allClaims.claim: A recent (May 2026) practitioner source names the radius-dilation mechanism explicitly with the industry term 'ranking radius' and ties it to website content, backlinks, reviews, and GBP — corroborating that organic authority lets a business 'compete farther from their physical address.' Directional, not a measured miles-per-link figure.
allClaims.stat: 'High-quality content, backlinks, strong reviews, and a properly optimized Google Business Profile all help businesses compete farther from their physical address'; authority can 'gradually increase what many SEO professionals call ranking radius.'
allClaims.snippet: A well-optimized site supported by a strong local strategy can gradually increase what many SEO professionals call 'ranking radius.' ... Businesses with strong reputations often outrank closer competitors because Google sees them as more authoritative and trustworthy.

allClaims.claim: Sterling Sky's independent 'near me' study sample is large and recent, lending weight to its pack-ranking conclusions — useful for sourcing the proximity-still-gates counterweight at scale.
allClaims.stat: Analyzed 8,186 businesses across 200 cities (100 large [pop 226k-8.8M], 50 mid-sized [91k-99k], 50 small [47k-50k]), 2025.
allClaims.snippet: We Analyzed 8,186 Businesses in 200 Cities. Here's What Actually Gets You Ranking for 'Near Me' in 2025.

allClaims.claim: Radius dilation is competition-density dependent, not authority-only: Google shows a business across a SIGNIFICANTLY WIDER radius in low-competition areas and a tight radius in dense markets. This is load-bearing for King Maker honesty — the radius-widening play works best in less-saturated NC/Triangle suburbs, and the office's own pack radius dilates where competition is thin, not everywhere equally.
allClaims.stat: 'Near me' results typically cluster under ~3 miles in urban areas, up to ~15 miles in rural regions; low-competition areas yield a 'significantly wider radius.'
allClaims.snippet: If your business is located in an area with a low competitive level, then Google is likely to show you as a result across a significantly wider radius than if your practice is just one of many in a single town.

pillars.title: Link-absorption capacity (deep site vs thin site)
pillars.section:
## T3 — Link-Absorption Capacity: Deep Site vs Thin Site

**Bottom line.** A deep, well-architected site is an *absorptive structure*. It converts link investment into rankings more safely and more efficiently than a thin site — not because more pages rank by themselves, but because more genuine pages give link equity more places to land and anchor text more ways to vary. King Maker ships that structure once. The structure is the one-time asset; it does not earn the links by itself.

**Internal linking causally moves organic traffic — this is measured, not theory.** A controlled SEO split-test on a large site found that increasing internal linking produced a **25% uplift in organic traffic** across category pages, with both the linked-to and the linked-from page groups gaining 20%+ ([searchpilot.com](https://www.searchpilot.com/resources/case-studies/seo-split-test-lessons-increasing-internal-linking)). Separate split-tests show the same mechanism at smaller magnitudes: adding related-article links lifted donor pages ~16% (95% probability of a positive effect) ([searchpilot.com](https://www.searchpilot.com/resources/case-studies/seo-split-test-lessons-increasing-related-article-links)), expanding a homepage footer's link set lifted the linked-to pages ~5% ([searchpilot.com](https://www.searchpilot.com/resources/blog/3-seo-split-tests-you-should-try)), and — directly relevant to a multi-city roofing spine — linking to **nearby location pages lifted those location pages ~7%** ([searchpilot.com](https://www.searchpilot.com/resources/case-studies/seo-split-test-lessons-nearby-location-links)). These are split-tests, so they are causal. A 5-page site has almost no internal links to add; a 40-50+ URL silo can build this mesh across every service-and-city target.

**Why depth = capacity, mechanically.** Internal links distribute PageRank as a fraction per outbound link, decaying with each click-hop from an authority page ([visively.com](https://visively.com/kb/content/internal-linking-architecture)). Google's own spokesperson confirms internal linking is how a site signals which pages matter — bury a page and Google reads it as unimportant ([searchenginejournal.com](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-john-mueller-rank-important-pages/345192/)). A deep, siloed site can route equity down topical paths to many rankable targets and surface them shallowly. A thin site has nowhere to route it.

**Why depth = safety under link investment.** Google names "links with optimized anchor text" and "excessive link exchanges" as link spam in its own spam policy ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)). Risk is assessed *relationally* — across the whole anchor-text distribution and link velocity, not link-by-link. A thin site funneling links into a homepage on the money keyword is forced into anchor concentration; practitioner consensus puts safe exact-match commercial anchors at **under ~5-10% of the profile** ([basesearchmarketing.com](https://www.basesearchmarketing.com/blog/right-ratio-of-exact-match-anchor-text-in-link-building/)), and a sudden same-anchor spike is itself a flagged pattern ([searchengineland.com](https://searchengineland.com/guide/link-velocity)). A deep spine spreads the same link budget across many topical URLs with varied, natural anchors — landing as diversity instead of stuffing.

**What the downside actually is — floor, not catastrophe.** Google's enforcement default against unnatural links is *devaluation*: SpamBrain neutralizes the credit so the gain disappears, which is distinct from a manual penalty (Dec 2022 link spam update; the "neutralize the impact of unnatural links" framing is corroborated via SE Roundtable / Authority Builders coverage of the update — [developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/12/december-22-link-spam-update)). So the honest claim is: a thin site **wastes** an aggressive link budget (devalued) and carries elevated demotion *tail*-risk — not a guaranteed competitor penalty. Sell the efficiency and safety, not a collapse.

**Floor vs ceiling.** *Floor (promise):* a deep silo of genuine pages routes link equity to many rankable targets and keeps exact-match anchors diluted across the profile — safer and more efficient absorption of any given link budget. *Ceiling (project, directional):* internal-mesh changes of this kind have produced 5-25% organic uplifts in controlled tests; vertical sources put on-page service-and-location clarity at ~36% of local *organic* weight (directional, agency-sourced, lineage to Whitespark/Moz survey work — not Google-confirmed).

**Hard boundary (load-bearing honesty).** Depth only converts to absorption capacity if every page is genuinely unique and valuable — Google explicitly rejects "more pages = more ranking" ([searchenginejournal.com](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-john-mueller-rank-important-pages/345192/)). A doorway-padded deep site fails the same way a thin site does. The asset is *depth of genuine pages + silo architecture*, gated by the real-job→page / delete-the-city-name test.

**What NOT to oversell:** never "thin sites get penalized" (devaluation is the base case); never a dollar figure or page count as a rank guarantee; never claim the site is the dominant local lever (GBP/reviews outweigh it for the pack); and the one-time deliverable is the absorptive *structure*, not the off-page links themselves.

loadBearing.claim: Increasing internal linking causally lifts organic traffic — a controlled SEO split-test produced a 25% organic uplift across category pages, with both linked-to and linked-from page groups gaining 20%+.
loadBearing.stat: 25% organic uplift; both page groups 20%+
loadBearing.snippet: Not only was this test positive, but it was one of our most positive tests to date resulting in a 25% uplift to organic traffic across level two and level three category pages... Both page groups alone also had estimated uplifts in the 20%+ range, which means the increased internal linking also benefited the pages being linked from.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the causal spine of the entire pillar: it proves internal linking MOVES organic traffic (split-test, not correlation). Everything else about deep-site equity routing rests on this being real. It is the headline slide/reel number.

loadBearing.claim: Internal links to nearby location pages causally lift the linked-to location pages — directly relevant to a multi-city roofing silo cascade.
loadBearing.stat: 7% organic uplift on location pages
loadBearing.snippet: This corresponded to a 7% uplift in organic traffic.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: It is the vertical-specific causal proof: the deep MULTI-LOCATION spine is exactly what a roofing site needs, and this test shows location-to-location internal links lift the location pages. A thin site cannot build this mesh. Connects the abstract mechanism to the actual product.

loadBearing.claim: Google's own spam policy names 'links with optimized anchor text' and 'excessive link exchanges' as link spam — the primary-source basis for thin-site over-optimization risk.
loadBearing.stat: Google-named violations: optimized anchor text, excessive link exchanges
loadBearing.snippet: Link spam is the practice of creating links to or from a site primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings... links with optimized anchor text... Excessive link exchanges ('Link to me and I'll link to you')...
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: It is the primary (Google first-party) anchor for the safety half of the offer: aggressive exact-match anchoring is named spam by Google itself, not vendor opinion. Lets us claim 'a thin site is forced toward a pattern Google calls spam' defensibly.

loadBearing.claim: Google's enforcement default against unnatural links is devaluation (credit neutralized via SpamBrain), not a guaranteed penalty — so thin-site over-optimization most often costs the GAIN, with demotion as the tail risk.
loadBearing.stat: links neutralized / credit lost, not penalized (Dec 2022 link spam update)
loadBearing.snippet: Google's December 2022 link spam update used SpamBrain to neutralize the impact of unnatural links; the 'turns them off rather than penalizes' framing is corroborated via SE Roundtable / Authority Builders coverage of the update.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the cardinal anti-oversell guardrail. It stops the offer from promising 'thin sites get penalized' (false-confidence/FTC exposure) and reframes the sell as efficiency+safety. NOTE: the primary blog URL returned only an archive shell on fetch this pass; the 'neutralize' wording is corroborated via secondary coverage — verify the verbatim quote against the live post before any slide/reel use.

loadBearing.claim: Google's spokesperson confirms internal linking signals which pages matter; burying a page signals low importance — and separately rejects 'more pages = more ranking,' so depth only counts if pages are genuinely unique/valuable.
loadBearing.stat: easily-findable pages treated as important; hidden pages treated as unimportant (J. Mueller, Google)
loadBearing.snippet: if there's something that you really really care about, you think is really important and you hide it away like that, then probably we'll think it's not as important. So if you think it's important then make sure it's really easily findable within your website.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Dual-purpose load-bearing: it is the Google-sourced basis for the deep-site equity-routing mechanism AND the honesty boundary (depth must be genuine pages, not a doorway pad). It ties the pillar to the anti-doorway gate, which is what keeps the whole offer defensible.

whatNotToOversell: Never claim 'thin sites get penalized' — Google's default enforcement against unnatural links is DEVALUATION (credit neutralized via SpamBrain), not a manual penalty. Frame it as wasted budget + elevated tail risk, never a guaranteed competitor collapse.

Never state 'more pages = more rank.' Google explicitly rejects page count as a ranking mechanism; depth only converts to link-absorption capacity if every page is genuinely unique/valuable (real-job->page, delete-the-city-name gate). A doorway-padded deep site fails like a thin one.

Never present a dollar figure ($5-10k/mo absorption) as a rank guarantee. It is a MECHANISM claim — a 40-50+ URL spine gives ~10x the anchor-distribution headroom of a 5-page site, so a larger budget lands as natural diversity instead of homepage anchor stuffing. Mechanism, not outcome.

Never imply the SearchPilot causal evidence covers off-page link acquisition. The clean causal proof is for INTERNAL links (fully site-controlled). External link earning — where velocity/over-optimization risk actually lives — is ongoing off-page work, out of scope. The one-time deliverable is the absorptive structure, not the earned links.

Never claim the site is the dominant LOCAL lever. Home-services sources consistently put GBP (~32% of Map Pack) and reviews (~20%) above on-page for the pack; the ~36% on-page figure is for local ORGANIC weight, is agency-sourced/directional, and traces to Whitespark/Moz survey lineage — not Google-confirmed. The pack stays a proximity-capped byproduct.
Treat exact-match anchor thresholds (<5-10% safe; >30% flag) and the per-hop equity math as practitioner-modeled/directional, not Google-confirmed numbers. Label them directional on any slide.

Deep alone is NOT automatically better — more links also dilute per-link equity. The claim is 'deep AND well-architected silo (topical silos, body-text contextual links, controlled counts),' which is the actual deliverable. A sprawling unstructured page-dump leaks equity too.
gaps: No primary Google source states an explicit 'safe anchor ratio' or 'link velocity threshold' — all specific percentages (5-10% exact-match, >30% flag, velocity spikes) are practitioner-modeled/directional. Treat as directional, never as a Google-confirmed line.

The '$5-10k/mo absorption' figure has no external source — it is an internal mechanism inference from anchor-distribution headroom (more URLs = more anchor variety). Frame as modeled, FLOOR = 'a deep site distributes link investment more safely than a thin one,' not a specific dollar capacity.

SearchPilot causal tests are on large enterprise/ecommerce/publisher sites, not small contractor/roofing sites — the direction transfers (internal links move organic) but the exact magnitudes (7-25%) are not measured in the roofing vertical.

Could not retrieve the Google Dec-2022 blog body verbatim via WebFetch (JS-rendered archive shell); the 'nullify the impact of unnatural links' wording is corroborated across multiple secondary sources and matches Google's known phrasing, but the exact one-line quote was confirmed via secondary coverage, not a direct read of the primary page text.

No clean study isolating 'thin site over-optimizes -> filtered' as a causal experiment — that mechanism is an inference chaining Google's spam policy + reasonable-surfer + anchor-distribution math; directionally sound but not a single measured result.

No PRIMARY, independent (Whitespark/BrightLocal/Moz/Sterling Sky) study directly measuring that a deep contractor/roofing site out-absorbs links vs a thin one — the deep-site link-absorption mechanism remains a SYNTHESIS of (causal internal-linking split-tests from round 1) + (anchor-concentration math) + (Mueller importance-signaling), not one head-to-head study. Label this as modeled/directional in the pitch.
No roofing- or NC/Triangle-specific quantified figure surfaced; best vertical data is generic home-services agency synthesis (hookagency/localmighty), which is vendor-incentive, not primary.

The 36% on-page local-ranking-weight figure could not be traced to its primary survey (Whitespark/Moz Local Search Ranking Factors) within this pass — verify the exact percentage against the primary survey before putting a hard number in a reel; treat as directional until then.

No quantified study isolating the harm to a THIN site specifically from a concentrated link push (the counterfactual). The risk is inferred from anchor-distribution norms + velocity red-flag patterns, not measured on a real thin-vs-deep pair. Promise the floor (safer routing), project the ceiling (uplift), never a guaranteed thin-site penalty.

Firecrawl was out of credits (HTTP 402) this entire pass; all evidence came via WebSearch + WebFetch. A future pass with credits could chase the primary local-ranking-factors survey PDF and any SearchPilot location-link aggregate directly.

counter.point: Google's enforcement default is DEVALUATION not penalty — SpamBrain 'turns off' the credit. So the thin-site 'spam-filter/velocity risk' is real but usually means lost gains, not a ranking collapse. Manual actions and Penguin-style demotions exist but are the tail, not the base case.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT promise 'thin sites get penalized.' Frame it as: a deep site SAFELY absorbs aggressive link investment because equity distributes across many URLs and anchors; a thin site WASTES the same budget (devalued) and carries elevated demotion tail-risk. Sell the efficiency + safety, not a guaranteed competitor penalty.

counter.point: The clean causal evidence (SearchPilot) is for INTERNAL links, which a site fully controls. External/inbound link acquisition — where over-optimization velocity risk actually lives — is largely an ONGOING off-page activity, out of pillar scope. The one-time shippable deliverable is the internal-mesh architecture + the rankable-URL inventory that makes future link investment safe.
counter.soWhat: Position T3 honestly as: King Maker ships the ABSORPTIVE STRUCTURE (deep silo + internal equity cascade + many anchor-able URLs). That is the one-time asset. It does not itself guarantee the off-page links get earned.

counter.point: Link COUNT -> rank is correlation; many 'factors' (incl. exact anchor ratios and the $5-10k/mo absorption figure) are practitioner-modeled, not Google-confirmed. The $5-10k absorption is a MECHANISM claim (a deep site has the surface area to spend it across silos without anchor concentration), not a guaranteed-ranking claim.
counter.soWhat: Never state a dollar figure as a rank guarantee. State: a 40-50+ URL spine gives ~10x the anchor-distribution headroom of a 5-page site, so a larger monthly link budget lands as natural-looking diversity instead of homepage anchor stuffing.

counter.point: More internal links also DILUTE per-link equity (100 links = 1/100 each) — a deep site is not automatically better; it must be ARCHITECTED (siloed, body-text contextual links, reasonable counts). A sprawling unstructured site can leak equity as badly as a thin one concentrates it.
counter.soWhat: The claim is 'deep + well-architected silo,' not 'deep' alone. The deliverable's value is the architecture (topical silos, contextual linking, controlled counts), which is exactly what King Maker bakes in vs a generic page dump.

counter.point: Google's own spokesperson (J. Mueller) explicitly rejects 'more pages = more ranking' as a mechanism: 'there's more to online success than just adding more pages ... it's important that things which you add actually bring new & unique value to the web.' Page DEPTH only converts to link-absorption capacity if each page is genuinely unique/valuable.
counter.soWhat: This is the load-bearing honesty boundary for the pillar AND the anti-doorway gate: the deep site only wins if its pages are real (real-job->page, delete-the-city-name test). A thin OR a doorway-padded deep site both fail. Frame the offer as 'a deep site of GENUINE pages absorbs links safely' — never 'more pages = more rank.' Promise the floor (safer equity routing + lower anchor concentration), not a page-count guarantee.

counter.point: Home-services/local SEO sources consistently say the site is NOT the dominant local lever: GBP ~32% of Map Pack weight and reviews ~20% outrank on-page; and even pro-depth guides warn duplicate city pages without unique local proof points actively hurt.
counter.soWhat: Consistent with the project spine (pack is a proximity-capped byproduct; the win is ORGANIC). Use these as the honest demarcation: the deep site maximizes ORGANIC regional dominance and safe link absorption — it does not by itself win the pack, and a depth play executed as boilerplate city pages backfires. Keep the claim scoped to organic + link-equity routing.

counter.point: Link-velocity sources note 'it's not the spike itself that's the problem; it's the quality and source of the links' — a sudden rise from viral content or PR can be perfectly natural and beneficial.
counter.soWhat: Tempers the spam-velocity argument: velocity alone is not disqualifying. The defensible claim is narrower — a CONCENTRATED, same-anchor, unrelated-source push at a thin site fits the manipulation pattern; the deep site's advantage is that it can absorb varied-anchor, topically-relevant links at natural velocity. Don't overclaim that any fast linking is penalized.

allClaims.claim: Internal-linking changes causally move organic traffic: a controlled SEO split-test on a large site found increased internal linking produced a 25% uplift in organic traffic across category pages, with both linked-to AND linked-from pages gaining 20%+. This is causal (split-test), not correlational, and is the core mechanism by which a deep site converts link equity into rankings.
allClaims.stat: 25% organic uplift; both page groups 20%+
allClaims.snippet: Not only was this test positive, but it was one of our most positive tests to date resulting in a 25% uplift to organic traffic across level two and level three category pages... Both page groups alone also had estimated uplifts in the 20%+ range, which means the increased internal linking also benefited the pages being linked from.

allClaims.claim: A deep site's MORE internal link sources is itself a ranking lever: a SearchPilot split-test adding related-article links showed a 95% probability of positive impact and a 16% uplift on the DONOR (linking-from) pages, with the combined groups showing a 90% probability of positive outcome and 11% uplift. More content = more pages that can both emit and absorb internal equity. (Honesty: recipient pages showed no detectable effect here, likely sample size.)
allClaims.stat: 16% uplift on donor pages (95% prob); 11% combined (90% prob)
allClaims.snippet: 95% chance of a positive impact on organic traffic, reporting a 16% uplift [donor pages]... No detectable impact on organic traffic [recipient pages]... 90% chance this change would result in a positive outcome with an 11% uplift [combined].

allClaims.claim: Internal links to NEARBY LOCATION pages causally lift organic traffic — directly relevant to a multi-city roofing site's silo cascade. A SearchPilot split-test adding links to nearby location pages produced a 7% organic uplift on the linked-to location pages. A deep multi-location spine has the URLs to build this mesh; a 5-page site does not.
allClaims.stat: 7% organic uplift on location pages
allClaims.snippet: This corresponded to a 7% uplift in organic traffic.

allClaims.claim: Google's own spam policy defines link spam as links created 'primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings' and explicitly names 'links with optimized anchor text' and 'excessive link exchanges' as violations. This is the PRIMARY-source basis for the over-optimization risk: aggressive exact-match anchoring is named spam by Google itself, not vendor opinion.
allClaims.stat: Google-named violations: optimized anchor text, excessive link exchanges
allClaims.snippet: Link spam is the practice of creating links to or from a site primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings... Advertorials or native advertising where payment is received for articles that include links that pass ranking credit, or links with optimized anchor text... Excessive link exchanges ('Link to me and I'll link to you') or partner pages exclusively for the sake of cross-linking.

allClaims.claim: Google's enforcement against unnatural links is primarily DEVALUATION, not penalty. The Dec 2022 link spam update used SpamBrain to 'nullify the impact of unnatural links' — ranking gains from spammy links are neutralized and the credit is lost, distinct from a manual penalty. This is the defensible framing: thin-site over-optimization most often costs the gain (devalued), with manual-action/Penguin demotion as the tail risk — NOT a guaranteed catastrophic penalty.
allClaims.stat: links neutralized/credit lost, not penalized (Dec 2022 update)
allClaims.snippet: Google reported it used SpamBrain to 'neutralize the impact of unnatural links'; widely reported: 'whatever effect they had on a website's rankings is now negated — this is different from penalizing... it only turns them off' (corroborated via SE Roundtable / Authority Builders coverage of the update).

allClaims.claim: Practitioner safe-anchor consensus: exact-match commercial anchors should stay under ~5-10% of the backlink profile; exceeding ~10% for a single phrase materially raises over-optimization risk. The bulk should be branded (40-60%), naked URLs (15-25%), generic/partial. A 5-page thin site funneling links to a homepage with the money keyword cannot hit this distribution — the limited URL set forces anchor concentration.
allClaims.stat: exact-match <5-10%; >10% per phrase = elevated risk
allClaims.snippet: keep exact match links down to less than 5-10%... [too many] can begin to look suspicious to Google's algorithm.

allClaims.claim: Internal links are a PageRank distribution system: link equity passes as a fraction per outbound link (a page with 10 links passes ~1/10 each; 100 links ~1/100), and equity decays with each click-hop from a high-authority source. A deep, siloed site routes equity down topical paths to many rankable targets; a thin site has nowhere to route it. Google has confirmed internal PageRank remains in the ranking system despite retiring the public toolbar metric.
allClaims.stat: ~1/N equity per outbound link; decays per hop
allClaims.snippet: a page with 10 internal links distributes roughly 1/10th of its equity per link, while a page with 100 internal links distributes 1/100th... Every page linked directly from the homepage receives more equity than pages accessible only through deeper navigation layers.

allClaims.claim: Google's 'reasonable surfer' model weights links by placement and click-probability: body-text contextual links carry the most weight, footer/sidebar links the least. This means a deep site's in-content topical silo links (high-weight) are both safer and more effective than a thin site's repeated nav/footer keyword links — the equity routing of a deep site is qualitatively superior, not just quantitatively larger.
allClaims.stat: body-text links weighted highest; footer/sidebar lowest
allClaims.snippet: Google's 'reasonable surfer' patent describes how link value varies based on placement, user behaviour, and click probability. The Reasonable Surfer model weights body-text links highest, footer and sidebar links lowest.

allClaims.claim: Unnatural-link risk is assessed RELATIONALLY across the whole profile — SpamBrain analyzes anchor-text distribution across all links to a target, the topical relevance of linking content, and historical velocity, not individual links in isolation. Practitioner disavow thresholds cited: exact-match commercial anchors >30% of profile, or >15-20% of referring domains showing network affiliation. A concentrated thin-site profile is exactly the relational pattern these systems flag.
allClaims.stat: risk flags: >30% exact-match anchors; >15-20% affiliated domains
allClaims.snippet: SpamBrain... analyses the relational patterns between the linking domain, the linked domain, the topic cluster of the linking content, the anchor text distribution across all links pointing to the target, and the historical behaviour of every domain in the network... exact-match commercial anchors account for more than 30% of the anchor profile.

allClaims.claim: Expanding internal link sources from a high-authority page (homepage footer) causally lifts the linked-to pages: a SearchPilot split-test found pages receiving links from an expanded homepage footer saw a ~5% organic uplift vs control. Confirms the 'more link targets fed by authority pages = measurable lift' mechanism that a deep site can exploit at scale and a thin site cannot.
allClaims.stat: ~5% organic uplift on footer-linked pages
allClaims.snippet: Pages that received links from an expanded homepage footer saw a 5% uplift in organic traffic compared to a control group.

allClaims.claim: Google's own spokesperson confirms internal linking is how a site signals which pages matter — and that burying a page deep signals LOW importance to Google. This is the primary-source basis for the deep-site mechanism: a deep site can route internal equity to many priority targets and surface them shallowly, while equally confirming that a page must be genuinely linked/surfaced (not just exist) to be treated as important.
allClaims.stat: Pages linked directly/easily from the homepage are treated as important; pages hidden behind archive layers signal low importance — 'if you think it's important then make sure it's really easily findable within your website' (J. Mueller, Google)
allClaims.snippet: On the other hand, if there's something that you really really care about, you think is really important and you hide it away like that, then probably we'll think it's not as important. So if you think it's important then make sure it's really easily findable within your website.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (Google spokesperson statement on how internal linking signals page importance)

allClaims.claim: Spam-velocity logic (the thin-site over-optimization risk, completing round 1's anchor-concentration thread): an abnormal SPIKE in backlinks — especially repeated identical anchor text and links from unrelated/low-quality sources — is itself a manipulation red flag independent of anchor ratios. A reputable trade source gives the concrete pattern Google's systems flag, and a normal small-site velocity baseline. A thin site that suddenly absorbs a concentrated, same-anchor link push fits the flagged pattern; a deep site can spread links across many topical targets with varied anchors and natural velocity.
allClaims.stat: 'a website goes from 10 backlinks to 400 in two days, without any newsworthy content or PR campaign. That's a big red flag'; 'if all 50 backlinks ... use the anchor text "best pet foods," it looks scripted'; normal small site ~5-15 backlinks/month
allClaims.snippet: a website goes from 10 backlinks to 400 in two days, without any newsworthy content or PR campaign. That's a big red flag ... if all 50 backlinks to your article about 'best foods for pets' use the anchor text 'best pet foods,' it looks scripted ... A small pet supply blog like Doobie & Co. might earn five to 15 backlinks per month
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (practitioner/trade synthesis of Google velocity/anchor red flags)

allClaims.claim: Vertical-specific support for the deep-site thesis in home-services/contractor local SEO: on-page service+location clarity (which only a deep multi-page spine can express) carries roughly 36% of local organic ranking weight — higher than links — and unique service-area pages outperform generic content. This is the roofing/home-services-adjacent figure round 1 lacked. NOTE vendor-incentive: this is an agency blog, not a primary independent study; the 36% local-pack factor lineage traces to Whitespark/Moz local survey work, treat the exact number as directional.
allClaims.stat: on-page (service + location clarity) ~36% of local organic ranking weight, 'higher than links'; GBP ~32% of Map Pack weight, reviews ~20%
allClaims.snippet: on-page elements tied to service and location clarity carry the most weight in local organic results, roughly 36%. That is higher than links.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (agency synthesis of local-ranking-factor survey data; exact % unverified to primary survey)

allClaims.claim: Practitioner safe-anchor distribution corroborator (independent of round 1's basesearchmarketing source): natural profiles run ~30-50% branded and only ~1-5% exact-match commercial anchors, with >10% exact-match for one phrase as the danger zone. A 5-page thin site funneling one-time links at a homepage money keyword is structurally forced toward anchor concentration it cannot dilute across URLs; a deep site has the page inventory to keep exact-match low while still absorbing the equity.
allClaims.stat: natural profile ~30-50% branded, ~1-5% exact-match; >10% exact-match for a single phrase = danger zone
allClaims.snippet: A natural link profile often includes 30–50% branded anchors and just 1–5% exact match anchors ... If your exact match ratio is above 10%, you are in the danger zone.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (practitioner consensus, vendor blog — corroborates round-1 basesearchmarketing thresholds)

pillars.title: Map-vs-organic ranking-factor weighting
pillars.section:
## T4 — Map-vs-Organic Ranking-Factor Weighting

**Bottom line:** Local rank splits into two different games with two different scoreboards. In **Local Organic**, on-page content plus links carry the majority of modeled ranking weight — about 57% combined (on-page 33%, links 24%), while the Google Business Profile is only ~7% ([BrightLocal 2026](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-local-algorithm-and-ranking-factors/), [AdviceLocal summary of Whitespark 2026](https://www.advicelocal.com/blog/2026-local-search-ranking-factors-maps-organic-ai/)). In the **Local Pack (Maps)**, the scoreboard flips: GBP plus reviews carry ~52% (GBP 32%, reviews 20%), on-page drops to 15%, links to 8% ([AdviceLocal](https://www.advicelocal.com/blog/2026-local-search-ranking-factors-maps-organic-ai/), corroborated by [Kyle Eggleston](https://www.kyleeggleston.com/blog/2026-local-seo-ranking-factors/)). A deep site plus one-time shippable off-page directly moves the levers that dominate organic. It does not move the levers that dominate the pack — those are gated by proximity, profile, and review velocity. So the engine of regional dominance is organic; the pack is a byproduct we capture inside the office radius but never center.

**The pack is proximity-capped — that is the structural ceiling, not an opinion.** A measured XGBoost study on ~3,200 businesses (R² ~92-93%) found proximity accounts for 55.2% of GBP visibility across positions 1-21, dropping to 36.2% in the top 10 where reviews and content relevance take over ([Search Atlas study, via secondary write-up](https://infinityrank.medium.com/local-seo-just-got-a-map-update-new-study-quantifies-what-actually-drives-google-business-profile-be4338ea1e52)). Proximity weight also varies sharply by vertical (law 69.4%, food ~30%), so any flat "proximity = X%" claim is wrong; cite the range, not a point. Sterling Sky's measured study (8,186 businesses, 200 cities) independently confirms that hiding your address correlates negatively with pack rank, and that this-month review velocity beats total review count ([Sterling Sky](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/what-gets-you-ranking-for-near-me-2025/)). Translation: no amount of site depth overcomes a closer competitor's geography in the pack. That is why we do not sell the pack as a site-driven win.

**On-page still helps even on the pack, which is why the deep site compounds.** Sterling Sky measured that landing pages with "more meaningful words" (substance, not volume) correlate with better pack rank ([Sterling Sky](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/what-gets-you-ranking-for-near-me-2025/)). So the deep site lifts the proximity-capped pack at the margin and wins organic outright — it works on both surfaces, harder on the one that scales.

**Click-reality check — promise the floor, not a fantasy.** In 2025, ~44% of local-search clicks went to the pack vs ~29% organic, ~19% paid ([Monday Digital](https://mondaydigital.com/blog/google-local-pack-traffic-statistics/)). The pack wins the plurality head-to-head — we do not pretend otherwise. The case for organic is scale and control: the pack is capped to one office radius and flat across the top 3 (CTR #1 17.8% / #2 15.4% / #3 15.1% — only ~3 points spread; [Monday Digital](https://mondaydigital.com/blog/google-local-pack-traffic-statistics/)), while organic scales region-wide. Zero-click is real and rising (~68% of U.S. searches end without a click, [Search Engine Land](https://searchengineland.com/google-zero-click-searches-2026-study-479717)) — but it de-centers the pack too, and Whitespark's third 2026 column shows AI-search visibility is won by the on-page + citations + links bundle (on-page 24%, GBP only 12%; [AdviceLocal](https://www.advicelocal.com/blog/2026-local-search-ranking-factors-maps-organic-ai/)). As clicks erode, durable visibility shifts further toward the deep site, not away from it.

**What NOT to oversell:** these splits are a modeled expert-opinion survey (47 experts, 187 factors; [Sam Bretzmann summary](https://sambretzmann.com/2026-local-seo-ranking-factors-overview/)), not Google-published weights — cite the direction (which levers dominate which surface), never the decimal as certified. Do not claim the pack is "60-90%" of clicks (it is ~44%). Do not promise pack top-3 (proximity-gated). Do not promise raw organic click-volume growth in a zero-click world — promise organic visibility/dominance across the region. Never PBNs or link schemes. Ongoing client-managed off-page is out of scope.

loadBearing.claim: In Local Organic, on-page content plus links carry the majority of modeled ranking weight (~57% combined), while the Google Business Profile is only ~7% — the deep site plus one-time shippable off-page directly controls the levers that win organic.
loadBearing.stat: Organic: on-page 33% + links 24% = ~57%; GBP only 7%
loadBearing.snippet: Local Organic: On-page 33%, Links 24%, Behavioral 10%, Personalization 8%, Google Business Profile 7%, Citations 7%. Most important factor for local organic: 'Dedicated page for each service.'
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the entire thesis of the organic-dominance offer — it is the headline number on the slide and the justification for selling a deep site over GBP optimization. If it falls, the offer's foundation falls.
loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: modeled (expert-opinion survey; BrightLocal restates the same Whitespark-lineage 47-expert survey, corroborates rather than re-measures)

loadBearing.claim: In the Local Pack (Maps), GBP plus reviews carry ~52% of modeled weight while on-page is only 15% and links only 8% — the pack rewards the GBP/proximity/review bundle, not site depth.
loadBearing.stat: Pack: GBP 32% + reviews 20% = ~52%; on-page 15%, links 8%

whatNotToOversell: The pack/organic percentage splits are a MODELED expert-opinion survey (47 experts, 187 factors), not Google-published weights — cite the direction (which levers dominate which surface), never the decimal as Google-certified. Treat every number as +/- several points.
Do NOT claim the pack is '60-90%' of local clicks — it is ~44% (Monday Digital, 2025). The pack wins the plurality head-to-head; the organic case is scale and control, not click-share victory.

Do NOT promise pack top-3 rankings — the pack is proximity-capped to the office radius (~5-7mi) and proximity is a hard geographic cap (55.2% of visibility pos 1-21, varying law 69.4% to food ~30%). No site depth overcomes a closer competitor.

Never claim a flat 'proximity = 55%' across the board — it varies sharply by vertical and by ranking band (36.2% in top 10). The 55.2% figure is positions 1-21, all-sector average, from a secondary write-up that must be corroborated against the primary Search Atlas source before reel use.

Do NOT promise raw organic CLICK-VOLUME growth — ~68% of U.S. searches are now zero-click. Promise organic VISIBILITY/dominance across the region (which the AI-search shift reinforces), not click counts.

The primary whitespark.ca report is JS-rendered and was not directly machine-readable; the figures rest on agency summaries (AdviceLocal, Kyle Eggleston, BrightLocal agree). A verifier should confirm against the rendered Whitespark report before FTC-exposed reel copy ships.
Explicitly EXCLUDE PBNs, link schemes, and any gray-hat off-page. Ongoing client-managed off-page is out of scope — do not pivot to it or caveat with it. Only one-time shippable off-page is in scope.

No NC / Triangle / Raleigh-Charlotte geo-specific ranking-factor data found. Regional proximity-radius behavior is inferred from national studies.

counter.point: The entire pack/organic split is an EXPERT-OPINION SURVEY (47 people scoring factors), not measured Google data. A skeptic can dismiss any single percentage as crowd-sourced opinion with no error bars published. Treat numbers as directional ranks (+/- several points), never as precise weights — promise the pattern (on-page+links dominate organic), not the decimal.
counter.soWhat: Frame in pitches as 'industry's largest expert consensus' and the DIRECTION (which levers dominate which surface), never as a Google-certified weight. The Sterling Sky measured study is the harder backstop for the proximity/velocity/content claims.

counter.point: Secondhand summaries disagree at the margins: one search-engine summary reported pack as on-page 19 / reviews 16 / links 15 (closer to older/2023 editions or a category mislabel), versus the 15/20/8 confirmed by two detailed sources. The primary whitespark.ca page is JS-rendered and was not directly machine-readable here — the figures rest on agency summaries of it.

counter.point: Proximity is the confound the survey-category buckets hide: in the PACK, GBP-category + proximity + address are top individual factors, and proximity is a hard geographic cap no amount of on-page/links overcomes within a competitor's tighter radius. So 'on-page 15% of pack' overstates how much a site can move the pack for a far-away searcher.
counter.soWhat: Reinforces the spine: do NOT sell the pack as a site-driven win — sell ORGANIC regional dominance (where on-page+links = 57%) and treat the pack as the proximity-capped ~5-7mi byproduct. Never naively sum proximity into a category bucket.

counter.point: Click-share (pack 44% vs organic 29%) means the PACK still wins the most local clicks head-to-head. A skeptic says 'so why not center the pack?' The answer is scale + control: the pack is proximity-capped to one office radius and flat across positions, while organic scales region-wide and is the only surface a $5-10k/mo deep-site + off-page budget can compound.
counter.soWhat: Position organic as the regional-scale ENGINE and the pack as the local near-default it also captures — rank the prizes, sell the bigger. Do not claim pack is '60-90%' of clicks; it is ~44%.

counter.point: ZERO-CLICK is the skeptic's strongest weapon: SparkToro/Similarweb (primary clickstream) found 68.01% of U.S. Google searches ended without ANY click in Jan-Apr 2026, up from 60.45% in 2024 — and AI Overviews appear on 20%+ of searches, cutting organic CTR by ~60% when present. A skeptic argues 'organic clicks are evaporating, so the deep-site organic prize is shrinking.'
counter.soWhat: It cuts BOTH ways and does NOT collapse the thesis: (1) zero-click de-centers the PACK too, and SparkToro explicitly names 'local business queries' + 'high-intent transactional searches' as categories that STILL benefit from SEO; (2) Whitespark's third 2026 column shows AI-search visibility is won by the on-page+citations+links bundle (a deep site delivers), not GBP — so as click-share erodes, the durable-visibility argument shifts FURTHER toward the deep site. Honest framing: do not promise raw organic click volume growth; promise organic VISIBILITY/dominance across the region, which the AI-search shift reinforces.

counter.point: The widely-quoted 'proximity = ~55%' figure is being passed around as if it's the single dominant ranking factor across the board — and a naive reading would say 'location beats everything, so the site barely matters.'
counter.soWhat: Two corrections protect the pillar from over-claim AND strengthen it. (1) The 55.2% is MAP/GBP visibility across positions 1-21 and falls to 36.2% in the top-10 (Search Atlas) — it is NOT an organic figure and NOT a top-rank figure. (2) It is sector-specific (law 69.4% vs food 30%), so a flat 55% claim is indefensible. Net: proximity dominance is a PACK phenomenon that decays at the top and varies by trade — exactly why the proximity-capped pack is a byproduct, not the regional engine. Never cite '55%' as a universal or organic number.

counter.point: GBP-maximalist sources note that 8 of the top 10 Local-Pack signals come directly from the Google Business Profile, and that some businesses rank in the pack with thin or no real website — implying 'just optimize GBP, skip the deep site.'
counter.soWhat: True FOR THE PACK only, and the pack is proximity-capped to one verified address (Sterling Sky: service-area polygon has zero ranking impact). 'GBP wins the pack' is fully consistent with — not contrary to — the thesis: the pack cannot scale past ~5-7 miles regardless of GBP quality, so a business that wants REGIONAL dominance must win organic, where on-page+links = ~57% and GBP is only ~7%. pillars.title: Map-pack EARLY-STAGE reality + the honest infiltration math
pillars.section:
## T5 — Map-Pack Early-Stage Reality: The Honest Infiltration Math

**Bottom line: the map pack is a low, slow-maturing channel at launch — not a couple jobs a week, not ten retail jobs out of the gate.** A new profile is penalized twice on day one: it is closer-competitor-capped to a small proximity bubble, and it loses clicks to higher-review competitors even at equal or better rank. Both penalties decay only over months as reviews accumulate. This is why King Maker centers **organic regional dominance** and treats the pack as a proximity-capped byproduct we deliver but never headline.

**Penalty 1 — proximity caps the pack to a bubble, and it is the one lever the business cannot directly pull.** Distance to the searcher is the dominant factor Google uses to assemble the pack ([whitespark.ca](https://whitespark.ca/guides/how-to-rank-in-surrounding-cities-or-towns-every-local-seo-strategy-you-need-to-know/)). A business sitting just outside a searcher's perimeter may not be considered relevant at all ([whitespark.ca](https://whitespark.ca/guides/how-to-rank-in-surrounding-cities-or-towns-every-local-seo-strategy-you-need-to-know/)). On geo-grid tools this shows as the "Proximity Halo" — green (top-3) at the office, fading to red two miles out, because a closer competitor wins each distant grid point ([localdominator.co](https://localdominator.co/what-is-geogrid-rank-tracker/)). The honest metric is therefore Share of Local Voice — the percentage of grid points where you rank top-3 — not a single "we rank #1 in [town]" check measured from the office pin ([localfalcon.com](https://www.localfalcon.com/blog/how-local-falcon-measures-your-local-rankings-and-visibility-across-ai-platforms-and-google-maps)). A fresh profile that honestly wins its own address can still have a low SoLV across the town.

**Penalty 2 — review asymmetry skips clicks past a thin profile even when it ranks.** In a controlled first-click test, pack position did not cleanly determine clicks — #1 won 14%, #2 won 12%, #3 collapsed to 1% — and the most-cited reason participants gave for their click was reviews and business longevity ([ilawyermarketing.com](https://www.ilawyermarketing.com/click-test-study-lsa-local-pack-organic-google-serps/)). BrightLocal's click study independently confirms the #3 cliff: position 3 took only 2.3–2.9% of clicks versus ~16–17% for #1 ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/research/local-services-ads-click-study/)). Star rating moves clicks independent of position — a 5-star listing earns ~25% more pack clicks than a 3-star one ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/research/review-search-click-through-study/)). A new profile with no rating loses clicks even when it ranks.

**The maturation curve.** A new GBP matures over months, not instantly. The most defensible single early milestone is ~10 reviews: across three businesses, Sterling Sky observed a small but noticeable Maps ranking bump exactly at the 9→10 review crossing — but no further bump at 10→11 or 16→31, so review count is a threshold effect, not a linear lever ([sterlingsky.ca](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/number-of-reviews-impact-ranking/)). A visible (not hidden) address and recent review volume are independently correlated ranking factors in the largest dataset — 8,186 businesses across 200 cities ([sterlingsky.ca](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/what-gets-you-ranking-for-near-me-2025/)). Practitioner consensus puts measurable movement at ~3–6 months, 6–12 in competitive markets — directional, not a controlled study ([sterlingsky.ca](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/what-gets-you-ranking-for-near-me-2025/)).

**Why organic is the bigger surface.** BrightLocal found organic results out-click the pack: 50.8% organic vs 32.3% pack with no Local Services Ads present, 43.9% vs 28.8% with them ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/research/local-services-ads-click-study/)). Organic position 1 alone (25.5–27.4%) out-pulls the entire pack #1 slot ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/research/local-services-ads-click-study/)). Organic is not capped to one office pin, so it is the larger, more scalable reach surface — the strategic reason the offer centers it.

**The honest job-shape (MODELED, not promised).** Composing the measured inputs — #3 pack CTR of 2.3–2.9% ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/research/local-services-ads-click-study/)), the review-driven click-skip, and the months-long ~10-review maturation gate — the early pack yield is a low curve in the range of ~1–2 jobs per month, maturing slowly toward ~10/month only after roughly two years with matched reviews and an expanded grid. **These are illustrative ranges built on measured CTR and review inputs, not a fixed count we promise.** Promise the floor (the proximity bubble); project the ceiling (an expanded grid) — never sell the ceiling out of the gate.

**One caveat to expect.** The skeptic's strongest card is the "44% click the map pack vs 29% organic" stat waved across vendor blogs as current. It traces to Moz's 2015 Snack Pack study — ~11 years old, pre-modern-SERP, and methodologically non-comparable to the BrightLocal click studies above. Both can be true: the pack wins clicks *when it appears for the proximity-bubble searcher*; organic wins the larger distance-unconstrained surface. Don't rest the pillar on "organic always out-clicks the pack" as settled.

**What NOT to oversell:** the pack is low and slow early — never a couple jobs a week out of the gate, never a roofing-specific click-to-job math, never the pack ranking number as the headline win. No PBNs, link schemes, or gray-hat — excluded explicitly. Off-page review/citation work that is ongoing client-managed fulfillment is out of scope here.

loadBearing.claim: Map-pack click-through is steeply front-loaded and the #3 slot captures almost nothing — being in the 3-pack at #3 with a thin review profile yields near-zero traffic.
loadBearing.snippet: Local Pack Position 1: 16.1% (with LSAs) / 17.3% (without LSAs); Position 2: 10.4% / 12.0%; Position 3: 2.3% / 2.9%.

loadBearing.claim: Reviews/social proof skip clicks past a higher-positioned but weaker-review listing — position does not cleanly determine clicks; the most-cited click reason was reviews and longevity.

loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: measured (first-click survey, n=1,001, single SERP image for 'car accident lawyer' — directional for roofing)

loadBearing.claim: Proximity to the searcher is the dominant pack factor and the one a business cannot directly improve — a closer competitor wins at a given location, structurally capping a fresh profile's pack reach to a bubble around its office.
loadBearing.stat: Proximity = top/dominant pack factor; 'not much a business can do to target this pillar'
loadBearing.snippet: "if your business is located even a little outside that border, Google may not consider it a relevant result for searchers located inside the perimeter" ... distance is one of three core factors (relevance, prominence, distance).

loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: directional (authority guidance, consistent with Google's distance/relevance/prominence framework)

loadBearing.claim: Organic results out-click the local pack and organic #1 alone out-pulls the entire pack #1 slot — organic is the larger, distance-unconstrained reach surface.
loadBearing.stat: Organic 50.8% / Pack 32.3% (no LSAs); Organic 43.9% / Pack 28.8% (with LSAs); Organic #1 = 25.5-27.4%
loadBearing.snippet: When LSAs absent — Organic results: 50.8%, Local Pack: 32.3%. When LSAs present — Organic results: 43.9%, Local Pack: 28.8%. Organic Position 1: 27.4% / 25.5%.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The single most offer-defining claim — it justifies centering organic. Directly contested by the stale 2015 '44% pack' stat, so it must be bulletproof and reconciled.

loadBearing.claim: A new GBP matures over months with ~10 reviews as the most defensible early ranking milestone — a measured bump at 9->10 reviews that did NOT repeat (10->11, 16->31), so count is a threshold not a linear lever.
loadBearing.stat: ranking bump at 9->10 reviews; none at 10->11 or 16->31
loadBearing.snippet: In all three cases, we saw a small but noticeable increase in their Maps ranking for the main keyword when the businesses went from 9 to 10 reviews ... [no bump] when a business went from 10 to 11 reviews.
