whatNotToOversell: The early pack channel is LOW and SLOW — never 'a couple jobs a week' or '10 retail jobs out of the gate'; the ~1-2 jobs/mo early and ~10/mo @ ~2yr figures are MODELED illustrative ranges, not promised counts.

Do NOT present pack CTR numbers as roofing-specific job math — both clean datasets are legal/SF service searches on mock SERPs; use them as SHAPE (front-loaded, review-modulated), directional for roofing only.

Do NOT assert a clean 'review count overrides position' percentage from the +25%/+39% BrightLocal study — it is 2016, mock-SERP, and varied STAR RATING, not review COUNT; frame as a star-rating/social-proof effect.

Do NOT treat 'organic always out-clicks the pack' as settled — the stale 2015 Moz '44% pack' stat is the skeptic's strongest card; reconcile (pack wins WHEN it appears for the bubble searcher; organic wins the larger surface), don't ignore it.
Do NOT cite the '55% proximity' point-figure — it never traced to a primary Whitespark table; assert proximity is the dominant factor qualitatively without the percent.

Label the 3-6 mo / 6-12 mo maturation timeline as practitioner-consensus/modeled, not a controlled study; lead with the measured 10-review threshold and address-visibility correlation as the hard anchors.
EXCLUDE explicitly: PBNs, link schemes, gray-hat. Ongoing client-managed off-page is out of scope; only one-time shippable off-page is in scope.
Promise the FLOOR (proximity bubble), project the CEILING (expanded grid via relevance/prominence) — never sell the expanded-grid ceiling out of the gate.
gaps: No roofing-specific (vs legal/generic) local-pack CTR-by-position or CTR-by-review-count dataset was found — all click studies are legal/multi-vertical mock-SERP. The roofing transfer is an assumption.

No single published study cleanly ISOLATES review COUNT (holding position + star rating constant) to quantify the '60-70% click-skip of a low-review #1 for a high-review #2/#3' — that magnitude remains modeled/reel-bound, supported only by qualitative participant reasoning (iLawyer) + star-rating proxies (BrightLocal).

No primary longitudinal study measuring a NEW GBP's month-by-month pack maturation curve (the 3-6/6-12 month figures are practitioner consensus). The 1-2 jobs/mo → ~10/mo @ ~2yr shape is a model, not a measured series.
The specific geo-grid fracture magnitudes (#5/#8/#14 across a town) are illustrative; no published roofing geo-grid case study with a fresh profile's actual SoLV-over-time was located.
The Whitespark '55% proximity' figure still lacks a primary-table citation — left excluded rather than asserted.

The honest job-shape numbers (~1-2 pack-sourced jobs/month early, maturing toward ~10/mo at ~2yr) remain MODELED — no single independent source ties geo-grid SoLV growth to dated lead/job counts on a maturation timeline. The WebFX action benchmarks (~10 calls/mo average) bound it directionally but are vendor-blended, not roofing-specific or new-profile-specific. Build the ramp as an explicit model (call-rate x pack-impression share x SoLV-growth-curve), label every node modeled, and promise the FLOOR.

No NC/Triangle or roofing-vertical-specific geo-grid dataset surfaced — all proximity/SoLV evidence is cross-vertical (plumber/HVAC/locksmith in the Sterling Sky set). The roofing-specific time-to-rank and pack-reach radius for the actual target metros is unverified; treat metro-specific claims as directional until a real Local Falcon scan of a target market exists.

The exact '3-6 months typical / 6-12 competitive' maturation window is practitioner-consensus (repeated across guides) but not anchored to a single controlled longitudinal study of NEW profiles; it is directional, not measured. Flag as such if used in the guarantee.

Did NOT find an independent eye-tracking/click study NEWER than the BrightLocal LSA study (round 1) that re-measures pack vs organic click share post-AI-Overviews — the 2025 AI Overview shift (Local Falcon: closer businesses appear 72.0% vs 68.5% within 4mi) may be reshaping pack click value in ways not yet captured. Worth a dedicated round on AI-Overview impact on local click distribution before reels lock.

counter.point: The two cleanest click-by-position datasets (iLawyer #3=1%, BrightLocal #3=2.3-2.9%) are for legal/SF service searches on mock SERPs, not roofing — and an earlier secondary summary cited a much flatter pack curve (#1 17.6% / #2 15.4% / #3 15.1%) that the PRIMARY page contradicts. Pack CTR numbers are directional for roofing, and the steep-vs-flat #3 question is unsettled.
counter.soWhat: Use pack CTR as SHAPE (front-loaded, review-modulated), not as a roofing-specific job math. Anchor only the qualitative review-skip + position cliff, with ranges.

counter.point: The BrightLocal review-CTR study (the +25%/+39% figures) is from 2016, uses mock SERPs, and varied STAR RATING — it did NOT isolate review COUNT. Several agency blogs wrongly attribute review-count claims (e.g. '240 vs 15 reviews') to it.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT assert a clean 'review count overrides position' percentage from this source. Frame as star-rating/social-proof effect; the count-override evidence is the qualitative iLawyer participant reasoning, not a number.

counter.point: Proximity can be partially overcome by relevance + prominence (Whitespark, Google's own framework), and review velocity is the fastest pack lever — so the pack is not permanently capped; it expands. A strict 'proximity-capped byproduct' framing under-sells what a sustained off-page engine can do to dilate the bubble.
counter.soWhat: Honest framing: pack reach is capped EARLY and expands SLOWLY with prominence; the floor is the proximity bubble, the ceiling is an expanded grid. Don't promise the ceiling out of the gate.

counter.point: The recurring '55% proximity' figure surfaced again in multiple search summaries attributed to Whitespark's 2026 survey, but it did not trace to a primary Whitespark table in prior verification — so it remains an unverified secondary citation.
counter.soWhat: Continue to EXCLUDE the 55% point-figure. Assert proximity is the single most important/dominant factor (well-supported qualitatively) without the specific percent.

counter.point: GBP maturation timelines (3-6 mo, 6-12 mo competitive) come from agency guidance, not a controlled longitudinal study; Google states no fixed timeline and rankings depend on market competitiveness. The ~10-review threshold (Sterling Sky/Joy Hawkins) is the most defensible single milestone.
counter.soWhat: Label the timeline as practitioner-consensus/modeled; lead with the measured 10-review trust threshold and the address-visibility correlation as the hard anchors.

counter.point: The most-cited 'pack dominates clicks' stat — '44% of local searchers click the Map Pack vs 29% organic / 19% paid / 8% more-results' — is the SKEPTIC'S STRONGEST card against this pillar's organic-out-clicks-pack thesis. It is reproduced as 'recent data' across dozens of vendor blogs but traces to Moz's 2015 'Snack Pack' study. It is ~11 years old, predates the modern local SERP, and uses a different methodology (survey/click-allocation) than the more recent BrightLocal eye/click studies round 1 cites. Treat it as stale and methodologically non-comparable, NOT as a current refutation — but expect prospects/competitors to wave it.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT let the pillar rest on 'organic always out-clicks the pack' as if settled — a credible-sounding 44% counter exists. Reconcile explicitly: the pack wins clicks WHEN it appears and for the proximity-bubble searcher; organic wins the larger, distance-unconstrained surface. Both can be true; the 2015 figure just isn't current evidence either way. This is exactly why the offer centers ORGANIC reach without claiming the pack is click-poor.

counter.point: Vendor case studies routinely show DRAMATIC, fast pack-driven lead jumps (e.g. a business invisible beyond 1.5mi at 4 organic calls/week expanding to 8-mi top-3 grid visibility and 47 inbound calls/week; a Georgia roofer '61 leads, 30% conversion in 30 days'). These are real-sounding and cut against the 'low, slow-maturing, 1-2 jobs/month' floor.
counter.soWhat: These are agency-marketing cases (selection bias, no control, unverifiable, post-optimization not launch-state) — they describe the CEILING after sustained work, which is consistent with this pillar's ceiling-projection, not its floor. Cite them ONLY as upside illustration, never as the expected early shape; promising 47 calls/week or 61 leads/30 days out of the gate is the FTC-exposed false-confidence trap this pillar exists to avoid.

counter.point: The review-count ranking lever is weaker and more bounded than a naive reading suggests: Sterling Sky's own controlled test found the ranking benefit of more reviews effectively PLATEAUS after ~10 (Law of Diminishing Returns), with no further bump from 16->31. So 'stack reviews to climb the pack' overstates the mechanism.
counter.soWhat: Strengthens honesty, not the optimism: the early ramp is gated on crossing ~10 AND on sustained recent VELOCITY (flow), not on amassing a large lifetime count. Frame the review engine as a recency cadence, not a count race — and don't imply hundreds of reviews keep buying rank.

allClaims.claim: In a controlled local-pack click test, position did NOT cleanly determine clicks: the #1 pack listing won 14%, #2 won 12%, and #3 collapsed to just 1% — and the most-cited reason participants gave for their click was reviews and business longevity, demonstrating the review-asymmetry click-skip where a stronger-review listing pulls clicks from a higher-positioned, weaker-review one.
allClaims.stat: Local pack first-click CTR: #1 = 14%, #2 = 12%, #3 = 1% (n=1,001); reviews/longevity = most-cited click reason
allClaims.snippet: "I typically skip directly past sponsored results, and I would be drawn toward search results that have a lot of reviews and have been around for a while." ... "They had very good reviews and were in business the longest" ... "ratings and reviews were the most common reasons participants gave for why they clicked where they did." Local pack: Listing #1 received 14%, #2 received 12%, and #3 only received 1% of clicks.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (first-click survey, n=1,001, single SERP image for 'car accident lawyer' — directional for roofing)

allClaims.claim: Pack CTR is heavily front-loaded and the #3 slot captures very little — BrightLocal's click study put local-pack position 3 at only 2.3-2.9% of clicks (vs ~16-17% for #1), so simply 'being in the 3-pack' at #3 with a thin review profile yields almost no traffic. This compounds the early under-delivery: a new profile that scrapes into #3 is near-invisible in click terms.
allClaims.snippet: Local Pack Position 1: 16.1% (with LSAs) / 17.3% (without LSAs); Position 2: 10.4% / 12.0%; Position 3: 2.3% / 2.9%.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (Mechanical Turk choice study, 5,500 testers, 5 SF service-area searches — directional)

allClaims.claim: The pack does NOT capture the lion's share of local clicks: BrightLocal found organic results out-click the local 3-pack. With Local Services Ads absent, organic took 50.8% of clicks vs 32.3% for the pack; with LSAs present, organic 43.9% vs pack 28.8%. Organic position 1 alone (25.5-27.4%) out-pulls the entire pack #1 slot — so organic dominance reaches more clicks than the proximity-capped pack.
allClaims.stat: Clicks by SERP feature — Organic 50.8% / Pack 32.3% (no LSAs); Organic 43.9% / Pack 28.8% (with LSAs); Organic #1 = 25.5-27.4%
allClaims.snippet: When LSAs absent — Organic results: 50.8%, Local Pack: 32.3%. When LSAs present — Organic results: 43.9%, Local Pack: 28.8%. Organic Position 1 CTR: 25.5% (LSAs present); 27.4% (absent).

allClaims.claim: Star rating measurably shifts pack clicks independent of position: going from a 3-star to a 5-star listing earns 25% more clicks from the Google local pack, and a 5-star vs 1-star listing earns 39% more. A fresh profile with no/low rating therefore loses clicks even when it ranks — the click-skip is a rating/social-proof effect, not just a position effect.
allClaims.stat: +25% clicks (3-star → 5-star); +39% clicks (1-star → 5-star); +28% (no rating → 5-star) in the local pack
allClaims.snippet: "Going from a 3-star rating to a 5-star rating gets a business 25% more clicks from Google Local Pack" ... "Having a 5-star rating earns a business 39% more clicks than having a 1-star rating."
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: modeled-ish (mock-SERP survey, 6,283 panelists, 2016; varied star rating, did NOT isolate review COUNT) — treat as star-rating effect, directional, dated

allClaims.claim: Proximity to the searcher is the dominant lever Google uses to assemble the local pack, and it is the one factor a business cannot directly improve — a closer competitor wins the pack at a given location regardless of effort. This is the structural reason a new profile's pack reach is geographically capped to a bubble around its office.
allClaims.stat: Proximity = top/dominant pack factor; 'not much a business can do to target this pillar'
allClaims.snippet: "if your business is located even a little outside that border, Google may not consider it a relevant result for searchers located inside the perimeter" ... distance is one of three core factors (relevance, prominence, distance); "while your address may be holding you back from competing on distance, it is frequently possible to overcome at least some of this disadvantage by building stronger relevance and prominence."
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (authority guidance, consistent with Google's own distance/relevance/prominence framework)

allClaims.claim: The 'Christmas tree' / proximity-halo fracture is real and observable on geo-grid tools: a business ranks green (top 3) at grid points near its office and fades to yellow/red farther out — e.g. #1 'across the street' but #10 two miles away — because a closer competitor wins each distant grid point. A single 'we rank #1 in [town]' check (measured from the office pin) hides this; the true Share of Local Voice (% of grid points in the top 3) is far lower for a fresh profile.
allClaims.stat: Grid pattern: green center → red edges ('Proximity Halo'); #1 across the street → ~#10 two miles away
allClaims.snippet: "A green center that fades to yellow and red shows that your rank is strong nearby but weaker farther away - this pattern is known as the 'Proximity Halo.'" ... "A client might rank #1 for a user standing across the street but drop to #10 for a user two miles away." Green = Top 3, Red = invisible (10+).
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured-pattern (geo-grid methodology); the specific #1/#10 figures are illustrative

allClaims.claim: Share of Local Voice (SoLV) is defined as the percentage of geo-grid points where the business ranks top-3 — so a fresh profile that wins only its immediate ~1-2 mile bubble has a LOW SoLV across a town even while honestly being 'number one' at its own address. The honest pack metric is SoLV/average-rank-across-the-grid, not a single-point rank.
allClaims.stat: SoLV = % of grid points in the Local 3-Pack; ARP = avg rank only where you appear; ATRP = avg across the whole grid
allClaims.snippet: "SoLV is the percentage of grid points where your business ranks in the top three positions." "ARP calculates your average ranking only across pins where your business appears." "ATRP includes the entire grid, assigning a default value to pins where your business does not appear." "Proximity is the single most important ranking factor in local search."

allClaims.claim: A new GBP does not rank in the pack instantly — it matures over months, with ~10 reviews acting as a concrete early trust threshold and a visible address (not hidden) materially helping. Independent practitioner consensus puts measurable pack movement at ~3-6 months, and competitive markets at 6-12 months. This is the time-shape behind 'low early, slow-maturing.'
allClaims.stat: 10 reviews = first trust/ranking milestone; visible address = 7th-ranked pack factor; ~3-6 mo (competitive 6-12 mo) to measurable movement
allClaims.snippet: Sterling Sky's 8,186-business / 200-city study found showing your business address, review ratings, recent review volume, and substantive landing-page content correlate with ranking for 'near me'; hiding the address correlated negatively (visible address = 7th most influential factor in their Local Search Ranking Factors report).
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (8,186-business correlation study) for the factors; the 3-6/6-12 month timeline is directional practitioner consensus, modeled

allClaims.claim: Review VELOCITY (recent review volume), not just lifetime count, is one of the correlated pack-ranking factors in the largest independent dataset — so the maturation curve is gated on a sustained review-acquisition engine, not a one-time burst. A fresh profile is behind on BOTH stock (count) and flow (velocity) at launch, which is why early pack contribution is structurally low.
allClaims.stat: Recent review volume + text-based reviews = independently-correlated 'near me' ranking factors (8,186 businesses)
allClaims.snippet: The study identifies six correlated factors including 'Recent review volume' and 'Text-based reviews' (alongside showing the address, review ratings, substantive landing-page content, and photos).

allClaims.claim: The honest early job-shape from the pack is a low, slow-maturing curve — NOT 'a couple jobs a week' and NOT '10 retail jobs out of the gate.' Mechanistically it is double-penalized at launch: (a) review-asymmetry click-skip (clicks flow to higher-review competitors even at equal/worse rank) and (b) proximity-grid fracture (top-3 only in a ~1-2 mile bubble). Both penalties decay only as reviews accumulate (months, past the ~10-review threshold) and as relevance/prominence expand the green bubble outward — a multi-quarter-to-multi-year ramp.
allClaims.stat: MODELED shape: ~1-2 jobs/MONTH early; maturing slowly toward ~10/MONTH only after ~2 years + matched reviews + expanded grid — claim the SHAPE + ranges, never a fixed count
allClaims.snippet: Composite of measured inputs: pack #3 CTR 2.3-2.9% and review-driven click-skip (iLawyer #3=1%) gate the early click yield; ~10-review trust threshold + months-long maturation gate the climb. Job counts are a downstream model, not a measured promise.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: modeled (job-count shape is a projection built on measured CTR + review/maturation inputs; the 1-2/mo and ~10/mo @ ~2yr anchors are illustrative ranges, NOT promises)

allClaims.claim: Because the pack is proximity-capped to a small radius while organic out-clicks the pack and is unconstrained by a single office pin, the organic channel is the larger and more scalable reach surface — the strategic reason King Maker centers ORGANIC regional dominance and treats the pack as a proximity-capped byproduct it delivers but never headlines.
allClaims.stat: Organic 43.9-50.8% of local clicks vs pack 28.8-32.3%; organic #1 (25.5-27.4%) > entire pack #1 slot
allClaims.snippet: Organic results: 50.8% (no LSAs) / 43.9% (LSAs) vs Local Pack 32.3% / 28.8%; Organic Position 1: 27.4% / 25.5%.

allClaims.claim: Independent case-study evidence pins the early-trust review threshold to a real, measured ranking bump: across three businesses, Sterling Sky observed a small-but-noticeable Maps ranking increase exactly when each crossed from 9 to 10 reviews — but the bump did NOT repeat from 10-to-11, and rankings did not climb further from 16 to 31 reviews (Law of Diminishing Returns). This sources the ~10-review early threshold AND honestly bounds it: count alone is not a linear ranking lever.
allClaims.stat: ranking bump at 9->10 reviews; none at 10->11 or 16->31
allClaims.snippet: In all three cases, we saw a small but noticeable increase in their Maps ranking for the main keyword when the businesses went from 9 to 10 reviews... we did not see the bump in local pack rankings we saw when a business went from 9 reviews to 10 reviews [at 10->11]... there really is not a ranking numbers increase when the listing went from 16 to 31 reviews.

allClaims.claim: The largest independent 'near me' ranking study (8,186 businesses across 200 cities — plumber/HVAC/locksmith/garage-door/lawn-care) found review VELOCITY beats lifetime count: 'the number of reviews you've gotten this month matters more than your total number of reviews,' and a client with 60+ monthly reviews who paused for just 18 days saw rankings 'fall off a cliff.' This is the measured engine behind the slow-maturing curve — a fresh profile is behind on FLOW, not just stock, and the ramp is gated on a sustained acquisition cadence.
allClaims.stat: 8,186 businesses / 200 cities; 18-day review pause = ranking collapse
allClaims.snippet: We Analyzed 8,186 Businesses in 200 Cities... The number of reviews you've gotten this month matters more than your total number of reviews... [a client with 60+ monthly reviews] stopped for 18 days [and] their rankings fell off a cliff.

allClaims.claim: Share of Local Voice is precisely defined by Local Falcon as 'the percentage of grid points where your business ranks in the top three positions,' and the tool separately reports Average Rank Position (only where you appear) vs Average Total Rank Position (whole grid, penalizing absence). This is the primary-source definition that makes the honest pack metric SoLV/ATRP across the grid — NOT a single 'we rank #1' check measured from the office pin, which structurally overstates a fresh profile's reach.
allClaims.stat: SoLV = % of grid points in top 3; ARP vs ATRP
allClaims.snippet: SoLV is the percentage of grid points where your business ranks in the top three positions... ARP (Average Rank Position): your average ranking only across pins where your business appears... ATRP (Average Total Rank Position): includes the entire grid with default values where your business doesn't appear, providing a more realistic view of overall visibility gaps.

allClaims.claim: Independent GBP benchmark data anchors the modeled early job-shape: the average profile generates ~59 actions/month split ~20 website clicks / 16 direction requests / 10 phone calls, and the conversion-from-views rate for service businesses runs 10-15% calls (vs 5-8% general). A fresh, low-visibility profile sits at the FLOOR of these benchmarks — single-digit monthly calls — which is the empirical basis for projecting the honest early shape as ~1-2 pack-sourced jobs/month, not a job a week. (Job-count translation is MODELED; the underlying action benchmarks are measured/third-party-blended.)
allClaims.stat: ~59 actions/mo; ~10 calls/mo; 10-15% service call-rate
allClaims.snippet: 5%-8% of viewers [click to call]; service businesses achieve 10%-15%... Businesses appear in local 3-pack for 20%-40% of relevant searches... Active businesses gain 2-5 reviews monthly.

allClaims.claim: BrightLocal's 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey quantifies the review-asymmetry click-skip on the consumer side: 31% of consumers will only use a business with 4.5+ stars (up from 17% the prior year) and 74% want reviews from the last three months. A fresh profile with few/old reviews is filtered out by roughly a third of buyers even when it ranks — independent demand-side corroboration that low early conversion is a social-proof effect, not just a position effect.
allClaims.stat: 31% require 4.5+ stars; 74% want reviews <3 months old
allClaims.snippet: 31% of consumers will only use businesses with 4.5+ stars (up from 17%)... 74% want reviews from the last three months.

allClaims.claim: Search Engine Land's proximity-bias guide gives a primary-publisher statement of the geographic ceiling: visibility is highest closest to the business and decays with device distance, and prominence can only sometimes overcome a nearer competitor. This corroborates the proximity-grid fracture as a structural cap on a fresh profile's pack reach — independent of the geo-grid tool vendors.
allClaims.stat: closer device = more visible; farther = less visible
allClaims.snippet: The closer a searcher's device is to a specific business location, the more visible that business will tend to be in local packs and maps. The further away the device is, the less visible the same business will typically be... As you take your device further away from the locale, you're likely to see your local rankings decrease.

allClaims.claim: Whitespark's 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors report (187 factors scored by 47 experts, published Nov 6 2025) is the current authoritative weighting and confirms the controllable/uncontrollable split: proximity dominates the pack but cannot be improved, leaving GBP signals (~32%), reviews (~16-20%, share rising), and on-page (~19%) as the levers. This dates round-1's Whitespark proximity claim to the newest edition and underpins the spine: a one-time-shippable enterprise site moves the controllable on-page/GBP/entity share, not the proximity cap.
allClaims.stat: 187 factors, 47 experts, pub 2025-11-06; reviews 16-20%
allClaims.snippet: Whitespark's 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey evaluated 187 factors by 47 top local SEO experts, published November 6, 2025... Reviews account for 16-20% of local ranking weight with that share rising year over year.

pillars.title: The sequencing — organic carries the pipeline months ~1-18
pillars.section:
## T6 — The Sequencing: Organic Carries the Pipeline (Months ~1–18)

**Bottom line:** Organic is the day-one and sustained engine. The map pack is a proximity-capped byproduct we deliver but never center. We build the website to carry the pipeline while the pack matures on its own slower, review-gated clock. This is a strategy SHAPE, not a dated rank guarantee.

**Why organic is the engine, not the second channel.** In a controlled local-SERP click study, organic results took the most clicks of any SERP type — 50.8% with no Local Services Ads present, 43.9% with LSAs present — ahead of the local pack at 32.3% / 28.8% ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/research/local-services-ads-click-study/)). Organic is not the smaller channel it is often assumed to be; it is the larger one.

**Why organic reaches the whole town and the pack cannot.** The local pack fractures geographically. Every pin on a geo-grid is a separate request from a distinct lat/long, so the same business can rank #1 at its office and fall to roughly #7–#10 a few blocks away ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/resources/geo-grid-ranking-tool-comparison-guide/)). City-intent organic does not fracture this way. In a 549-search / 61-pin study, once a city modifier was added the top-5 organic positions held constant across every test pin ([sterlingsky.ca](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/2025-update-how-proximity-impacts-google-organic-results/)). A town-named `/locations/[city]` page therefore serves the whole town on the same terms regardless of where the searcher stands — the location-independent reach the pack structurally cannot deliver. This is the documented way one website covers a metro of surrounding cities where a service-area business has no physical address and is "extremely unlikely" to appear in the 3-pack ([sangfroidwebdesign.com](https://www.sangfroidwebdesign.com/local-seo/city-pages/)).

**Why the website is the lever for organic — and only a partial lever for the pack.** The two channels run on different ranking-factor weights. BrightLocal's local-algorithm breakdown puts Local Organic at On-page 33% / Links 24% / Behavioral 10%, versus Local Pack at Google Business Profile 32% / Reviews 20% / On-page 15% ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-local-algorithm-and-ranking-factors/)). A well-built site (on-page + one-time links) moves organic directly; the pack is gated on GBP completeness and review accumulation. Google's own docs confirm the channels are entangled, not separate: "Your position in web results is also a factor, so search engine optimization (SEO) best practices apply" ([support.google.com](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091)). Organic is the leading edge of the same engine — as organic authority lands it pulls the pack up over time. We do not claim the pack is dead weight for 18 months; it begins maturing as organic prominence accrues.

**The honest ramp — floor and ceiling.** Organic compounds; it is not instant. Only 1.74% of newly published pages reach Google's top 10 within a year, and the average #1-ranking page is five years old ([ahrefs.com](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-rank-in-google-and-how-old-are-top-ranking-pages/)). That is the head-term reality, and we never promise around it. But the same study shows 40.82% of pages that do reach the top 10 get there within one month ([ahrefs.com](https://ahrefs.com/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-rank-in-google-and-how-old-are-top-ranking-pages/)) — the mechanism by which lower-competition, long-tail, town-named pages can rank in weeks-to-months. So:
- **FLOOR (promise this):** long-tail and city-intent pages move within months. Roofing-vertical agency consensus reports ranking movement typically within 3–6 months ([gomarketing.com](https://gomarketing.com/blog/how-roofing-companies-rank-1-in-local-google-search-in-2026/)) — directional, vendor-incentive, label it as such.
- **CEILING (project, do not promise):** head-term regional dominance compounds over ~6–18 months as authority accrues.

**Why organic must carry months 1–18.** The pack is the slow, maintenance-heavy channel it has to wait on. Agency consensus puts competitive top-3 map-pack placement at 6–12 months of consistent effort, with reviews compounding rather than boosting instantly ([bluemonkfish.com](https://bluemonkfish.com/how-long-does-local-seo-take/)) — and positions decay over 2–4 months without ongoing review/freshness signals (same source; directional, agency-sourced, not measured). Organic ranking, once earned, is the more stable, town-wide, durable spine. That is the sequencing: organic carries the pipeline while the pack heals and matures underneath it.

**What NOT to oversell:** Do not claim "organic ignores proximity." The measured, defensible claim is narrow — a *city-modified / explicit-intent* organic query ranks stably across the town; bare "near me" / implicit queries still shift, and Sterling Sky's own 2022 data showed proximity then hit organic *harder* than the pack ([sterlingsky.ca](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/2025-update-how-proximity-impacts-google-organic-results/)). Sell the SHAPE and the FLOOR, never a month-X rank guarantee.

pillars.section:
## T7 — The Organic Lead-Quality Differential (High-Ticket Only)

**Bottom line.** For considered, high-ticket roofing jobs ($15-30k), an organic-owned visitor is a better lead than a map-pack lead — but not because organic "converts at a higher rate." At the raw session level, organic and paid search convert almost identically (organic 4.8% vs paid 5.1% in Construction & Engineering, across 110M+ sessions tracked) ([Ruler Analytics](https://www.ruleranalytics.com/blog/insight/conversion-rate-by-industry/)). The edge is four mechanisms — intent split, ticket size, owned environment, and de-risking — not a conversion-rate number. Lead with the mechanisms; never lead with "organic converts higher."

**The intent split.** The pack is a side-by-side, three-pin commodity surface with one-tap call buttons — it structurally feeds comparison-shopping ([Tara Saka](https://tarasaka.com/google-maps-seo-for-roofers/)). Considered buyers run a bake-off: ~70% of homeowners compare 2-3 quotes, ~85% compare three or fewer, and ~65% call pricing "very important" ([Modernize 2024](https://modernize.com/homeowner-insights/contractor-selection-trends)). A visitor who navigated to one brand's owned site has already partially self-selected out of the side-by-side. This does not *eliminate* the bake-off — even considered buyers are price-aware — it improves win probability by letting the brand frame value before price enters.

**The owned environment.** High-ticket buyers research a brand's public presence — content, portfolio, evidence of results — before they make contact ([practitioner; high-ticket psychology](https://medium.com/@tiffygwrites/the-quiet-lurker-buyer-understanding-high-ticket-buyer-psychology-01d2f8e57d37)). They weigh value and outcomes over lowest price and research for weeks ([Spear](https://www.getspear.ai/blog-post/high-ticket-sales-a-playbook-of-strategies-to-win-the-game)). An organic visitor converts on the brand's E-E-A-T-rich turf, not in a multi-pin grid. Caveat: high-ticket buyers are *more* demanding, not less — the owned site has to actually demonstrate authority for this to pay.

**The intent-quality gradient (directional support).** Self-initiated, intent-rich contact closes far better than interruptive contact: referral close rates run above 50%, ad-response under 20% ([Hook benchmark]). Exclusive high-intent contractor leads close 23% at $8,400 (roofing) and 31% at $22,000 (windows) versus a shared-lead floor of ~6-10% ([LeadGen Jay](https://leadgenjay.com/blog/best-lead-services-for-contractors-2026-7-expert-tested-winners)). The much-restated "14.6% inbound vs 1.7% outbound" pair is directional color only — it is inbound-vs-outbound, not organic-vs-pack ([restated benchmark](https://blog.nimblo.ai/enterprise-seo-lead-generation-14-percent-close-rate/)). None of these is a direct organic-vs-pack measurement; they establish the general principle organic-owned leads exploit.

**De-risking.** A map pin is a rented asset. GBP suspension reports surged 80%+ since 2023 ([Search Engine Roundtable](https://www.seroundtable.com/google-business-profile-suspensions-increase-40169.html)), and appeal wait times ran 5-6 weeks in early 2025 with no guaranteed reinstatement ([Sterling Sky](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/top-reasons-google-my-business-suspended-your-listing/)). This is a real, rising risk with a multi-week recovery — measured, not epidemic. **Do not assert "35% of profiles suspended yearly"** — that figure traces to no primary source. An owned domain carries no such suspension exposure.

**The cost curve.** Once a domain ranks, organic CPL floors at roughly $10-90 versus paid search ~$165 and roofing LSA ~$60-120, and effective CPL *drops* as the asset matures — the inverse of rented channels ([benchmark range](https://www.estatehub.io/articles/2026-benchmarks-lead-conversion-rates-home-services)). Promise the floor; project the maturity curve as the ceiling.

**Two hard conditions on all of the above.** (1) The differential is **conditional on actually ranking for money terms** — ~90% of pages get zero Google traffic, and most SEO fails by targeting informational not commercial queries ([Marketing Eye](https://www.marketingeye.com/blog/why-most-seo-strategies-fail-to-generate-leads.html)). The quality differential is a *consequence of ranking*, never automatic from "having a good site" — which is why the offer must be tied to a ranking outcome. (2) It is **scoped to considered/high-ticket only.** For urgent jobs (active leak, storm), pack speed wins — first responders get ~5x the hire rate ([Thumbtack via LeadGen Jay](https://leadgenjay.com/blog/best-lead-services-for-contractors-2026-7-expert-tested-winners)). And organic takes 6-12 months to mature, so the build period needs a bridge for near-term volume.

**What NOT to oversell:** Do not claim organic "converts at a higher rate" (it converts at parity with paid) or quantify "arrives pre-sold" (the ~70% figure is modeled, not measured); the owned site improves win probability in a bake-off, it does not erase the bake-off.

pillars.title: Zero-pack long-tail volume (organic-only territory)
pillars.section:
## T8 — Zero-Pack Long-Tail Volume (Organic-Only Territory)

**Bottom line: roughly 70% of searches return no map pack at all, and the pack-free majority is research/cost/comparison territory a thin pack-optimized site is structurally blind to.** A deep `/resources` + cost-guide + glossary silo is the only business-owned asset eligible to compete there. We promise eligibility and authority on that territory — not a traffic windfall. That distinction is the whole defensibility of this pillar.

**The pack owns the bottom funnel. We never contest it.** In a June 2026 SERP study of UK trades, the roofing vertical showed a local pack on 97.4% of genuine hire-intent queries — but only after research/cost/comparison/jobs/training/brand "noise" was filtered out of the keyword set ([studio36digital.co.uk](https://studio36digital.co.uk/uk-local-seo-statistics-2026/)). That filtered-out slice is exactly where the silos play. The two are separate demand pools, not competitors for the same SERP. "Roofer near me" and "[city] roof repair" belong to the pack; "metal vs asphalt roof cost" and "how to file a roof insurance claim" do not.

**The non-pack territory is large, not niche.** Across a 1,000-keyword Ahrefs panel (22 industries, ~404M monthly searches, Oct 2025), only 29.7% of searches triggered a Local Pack — so roughly 70% returned none ([studio36digital.co.uk](https://studio36digital.co.uk/98-7-of-uk-searches-display-serp-features/)). Google's own long-cited figure is that ~46% of searches have local intent, implying ~54% do not ([seroundtable.com](https://www.seroundtable.com/google-46-of-searches-have-local-intent-26529.html)). Both are directional for US roofing — the 29.7% is a UK all-vertical average and the 46% is a 2018 Google statement, not a fresh measurement — so we anchor the offer on the measured intent split below, not on a precise roofing pack-trigger percentage.

**The measured anchor: a thin site has no eligible content to rank on research queries.** BrightLocal's controlled study (8,000 results, 800 manual searches, 20 verticals × 20 US cities) found business websites appear in 61% of top-10 organic results for *transactional* queries but only 32% for *informational* ones — where directories (37%) and content sites outrank them ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/research/business-listings-visibility-study/)). The way to surface on research queries is deep informational content. A pack-optimized transactional site has nothing to enter. Firsthand SERP checks confirm the shape: "roof replacement cost" and "metal vs asphalt roof" return editorial guides and calculators — This Old House, Angi, the JLC Cost-vs-Value Report — with no map pack ([thisoldhouse.com](https://www.thisoldhouse.com/roofing/shingles-vs-metal-roof-cost)); "how to file a roof insurance claim" returns manufacturer and .gov authority pages — GAF, Texas TDI ([gaf.com](https://www.gaf.com/en-us/plan-design/roofing-insurance-claims), [tdi.texas.gov](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/tips/replacing-your-roof.html)).

**The honest counter-pressure: AI Overviews are eating this lane hardest.** AIO coverage ran ~6.5% of queries in Jan 2025, peaked near 25% mid-year, and settled ~16% by Nov — and ~91% of early-2025 AIOs were informational-intent ([searchengineland.com](https://searchengineland.com/google-ai-overviews-surge-pullback-data-466314), corroborating the Semrush 10M-keyword dataset). AIO cut organic CTR on informational queries an estimated 38–61% across 2025 studies, with US zero-click already ~58.5% ([searchengineland.com](https://searchengineland.com/google-ai-overviews-drive-drop-organic-paid-ctr-464212)). So a chunk of pack-free research demand is increasingly answered on-SERP and never clicks through.

**Floor vs ceiling.** *Floor (promise this):* deep silos make the domain ELIGIBLE on a query category a thin competitor cannot appear on at all — qualified-coverage breadth, AI-Overview citation surface (cited brands see ~+35% CTR), and an entity/authority signal that lifts the whole domain including the pack-served transactional pages. *Ceiling (project, don't promise):* incremental research-query clicks on the AIO-resilient slice — commercial-investigation, cost/comparison, and localized long-tail variants, which are far less AIO-exposed than definitional lookups. Individual research keywords are low-volume long-tail; the payoff is breadth of qualified coverage and topical authority, not raw traffic. This is a one-time shippable content asset — no PBNs, no link schemes, no gray-hat, all explicitly excluded.

**What NOT to oversell:** Do not promise raw research-query click volume — AIO and zero-click erode it. Do not assert a precise roofing pack-trigger percentage — that figure is directional. Do not claim research queries *never* show a pack — claim they *disproportionately* favor organic/content/AI surfaces a thin site can't occupy. Do not center the map pack — it is a proximity-capped byproduct we deliver but never sell as the engine.

loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the load-bearing HONESTY claim — the strongest counter-evidence. Including it on-slide is what makes the pillar FTC-defensible: it forces the floor/ceiling framing and stops us promising research-query traffic we can't guarantee. Independent editorial corroboration of the vendor (Semrush) dataset.

whatNotToOversell: Do not promise raw research-query CLICK volume as the payoff — AI Overviews and zero-click (~58.5% US, informational ~74%+) erode it; promise eligibility + authority + AIO-citation surface, project clicks only on the AIO-resilient commercial/cost/localized-long-tail slice.

Do not assert a precise roofing pack-trigger percentage — the 29.7% figure is a UK all-vertical Oct-2025 panel average and the 46% local-intent figure is a 2018 Google statement; both are directional, not measured roofing constants.

Do not claim research queries NEVER show a pack — claim they DISPROPORTIONATELY favor organic/content/AI surfaces a thin site can't occupy; the informational/transactional boundary is fuzzy and Google is pushing AIO down-funnel.

Do not frame the silo as a traffic-majority play — individual research keywords are low-volume long-tail; the value is breadth of qualified coverage + topical authority that also feeds Prominence (which dilates the pack), not raw traffic.
Do not center the map pack as the engine — it is a proximity-capped (~5-7mi) byproduct we deliver but never sell as the win; the spine is organic regional dominance.

Do not claim the broadest commercial heads (e.g. 'best roofing companies') as a winnable silo target — those are dominated by large publisher listicles/directories; the realistic win is localized + specific long-tail variants.
No PBNs, link schemes, or gray-hat — explicitly excluded; the silo is a one-time shippable on-page content asset, not an ongoing off-page program.
gaps: No US-specific, roofing-vertical SERP-feature panel measuring exact local-pack trigger rate on research vs transactional roofing queries (the studio36 panel is UK + all-vertical; BrightLocal is multi-vertical, 1 informational + 1 transactional keyword each). A purpose-built DataForSEO/Ahrefs pull on a roofing research-query set would convert 'directional' to 'measured'.

No measured search-VOLUME quantification of the zero-pack roofing research long-tail (how many monthly searches the /resources + /glossary silo could realistically address) — needed to size the opportunity without overstating it.

AI-Overview CITATION-share data for contractor research content specifically (does deep silo content get cited in AIOs for roofing queries?) is unmeasured — load-bearing if we sell the silo as an AI-citation surface.
The exact share of roofing research queries answered fully on-SERP (zero-click) vs still driving a click is unknown for this vertical — affects the honesty of any traffic projection.

No US (let alone NC/Triangle) roofing-specific SERP-feature study found — the cleanest roofing local-pack figure (97.4%) is from a UK dataset (studio36, June 2026). US roofing pack frequency is reasonably assumed similar for hire-intent but is NOT independently measured; treat the 97.4% as directional for US/NC.

No measured figure for what % of ROOFING research/commercial-investigation queries specifically suppress the local pack (the seed target). The evidence is inferential: studio36 filtered those queries OUT (so they aren't in the 97.4% denominator) + firsthand SERP checks show no pack on cost/comparison/best-of heads. A precise 'X% of roofing research queries show no pack' number would require a custom SERP-feature pull (DataForSEO/Semrush) and remains un-sourced.

The AIO-resilience split (informational ~35%+ AIO trigger vs transactional ~6%) comes from a single vendor-adjacent aggregator (Digital Applied); a fully independent primary breakdown of AIO trigger rate by intent for the HOME-SERVICES vertical specifically was not located — corroborate before putting the 6%-vs-35% contrast in a reel.
The 'AIO-cited brands see +35% CTR' silver-lining stat is single-sourced and not yet verified at a primary; do not make it load-bearing without a second corroborator.

Quantified silo upside (e.g. 'capture N incremental monthly research sessions') is NOT modeled here — this round establishes the territory EXISTS and is pack-free + partially AIO-exposed; the $ / session projection belongs in the claim-library modeling pass, labeled modeled.

counter.point: The organic-only research lane is the SAME lane AI Overviews and zero-click are eroding hardest. AI Overviews cut organic CTR on informational queries by an estimated 38-61% across multiple 2025 studies (Seer 61% on 3,119 informational queries; a randomized field experiment 38% with zero-click rising 54%->72%), and ~58.5% of US searches already produce no click. So 'we own the zero-pack research territory' must be sold as QUALIFIED-INTENT COVERAGE + AI-citation surface, not as a guaranteed click/traffic windfall.
counter.soWhat: Promise the floor: deep silos make the site ELIGIBLE on a category of queries a thin pack-only competitor cannot appear on at all (coverage + AI-Overview citation + brand-preference seeding). Do NOT promise it as a traffic majority — many of these queries are low-volume and increasingly answered on-SERP.

counter.point: Research/commercial keywords are individually LOW-VOLUME and long-tail. The value is breadth of qualified coverage and topical authority, not raw traffic — overstating 'long-tail volume' contradicts the KM_VALUEPROP long-tail correction. The pack still captures the high-volume, high-intent bottom-funnel ('roofer near me', '[city] roof repair').
counter.soWhat: Frame the silo as the topical-authority + qualified-coverage engine that also feeds Prominence/organic rank (which in turn dilates the pack), not as a traffic-majority play.

counter.point: The headline 29.7% pack figure is a UK, all-vertical Ahrefs-panel average; US roofing-specific pack-trigger rates are not directly measured here and SERP features shift month to month. Exact pack-suppression % for roofing research queries is directional, not a measured constant.
counter.soWhat: Use ranges and 'directional', anchor the bulletproof claims on the BrightLocal intent split (measured) + firsthand SERP checks, and avoid asserting a precise roofing pack-trigger percentage.

counter.point: Some 'cost' and 'best' queries are migrating into commercial/transactional AIO and even occasionally surface local units; the informational/transactional boundary is fuzzy and Google is pushing AIO down-funnel (transactional AIO share rose from 2% to 14% in 2025).
counter.soWhat: Don't claim research queries NEVER show a pack; claim they DISPROPORTIONATELY favor organic/content/AI surfaces a thin site can't occupy.

counter.point: STRONGEST COUNTER — AI Overviews are eating the informational/research lane the silos target. Ahrefs (Nov 2025) found ~99.9% of informational keywords now trigger an AI Overview; Digital Applied (2026) puts AIO on 35%+ of informational queries vs only ~6% of transactional, and 25.11% of ALL Google searches in Q1 2026. Informational queries run ~74% zero-click (definitions ~86%, factual lookups ~91%). So a chunk of the pack-free research demand is increasingly answered ON the SERP, never clicking through to the silo at all.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT promise raw research-query CLICK volume as the silo payoff. Reframe the silo value honestly on THREE bounded planes: (1) the resilient slice — commercial-investigation + cost/comparison + localized long-tail queries are far LESS AIO-exposed and remain clickable; (2) AI-citation capture — brands cited in an AIO see ~+35% CTR, and deep credentialed silo content is what gets cited, so the silo becomes the AIO-citation asset, not just a blue-link asset; (3) entity/authority signal that lifts the whole domain (incl. the transactional pages the pack does serve). Promise the FLOOR (authority + AIO-citation eligibility + long-tail capture), project the CEILING (research-query clicks where AIO is absent).

counter.point: PRIMARY/ACADEMIC corroboration of the AIO threat — a pre-registered randomized field experiment (Agarwal & Sen, Indian School of Business + Carnegie Mellon; 1,065 US desktop Chrome users via Prolific, Jan-Feb 2026, SSRN working paper) found AI Overviews cut organic clicks on triggered queries by 38%, with zero-click rising from 54% to 72% when an AIO was shown. This is the most rigorous (causal, not correlational) evidence and it does NOT distinguish transactional vs informational — so we cannot claim the transactional resilience from THIS study.
counter.soWhat: This is the skeptic's best weapon: a causal study showing AIO materially suppresses clicks. Concede it cleanly. Our defense is that the resilience split (AIO hits informational far harder than transactional/local) comes from SEPARATE SERP-feature studies, not this experiment — and that the pack itself sits BELOW the fold of these effects (the pack is a local-intent feature largely untouched by the informational-AIO dynamic). Never overstate: the silo's research-click value is genuinely compressing year over year.

counter.point: BOUNDED COUNTER on the 'pack-free' framing itself — the studio36 roofing 97.4% / trades 95.6% figure proves that for genuine hire-intent roofing queries the pack is near-universal. A skeptic can say: 'the money queries ARE pack queries, so a thin pack-optimized site captures the high-value demand and your silo only wins low-intent traffic.'
counter.soWhat: This is true and we should NOT fight it — it is consistent with the doctrine (the pack is a proximity-capped byproduct we deliver; the silo plays the complementary research/comparison/long-tail layer). The rebuttal is the organic-dominance spine: the pack is proximity-capped (~5-7mi) and cannot scale a $5-10M regional operation, whereas deep organic silos rank across the whole region on the larger research+commercial-investigation volume pool. The silo is the SCALE engine; the pack is the local default. Don't sell the silo as a pack substitute — sell it as the regional-scale layer the pack structurally can't be.

pillars.title: The two execution conditions
pillars.section:
## T9 — The Two Execution Conditions

**Bottom line.** Organic regional dominance is not bought, it is built — and it rests on two client-executed conditions King Maker installs as systems but does not run forever: (1) a **universal, unscreened review-velocity machine**, and (2) a **legitimate, earn-don't-buy off-page authority program** seeded by the one-time on-site link architecture we ship. The two move different surfaces and are not interchangeable. Reviews are the fast lever; off-page links are the slow compounding engine. Centering organic is correct on the math: with no Local Services Ads present, organic takes 50.8% of local-search clicks versus 32.3% for the map pack (https://www.brightlocal.com/research/local-services-ads-click-study/). The pack is a real but proximity-capped minority — a byproduct we deliver, never the headline.

**Why the two conditions are not the same lever.** In Whitespark's 2026 model, review signals are ~20% of the pack but only ~8% of local organic, while link signals are ~24% of organic versus ~8% of the pack (https://thestacc.com/blog/local-seo-ranking-factors/). So a review mandate is primarily a pack-deficit healer; an off-page link program is primarily the organic-dominance engine. Treat those weights as directional ratios from an expert survey, not measured coefficients — they argue direction, not magnitude.

**Condition 1 — Review velocity (the fast lever).** Recency, not raw count, is what moves and protects ranking. Review recency rose from ranking factor #93 in 2023 to #11 in 2026, the single largest positional jump in Whitespark's study (https://thestacc.com/blog/local-seo-ranking-factors/). Sterling Sky's case-study tracking shows a noticeable bump around the 10-review mark and warns rankings can decline after roughly three weeks of dormancy (https://www.sterlingsky.ca/number-of-reviews-impact-ranking/) — small-sample observation, so we frame it as "sustained velocity protects ranking; dormancy risks decline," not a guaranteed drop/recovery curve. The mandate must be **universal and unscreened** to be legal: the FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect Oct 21, 2024, carries civil penalties up to $51,744 per violation, and bans review suppression, incentivized reviews, and gating (https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/08/federal-trade-commission-announces-final-rule-banning-fake-reviews-testimonials). King Maker ships an ask-everyone system — never a happy-customer filter.

**Condition 2 — Off-page authority (the slow compounding engine).** Links have a demonstrated causal effect on organic, not just correlation: Ahrefs disavowed 3,476 links to three of its own pages and watched traffic fall 13.3%–18%, recovering to ~99% when the disavow was removed (https://ahrefs.com/blog/impact-of-links/). The **one-time, in-scope** piece King Maker ships directly is the on-site link architecture: SearchPilot split-tests show +5% to +25% organic uplift, and a roofing-relevant test adding links to the 6 nearest geographic regions across ~8,000 location pages produced +7% organic uplift on the linked pages (https://www.searchpilot.com/resources/case-studies/seo-split-test-lessons-nearby-location-links). Ongoing earned links are client-managed fulfillment and out of scope — we build and instrument the machine; the client feeds it. **Honest timeline:** first impact ~8–10 weeks after acquisition, full compounding over 6–12 months (https://outreachz.com/blog/link-building-results-timeline/). No PBNs, no link schemes, no gray-hat — excluded explicitly.

**Pricing the off-page program — floor and ceiling.** $5–10k/mo is enterprise-tier, not typical. SE Ranking's survey of 260 agencies: 64% charge under $1k/mo, 20% $1–2k, 13% $2–5k, only ~2% above $5k (https://seranking.com/blog/seo-pricing/). Ahrefs' poll of 439 providers corroborates: ~$3,209/mo average, 68.8% at $2k/mo or less (https://ahrefs.com/blog/seo-pricing/). So the **floor** is a legitimate program at the typical $1–2k/mo; the **ceiling** is $5–10k/mo for genuine enterprise regional domination. The pillar SEED's "~19% of providers at $5k+/mo" does not survive the primary distribution — the honest figure is ~2%.

**The mechanism that links the two conditions.** Google's prominence framework treats backlink authority and web presence as signals that can let a business outrank closer competitors in the pack (https://thestacc.com/blog/local-seo-ranking-factors/). That is how an organic-first program indirectly lifts the pack — indirectly. Do not over-claim a direct pack-weight from links; links are only ~8% of the pack model.

**What NOT to oversell.** The Whitespark weights are expert-survey opinion, not causal coefficients — never quantify rank movement from them. The Sterling Sky cliff is small-sample, not a published magnitude. The off-page timeline means neither condition reliably moves organic by day 90 — tie any 90-day bar to the fast levers (review velocity, GBP, on-site ship) and let links back the 6–12mo claim. Google's Mueller has signaled links may de-weight over time (https://searchengineland.com/links-may-be-less-important-to-the-google-search-ranking-algorithm-in-the-future-389364) — sell "earn authority that compounds," not "links = 24% forever." And both conditions are client-executed requirements, not King Maker guarantees: we ship the system; the guarantee is conditional on the client running it.

whatNotToOversell: Whitespark LSRF weights (20%/8%/24%) are expert-opinion survey numbers, not measured causal coefficients — use them only for DIRECTION (reviews->pack, links->organic), never to promise a specific number of pack positions or rank movement.

Sterling Sky's 'Magic 10' and '18-day cliff' come from small-sample case tracking with no published magnitude — frame as 'sustained velocity protects ranking, dormancy risks decline,' not a guaranteed drop/recovery curve.

Neither condition is fast: links take ~8-10 weeks to first impact and 6-12 months to compound — do NOT tie a 90-day guarantee to off-page links; back the 90-day bar with review velocity + GBP + the one-time on-site ship instead.
$5-10k/mo is the CEILING (~2% of agencies), not a requirement — sell a $1-2k/mo floor scaling up; do not anchor the offer at $5-10k. The SEED's '~19% at $5k+' is wrong; the honest figure is ~2%.

Do not promise links as a fixed ~24%-of-organic lever in perpetuity — Google's Mueller signaled link weight may drop; sell 'earn authority that compounds' and lean on link relevance + internal architecture, not raw link volume.

Both conditions are CLIENT-EXECUTED requirements, not King Maker guarantees — KM ships and instruments the system; the guarantee is conditional on the client running the velocity machine. Ongoing earned links + ongoing review collection are out of scope.
The roofing +210% / 38-reviews / 4-5-calls-a-day case is a single unaudited vendor self-report (source_type vendor-incentive) — use it only as directional color, never as a promised outcome.
Do not over-claim a direct pack lift from links — links are only ~8% of the pack model; the pack benefit is INDIRECT, via Google's prominence framework, and should be stated as such.
Never PBNs, link schemes, or any gray-hat off-page tactic — excluded explicitly; the off-page program is earn-don't-buy only.
gaps: No primary, quantified study isolating how much a defined $5-10k/mo legitimate off-page spend moves organic rank specifically for ROOFING/home-services in a single metro (the link-impact evidence is general-web, not roofing-vertical-specific).

The exact magnitude/recovery curve behind Sterling Sky's '18-day cliff' is not published with numbers; the dramatic framing rests on case-study observation, not a controlled before/after with effect sizes.
No direct measurement of how much an improved organic/prominence profile dilates effective PACK radius (the proximity-override claim is mechanistic/Google-stated, not quantified).

Whitespark primary report page is JS-rendered and returned only navigation via fetch; all Whitespark weight figures are sourced via independent corroborators (theStacc) rather than the primary PDF — the numbers match warm context but a direct primary capture is still pending.

Could not load the FTC press-release page body directly (used SE-search-surfaced text + corroborating law-firm advisories); the $51,744 figure and Oct 21 2024 effective date are well-corroborated across Alston & Bird / DWT but a primary .gov body capture was blocked this pass.

No INDEPENDENTLY AUDITED roofing-vertical case study isolating the marginal organic-traffic lift attributable to reviews vs links vs on-page — all roofing case studies found are vendor-self-reported (D&D, WebTechs 1072%, etc.) and bundle all tactics, so they cannot cleanly quantify either condition's individual contribution. Treat all roofing case-study percentages as directional vendor claims, never as a promised floor.
No NC/Triangle-specific (Raleigh/Durham/Charlotte) ranking or review-velocity dataset surfaced; the geography-specific proof remains modeled/general rather than local-market measured.

The exact quantified ORGANIC-traffic range attributable specifically to a one-time review mandate (as opposed to ongoing) is not isolable from sources — review effects are measured on revenue/conversion (causal) and on pack rank (correlational/plateauing), but a clean 'reviews -> X% organic' elasticity does not exist in the literature. The pillar should not promise a review-driven organic floor.

FTC.gov primary pages (press release + business-guidance blog) block automated fetch (403); the Dec 22 2025 enforcement + $53,088 figure are confirmed via a top-tier law-firm secondary (Covington/Inside Privacy) rather than the .gov original — worth a manual click-through to the FTC press release to capture the verbatim primary before any FTC-exposed reel uses it.

Mueller's link-deweighting statement is from 2022; no 2025-2026 Google first-party confirmation found that links have materially dropped — so the forward-looking caveat is directional, and round-1's causal Ahrefs evidence that links still move traffic remains the current-state anchor.

counter.point: Whitespark's LSRF weights are an EXPERT-OPINION SURVEY, not measured causal coefficients. The 20%/8%/24% numbers are practitioners' aggregated guesses about relative importance — useful as directional ratios but they cannot support a precise promise like 'a review mandate adds X pack positions.'
counter.soWhat: Use the weights only to argue DIRECTION (reviews -> pack, links -> organic) and never to quantify rank movement. Pair every weight with a measured source (Ahrefs disavow, SearchPilot, Sterling Sky) when making an impact claim.

counter.point: The Sterling Sky 'Magic 10' and '18-day cliff' findings come from small-sample case-study tracking, not large controlled experiments, and Sterling Sky itself flags diminishing returns past 10 reviews. The dramatic 'fell off a cliff' language is not backed by published quantified magnitude in the article body.
counter.soWhat: Frame the review mandate as 'sustained velocity protects ranking; dormancy risks decline' — a defensible floor — rather than promising a specific drop/recovery curve.

counter.point: The off-page TIMELINE (8-10 weeks to first impact, 6-12mo to compound) means neither condition is fast. A guarantee tied to a 90-day window is in tension with the honest off-page timeline — links may not have moved organic materially by day 90.
counter.soWhat: Tie the early-window guarantee to levers that move fast (review velocity, GBP optimization, on-site/internal-link ship) and let the slow off-page link compounding back the 6-12mo organic-dominance claim, not the 90-day bar.

counter.point: $5-10k/mo is so far above market (~2% of agencies, per SE Ranking) that anchoring the offer there risks pricing objections; most clients will and should run a smaller off-page budget. The condition is real but the dollar figure is a ceiling, not a floor.
counter.soWhat: Present off-page as a scalable input ('a legitimate campaign starting at typical $1-2k/mo, scaling to $5-10k for enterprise regional domination'), not a fixed $5-10k requirement.

counter.point: ONGOING earned links + ongoing review collection are CLIENT-MANAGED fulfillment, which the pillar scope explicitly puts out of bounds. KM can ship the machine (review-request system, internal-link architecture, find-a-pro link setup) but cannot itself guarantee the client keeps feeding it.
counter.soWhat: Position the two conditions honestly as REQUIREMENTS the client must execute (KM builds and instruments the system); the guarantee is conditional on the client running the velocity machine KM ships.

counter.point: The strongest skeptic's case against over-weighting links: Google's John Mueller stated (Nov 4, 2022) that the weight on links 'will drop off a little bit' over time and 'won't be such a big factor as sometimes it is today,' adding 'that's something that's been changing quite a bit' already.
counter.soWhat: Bounds the off-page-link claim. Do NOT promise links as a fixed ~24%-of-organic lever in perpetuity — frame the off-page engine as 'earn authority that compounds' and lean on the link-RELEVANCE/quality + internal-architecture pieces (which Mueller endorses) rather than raw link volume. Keeps the pillar honest if Google de-weights links further. Round-1's Ahrefs disavow causal study still proves links matter NOW; this just caps the forward-looking claim.

counter.point: The in-scope one-time on-site lever (location/service pages + internal links) has a hard failure mode: city pages that swap names across boilerplate, lack real local proof (no address/team), or exist only to funnel users are DOORWAY pages — explicitly penalized by Google since 2015 and hit at scale by the March 2024 Core Update + SpamBrain. Spreading authority across thin satellite pages can LOWER rankings.
counter.soWhat: This is the boundary condition on the one-time shippable off-page/on-site work. The SearchPilot +7% nearby-links uplift (round 1) only holds for pages with genuine localized content (real testimonials, regional photos, local team, clear nav). KM must ship differentiated, navigable, conversion-real location pages — the 'delete-the-city-name test' / anti-doorway gate in the build doctrine is the thing that keeps the on-site lever a net positive instead of a penalty risk.

counter.point: Review-count/velocity 'ranking impact' studies are largely observational, so they are vulnerable to confounding — the businesses gaining reviews fastest are often also the ones doing everything else right (more jobs, better GBP, more links), so attributing the rank lift purely to reviews risks correlation-as-causation. Sterling Sky's own 'Magic 10' work shows reviews plateau as a ranking lever after a threshold.
counter.soWhat: Forces the honest framing: the DIRECT causal evidence for reviews is on REVENUE/conversion (Luca 5-9%, the buyer-behavior surveys), while the ranking effect is real but partly correlational and plateaus. So pitch the review mandate primarily as a pack-deficit healer + conversion/revenue engine (causal) and only secondarily as an unlimited organic-rank lever. Avoids an FTC-exposed overclaim that 'more reviews = more rank, linearly.'
