counter.soWhat: KM's funnel must be explicitly single-path/unscreened by design — every customer gets the same Google link. This is a build constraint, not a config option to leave to the client.

counter.point: A site-side aggregateRating could mislead a client into expecting Google stars; if framed as 'star results' it is both ineffective and a potential FTC deceptive-claim exposure for KM.
counter.soWhat: Position site-side reviews strictly as content/E-E-A-T/AI-answer signal; reserve actual star rich-results talk for Product/service schema where legitimately applicable.

counter.point: Reviews-to-ranking is correlation, not proven causation. Search Engine Land and the Sterling Sky case studies themselves caution that feature importance indicates correlation, and a commenter on Sterling Sky's recency study noted the ranking lift could stem from increased profile ENGAGEMENT (the act of soliciting reviews) rather than the reviews per se. One proposed mechanism is indirect: ratings lift click-through, and Google's algorithm reacts to click patterns.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT sell reviews as a deterministic ranking dial. Frame the machine as moving a heavily-correlated signal with strong practitioner consensus — promise the floor (clears the low roofing bar, drives recency-conversion), project the ceiling (ranking lift) as a probable outcome, not a guarantee.

counter.point: Proximity to the searcher remains the dominant local-pack factor (~55% per Whitespark framing), while reviews are only ~16-20% of weight. Reviews cannot overcome a proximity gap in the map pack.
counter.soWhat: Reinforces the pillar spine: the pack is a proximity-capped byproduct. Center the review machine on ORGANIC regional dominance and conversion (where reviews carry full weight as trust + content + AI-entity signals), and treat any pack lift as a bonus, never the headline promise.

counter.point: Sterling Sky's 'Magic 10' finding shows diminishing returns: the measurable bump came crossing 9->10 reviews, and 'the boost does not necessarily continue if you keep getting more reviews.' Raw-volume promises past the early floor are not supported.
counter.soWhat: The machine's value is VELOCITY/recency + clearing the early floor fast, not an ever-climbing total. Sell consistency, not a vanity review count.

counter.point: Recency case-study evidence is observational, not controlled: 'individual examples may not serve as definitive proof of how Google's algorithm operates.' The velocity claim rests on repeated practitioner observation plus large-N correlation, not an RCT.
counter.soWhat: Label velocity/recency claims as measured-correlation + directional-consensus, never as a controlled causal result. Honesty protects the FTC-exposed offer.

allClaims.claim: Review velocity (consistent, recent reviews) is the fastest local-pack lever; rankings 'fall off a cliff' if a business stops collecting reviews for even ~three weeks, and recover when collection resumes. This validates the velocity-machine spine: the mechanism must produce a STEADY drip, not a one-time spike.
allClaims.stat: Maps ranking can drop within ~3 weeks of review dormancy
allClaims.snippet: Consistent monthly reviews (recency) are more impactful than having a large, stagnant total... Rankings can 'fall off a cliff' if you stop receiving reviews for even three weeks; stay consistent.

allClaims.claim: Sterling Sky's 2025 controlled study found a small but noticeable Maps-ranking bump when a business crossed from 9 to 10 reviews (the 'Magic 10'), with diminishing returns after — confirming an early floor target the machine should clear fast, while velocity (not raw total) carries ongoing weight.
allClaims.stat: 9 → 10 reviews = ranking bump in all 3 test cases; no bump 10 → 11
allClaims.snippet: In all three cases, we saw a small but noticeable increase in their Maps ranking for the main keyword when the businesses went from 9 to 10 reviews... We did not see the bump in local pack rankings we saw when a business went from 9 reviews to 10 reviews [moving from 10 to 11].

allClaims.claim: Reviews with written text + keywords boost local SEO far more than star-only ratings — so the request flow should nudge a written review, not just a star tap. This also means self-published reviews are valuable as on-page CONTENT and an AI/entity signal even though they cannot show stars (see ineligibility claim).
allClaims.stat: text reviews > star-only for ranking
allClaims.snippet: Reviews with actual text and keywords boost SEO far more than star-only ratings.

allClaims.claim: Review GATING (pre-screening by satisfaction — happy customers get the Google link, unhappy ones get a private form) explicitly violates Google's Maps UGC policy: businesses must not discourage negative reviews or selectively solicit positive ones. The KM mechanism MUST send every customer the same unscreened ask.
allClaims.stat: policy prohibition (no penalty stated by Google)
allClaims.snippet: Discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive reviews from customers [is prohibited]. ... merchants should not require or pressure users to leave ratings or write reviews while on the premises.

allClaims.claim: The FTC's final Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (effective Oct 21, 2024) bans review suppression and incentivizing reviews of a particular sentiment, carrying civil penalties up to ~$51,744 per violation — making gating a federal-law exposure, not just a platform-ToS issue. This is the FTC-exposure rail the offer must respect.
allClaims.stat: up to $51,744 per violation; effective Oct 21, 2024
allClaims.source_type: legal-analysis (law firm, citing FTC final rule)
allClaims.snippet: The rule was passed by the FTC on a 5–0 vote and went into effect on October 21, 2024. ... gives the FTC authority to pursue significant monetary penalties against violators – currently $51,744 per violation ... The purchasing or incentivizing of reviews of a particular sentiment. For example, a business cannot provide compensation to its customers for making a positive review.

allClaims.claim: Self-serving reviews placed on the reviewed entity's own site are INELIGIBLE for Google star review-snippet rich results — for LocalBusiness or any Organization type — whether marked up directly or via an embedded Google/Facebook widget. So a site-side aggregateRating will NOT render stars in Google search; ship it as content / AI-answer / entity signal, never sold as 'star results.'
allClaims.stat: 0 star rich-results from self-hosted LocalBusiness reviews
allClaims.snippet: If the entity that's being reviewed controls the reviews about itself, their pages that use LocalBusiness or any other type of Organization structured data are ineligible for star review feature. For example, a review about entity A is placed on the website of entity A, either directly in their structured data or through an embedded third-party widget (for example, Google Business reviews or Facebook reviews widget).

allClaims.claim: Independent corroboration of the aggregateRating limit: BrightLocal confirms LocalBusiness review markup won't generate stars regardless of source, and recommends Product/Service-level schema as the eligible path. The shippable move is Product/service-scoped schema where genuinely applicable, not a whole-company self-rating.
allClaims.stat: LocalBusiness self-reviews = no stars; Product schema = eligible
allClaims.snippet: Even if you add LocalBusiness review markup to your website, it won't generate the star ratings in Google search that business owners hope for... The key is to focus on products or services offered by your business rather than the company as a whole.

allClaims.claim: Google itself provides the canonical review-request primitive: a first-party shareable review LINK and downloadable QR CODE from the Business Profile ('Get more reviews'). The KM /review funnel should route to THIS official link/place-ID URL — not a third-party intermediary — so the QR on trucks/invoices/door-hangers lands customers directly on the Google review form.
allClaims.stat: official Google link + QR available
allClaims.snippet: To make it easier for customers to leave reviews on your Business Profile, you can create and share a link or QR code to request reviews. ... Offering incentives, like free or discounted goods or services, to customers in exchange for reviews is considered fake engagement and is strictly prohibited.

allClaims.claim: Post-job SMS requests convert far better than email, supporting an SMS-first request flow fired within 24-48h of job completion: SMS ~98% open vs ~20-30% email, and review-completion ~12-20% (SMS) vs ~3-8% (email). KM ships the funnel + QR; the client runs the send.
allClaims.stat: SMS ~98% open / 12-20% review completion vs email ~20-30% / 3-8%
allClaims.snippet: SMS shows an open rate of 98% versus 20-25% for email... For review completion specifically, SMS achieves a 12-20% review completion rate versus 3-8% for email.

allClaims.claim: Timing discipline for the post-job flow: fire within 24-48h while the experience is fresh, keep it to ~two sentences + the link, personalize with name/job, and cap follow-ups at a single reminder 3-5 days later (more damages the relationship). These are the request-flow parameters the machine encodes.
allClaims.stat: send 24-48h; 1 reminder at 3-5 days; ~98% of texts read within 3 min
allClaims.snippet: Send within 24 to 48 hours of delivery or service completion for SMS... A single reminder 3 to 5 days later is standard practice. Sending more than one follow-up damages the customer relationship and increases unsubscribe rates.

allClaims.claim: Physical QR/NFC review cards and vehicle/invoice decals materially lift review volume at the point of peak satisfaction (job completion) — vendor field data cites 3-5x volume vs manual asks and dual-mode (QR+NFC) cards out-converting single-mode. KM ships the QR artifacts (trucks, invoices, door-hangers); flag the multiplier figures as vendor-incentive, treat the DIRECTION (point-of-job physical ask works) as the durable claim.
allClaims.stat: 3-5x review volume claimed (vendor); QR+NFC dual-mode ~68% higher completion vs QR-only (vendor field study)
allClaims.snippet: Businesses using them report review volume increases of 3-5x compared to manual requests... For service businesses, tradespeople and home services... can tap the card at the end of the job while the customer is still impressed.

allClaims.claim: Genuine, UNINCENTIVIZED solicitation of reviews is explicitly permitted by Google — so the universal post-job ask is policy-clean as long as it is not gated and offers no incentive. This is the affirmative green-light the KM mechanism operates inside.
allClaims.stat: permitted: solicit genuine experience without incentives
allClaims.snippet: Solicit or encourage the posting of content that does represent a genuine experience, without offering incentives [is permitted].

allClaims.claim: Review velocity (new reviews per month) outweighs total review count: a business earning ~20 fresh reviews monthly outranks one with 200 reviews from two years ago. In the Local Search Ranking Factors survey, review velocity rose from roughly factor #93 to #11 — confirming the KM machine must produce a steady monthly drip, not a one-time backfill.
allClaims.stat: velocity jumped from ~#93 to #11; 20 fresh/month beats 200 stale
allClaims.snippet: Review velocity jumped from factor #93 to #11 in recent local search ranking factors... a business with 200 reviews from two years ago will rank lower than a business that earns 20 fresh reviews every month.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (practitioner survey consensus, Whitespark/Darren Shaw 2026 LSRF report)

allClaims.claim: Whitespark's Darren Shaw rates review RECENCY a top-5 local ranking factor for 2025 (up from #20 in the 2023 LSRF survey), and warns that a business not getting new reviews consistently will be quietly out-ranked. This is the single strongest independent endorsement of the velocity-machine spine.
allClaims.stat: recency = top-5 factor 2025 (was #20 in 2023)
allClaims.snippet: In the 2023 Local Search Ranking Factors, Review Recency ranks as the #20th most valuable local ranking factor... I think Google has cranked the dial on this factor. I'd put review recency in my top 5 most important ranking factors of 2025.

allClaims.claim: Sterling Sky's 2025 'near me' study analyzed 8,186 businesses across 200 cities and found reviews-this-month matters more than total review count: a dental client pulling 60+ reviews/month dominated, but rankings 'fell off a cliff' during an 18-day pause. This is a larger-N independent corroborator of the velocity spine — and the 18-day figure sharpens round 1's ~3-week cliff estimate.
allClaims.stat: 8,186 businesses / 200 cities; 18-day pause = ranking cliff
allClaims.snippet: The number of reviews you've gotten this month matters more than your total number of reviews... a dental client with 60+ reviews a month dominated rankings, but their rankings fell off a cliff during an 18-day pause.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (8,186-business correlation analysis) + observed client case

allClaims.claim: Sterling Sky's same 8,186-business study independently confirms that reviews with written TEXT outperform star-only ratings for local ranking, and that hiding a business address negatively correlates with pack ranking. Corroborates round 1's 'nudge written reviews' request-flow design from a larger independent dataset.
allClaims.stat: text reviews > star-only; address-hiding hurts ranking
allClaims.snippet: reviews with actual text had a stronger impact on rankings... a negative correlation between hiding your address and ranking well in the local pack.

allClaims.claim: Roofing-vertical benchmark (study of 34,111 US roofing GMB profiles): the average roofing contractor has just 22 reviews, 49.29% have 4 or fewer, and 23.19% have ZERO reviews. The bar is low — a steady velocity machine clears the field fast. Average roofing star rating is 4.5 (4.6 for those with 5+ reviews).
allClaims.stat: avg 22 reviews; 49.29% have <=4; 23.19% have 0; 4.5 stars avg
allClaims.snippet: 34,111 Google My Business profiles for roofing companies in the United States... 22 - The average number of reviews for a roofing contractor... 49.29% of roofing contractors have 4 or fewer reviews... 23.19% of roofing contractors have 0 reviews... average 4.5-star rating.

allClaims.claim: The FTC final rule (effective Oct 21 2024) does NOT ban incentivized review requests outright — it bans only incentives CONDITIONED on a particular sentiment. Offering a small reward for any review is permitted; offering it for a five-star review (or 'tell us how much you loved it') is illegal. The KM ask can carry a neutral incentive if it never conditions on sentiment — important refinement of round 1's blanket 'incentivizing banned' framing.
allClaims.stat: incentives allowed if sentiment-neutral; sentiment-conditioned = illegal
allClaims.snippet: a business that offers customers $5 off a future purchase in exchange for a product review is not inherently unlawful... for that same business to offer customers $5 off a future purchase in exchange for a five-star review (or the equivalent) [is prohibited].

allClaims.claim: Concrete enforcement precedent for the no-gating rail: the FTC fined Fashion Nova $4.2M for suppressing reviews under four stars — proof that review-gating carries real, dollar-quantified federal liability (independent of, and predating, the 2024 rule's per-violation penalties up to ~$51,744). The KM mechanism's universal unscreened ask is the compliant posture.
allClaims.stat: Fashion Nova fined $4.2M for blocking sub-4-star reviews
allClaims.snippet: Fashion Nova was fined $4.2 million for blocking reviews under 4 stars... suppressed negative feedback by not publishing reviews with ratings below four stars.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (FTC enforcement action; figure surfaced via secondary, attributed to FTC)

allClaims.claim: Consumer-side recency demand quantified (GatherUp): 54% of consumers say a review must be a month old or less to impact their decision; +27% accept the past 6 months (81% combined depend on reviews <=6 months old); and 44% are most influenced by a brand's MOST RECENT review. This is the demand-side proof that the velocity drip also drives conversion, not just ranking.
allClaims.stat: 54% want <=1mo; 81% <=6mo; 44% weight the most-recent review
allClaims.snippet: 54% of consumers say that a review must be a month-or-less old for it to impact their decision... An additional 27% consider reviews from the past 6 months to be relevant... 44% of customers are most influenced by your brand's most recent review content.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (consumer survey; vendor-published, flag for incentive)

allClaims.claim: BrightLocal's 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey puts review signals at ~20% of local-pack weight (up from 16% in 2023), and a 4.5-star business can earn up to ~25% more clicks than a 3.5-star one. Confirms reviews are a rising — but bounded — lever; KM should rank reviews as a top-tier on-page-adjacent signal without over-claiming it as the dominant factor.
allClaims.stat: reviews ~20% of pack weight (was 16%); 4.5 vs 3.5 stars = ~25% more clicks
allClaims.snippet: Reviews have grown in importance for local pack rankings, from 16% in 2023 to 20% today... A company with a 4.5-star average can earn up to 25% more clicks compared to one with a 3.5 rating.

pillars.title: Other one-time levers
pillars.section:
## L6 — Other One-Time Levers

**Bottom line.** Beyond the site itself, a launch can ship a fixed bundle of one-time off-page assets. Two of them move organic dominance and are near-deterministic to deliver: a GBP optimization kit (correct primary category + all relevant additional categories + every service + a seeded real-job photo set) and credential-gated relevance links (manufacturer find-a-pro directory, chamber/sponsorship directory). One has the highest ceiling but is *earned, not guaranteed*: reactive digital PR. And one is table-stakes hygiene only, not a rank-mover: directory citations + aggregator NAP. We promise the floor — the assets ship — and project the ceiling as a range.

**The GBP optimization kit is the highest-leverage controllable lever, and it is one-time.** The primary GBP category is the consensus #1 local-pack ranking factor in Whitespark's expert survey, six years running, and the wrong primary category is the single most impactful *negative* factor ([whitespark.ca/google-business-profile-guide/categories](https://whitespark.ca/google-business-profile-guide/categories/)). On Whitespark's tier list, primary category sits in S-tier with reviews; photos and additional categories sit in A-tier; the description and Q&A have no ranking impact and are honest to set as conversion-only ([whitespark.ca tier list](https://whitespark.ca/blog/how-to-outrank-99-of-local-competitors-google-business-profile-tier-list/)). These weights are *modeled* — opinion-aggregation from a survey, not a measured correlation study — so the claim is "we ship the consensus #1 controllable lever," never "this guarantees a rank lift." Photos carry a widely-cited Google-attributed engagement lift (≈42% more direction requests, ≈35% more clicks), but that figure could not be pinned to a live Google-owned URL — treat it as directional, not first-party-verified ([whitespark.ca/google-business-profile-guide/photos-videos](https://whitespark.ca/google-business-profile-guide/photos-videos/)). Scope discipline: only the *one-time* optimization is in scope. Review velocity and posting cadence are client-owned and ongoing — out of L6, never sold as a KM deliverable.

**Credential-gated relevance links are the near-deterministic equity lever.** The GAF certified-contractor directory (GAF = North America's largest roofing manufacturer) is the highest-relevance roofer link because it is on-topic *and* credential-gated — it cannot be bought as a raw link ([gaf.com/roofing-contractors](https://www.gaf.com/en-us/roofing-contractors/residential)). Chamber-of-commerce membership and local sponsorship directories add permanent, hyper-local, dofollow links where local relevance can outweigh raw domain authority ([linkdoctor.io/local-link-building-2](https://linkdoctor.io/local-link-building-2/)). These feed the *organic* spine: links contribute ≈19% of local ranking after on-page and GBP, and far more to organic than to the proximity-capped pack ([linkdoctor.io, citing Moz](https://linkdoctor.io/local-link-building-2/)).

**Reactive digital PR is the highest ceiling — but earned, not guaranteed.** KM ships the *assets* (pitch templates, an expert-quote bank, a local storm/replacement-cost data angle, a HARO/Featured source profile) — placement depends on a journalist choosing it. Editorial links land at DR 70–90+ in a 4–24h news window ([reporteroutreach.com/blog/newsjacking](https://www.reporteroutreach.com/blog/newsjacking) — vendor-incentive), and data-driven campaigns earn a median 24 backlinks vs 8 for non-data (Fractl — [frac.tl/hiring-digital-pr-agency](https://www.frac.tl/hiring-digital-pr-agency/), vendor-incentive). HARO is free again under Featured since April 2025 ([mentionagent.ai/blog/haro-alternatives](https://mentionagent.ai/blog/haro-alternatives/)). Frame this as an asset + outreach machinery with an *earned* outcome — floor is the asset shipping, not a placement.

**Citations are hygiene, not a rank-mover — say so.** A one-time core submission (top 30–50 directories + the three data aggregators: Foursquare, Data Axle, TransUnion/Localeze) is foundational and does *not* need recurring fees for a single-location business — Darren Shaw: "get the work done and just be done with it" ([whitespark.ca/blog/do-citations-matter-local-seo](https://whitespark.ca/blog/do-citations-matter-local-seo/)). But several top independent experts call citations "almost a non-factor" today, and mass citation-building is counterproductive — ~50 at once produced no pack lift and duplicate listings get deindexed ([ricketyroo.com/blog/do-citations-still-matter-local-seo](https://ricketyroo.com/blog/do-citations-still-matter-local-seo/)). Position the citation set as clean, consistent, indexed NAP hygiene — a quality core, never a count of hundreds.

**Hard exclusions — no gray-hat.** Google's spam policy prohibits buying/selling links, excessive exchanges, automated link creation, and PBN/link-farm/guest-post networks; paid or placed links must carry `rel="sponsored"`/`rel="nofollow"` ([developers.google.com spam-policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)). The seed's "scholarship links" and "PR-with-optimized-anchors" fall under the same prohibition — earned PR links use natural/branded anchors, never money-keyword anchors. GBP business-*name* keyword stuffing is also out: Google removed thousands of listings in 2024 and now auto-flags it ([birdeye.com/blog/google-business-profile-guidelines-2025](https://birdeye.com/blog/google-business-profile-guidelines-2025/)). We optimize the category, not the name. Never PBNs, link farms, expired-domain links, or paid dofollow links.

**One-time vs ongoing.** In scope (one-time, shippable): GBP optimization kit, manufacturer + chamber/sponsorship directory links, PR/HARO asset pack, core citation + aggregator submission. Out of scope (ongoing, client-owned): review velocity, GBP posts, recurring link campaigns.

**Dofollow/equity vs citation.** Equity (dofollow, rank-moving): manufacturer directory, chamber, most sponsorship pages, earned editorial PR. Citation (NAP consistency, often nofollow, hygiene-only): the aggregator/directory set; many trust-badge directories (e.g. BBB) are nofollow and not direct ranking factors.

**Approximate one-time cost.** Chamber membership ~$300–600/yr; local sponsorships ~$250–1,000 each; manufacturer certification is credential-driven (labor, not a link fee); core citation set ~$4–per-listing tier (Whitespark) or labor; PR/HARO assets are labor. Low hundreds to low thousands one-time, depending on the sponsorship tier chosen.

**Impact vs effort.** Highest impact / lowest effort: GBP primary category + categories (modeled #1, near-zero effort). High impact / low effort: manufacturer + chamber directory links (deterministic equity). Highest ceiling / highest variance: reactive PR (earned). Lowest impact / do-once-and-stop: citations (hygiene). Spend effort top-down that list.

**What NOT to oversell:** the GBP weights are a modeled expert survey, not measured rank lift; the 42%/35% photo stat is Google-attributed but not first-party-verified; PR/HARO placements are earned and never guaranteed; citations are hygiene, not a ranking lever — never promise a count of hundreds; and no PBN, link-scheme, optimized-anchor, or name-stuffing tactic ships, ever.

loadBearing.claim: The primary GBP category is the consensus #1 local-pack ranking factor and a one-time shippable configuration asset; the wrong primary category is the single most impactful negative factor. KM ships the correct primary + all relevant additional categories as a launch GBP-optimization kit.
loadBearing.stat: Primary GBP category ranked #1 local-pack factor (Whitespark expert survey, 6 years running); wrong primary category = #1 negative factor
loadBearing.snippet: the #1 most important local search ranking factor ... [2026 Local Search Ranking Factors report]
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Anchors the offer's single highest-leverage one-time off-page deliverable; goes on the pitch slide as 'the consensus #1 controllable lever.'

loadBearing.claim: Google's spam policy prohibits link schemes — buying/selling links, excessive exchanges, automated link creation, PBNs/link farms/guest-post networks — so KM never ships gray-hat links; paid/placed links must use rel=sponsored or rel=nofollow.
loadBearing.stat: Prohibited: buying/selling links, excessive exchanges, automated link creation; paid links require rel=sponsored/nofollow
loadBearing.snippet: Buying or selling links for ranking purposes... Excessive link exchanges... Using automated programs or services to create links to your site... qualified with a rel="nofollow" or rel="sponsored" attribute
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The FTC-exposed compliance backbone of the pillar — defines what KM will NOT do; protects the offer from being a link-scheme liability. Verbatim-confirmed against the live Google page this pass.

loadBearing.claim: Manufacturer find-a-pro directories (GAF, largest NA roofing manufacturer) are a credential-gated, on-topic one-time link asset — the highest-relevance roofer link because it is topical AND not buyable as a raw link. KM ships the certified-directory listing in the launch kit.
loadBearing.stat: GAF = North America's largest roofing manufacturer; public crawlable contractor directory keyed by ZIP/state
loadBearing.snippet: Find a residential roofing contractor near you ... GAF is North America's largest roofing manufacturer.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The near-deterministic dofollow equity lever — the part of the earned-link story KM can actually promise as a floor, distinct from earned PR which is not guaranteed.

loadBearing.claim: A one-time core citation + aggregator submission is foundational hygiene, NOT a rank-mover, and does not require recurring fees for a single-location business — per independent local-SEO authority Darren Shaw.
loadBearing.stat: One-time, no recurring fee for single-location; top 30-50 directories is the value band
loadBearing.snippet: "I also don't think you need to pay recurring fees for listings, unless you are a multi-location operation with 100 plus locations" ... "you can get the work done and just be done with it"
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Keeps the offer honest — citations are positioned as table-stakes hygiene, never sold as an organic rank lever. Prevents an FTC-exposed over-claim and the counterproductive volume play.

loadBearing.claim: Reactive digital PR / data-study assets have the highest link ceiling (DR 70-90+ editorial, median 24 vs 8 backlinks for data campaigns) but the links are EARNED — KM ships the asset + outreach machinery, not a guaranteed placement.
loadBearing.stat: Editorial links DR 70-90+; data-driven campaigns median 24 backlinks vs 8 non-data (~3x)
loadBearing.snippet: data-driven campaigns earn a median of 24 backlinks per campaign, compared to 8 for non-data campaigns
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The 'highest ceiling' lever in the offer — must be framed as earned with a real floor (asset ships) to avoid promising placements KM can't guarantee. Both figures are vendor-incentive benchmarks needing the earned-not-guaranteed caveat.

whatNotToOversell: GBP per-element weights (primary category #1, S/A/D tiers) are a MODELED expert-survey aggregation, not a measured correlation study — label modeled, never claim a guaranteed rank lift from the kit.

The 42%/35% GBP-photo engagement stat is Google-attributed and industry-ubiquitous but could NOT be pinned to a live Google-owned URL this pass — present as 'Google-attributed, directional,' not first-party-verified.

PR / newsjacking / HARO / sponsorship-press links are EARNED — placement depends on a journalist or organizer; promise the asset + machinery, never the placement. The DR 70-90+ and median-24 figures are best-case vendor-incentive benchmarks.

Citations are hygiene, not a ranking lever — multiple top independent experts call them 'almost a non-factor.' Never center them as an organic-dominance driver and never promise a count of hundreds of listings (mass building is counterproductive; duplicates get deindexed).
GBP is client-owned/ongoing — only the one-time optimization (categories, services, seed photos, setup) is shippable; do not over-promise managed reviews/posts as a KM deliverable.

NO gray-hat, ever: no PBNs, link farms, expired-domain links, paid dofollow links, scholarship-link schemes, optimized-anchor placed links, or GBP business-name keyword stuffing — all are Google spam-policy violations and FTC/suspension exposure.

verdicts.claim: The map pack ranks from a business's verified physical address, not its listed service area — the service-area setting is visual only and has no ranking impact. This anchors each office's pack reach to one geographic point.

verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (case study); corroborated by Google first-party docs (support.google.com/business/answer/7091)
verdicts.externalSignal: Sterling Sky's cited page resolves live and contains the captured snippet verbatim ("the ranking is based on the address at which the business verified the listing. The only impact that the service area has is visual"), backed by their own empirical GBP test (Toronto service area, ranks from Uxbridge physical address). Independently corroborated by Whitespark ("service areas have no impact on rankings at all... their ranking radius will be based on the address that they originally verified their business at") and multiple SEO agencies (Rio SEO, OllyOlly, etc.) — unanimous practitioner consensus.
verdicts.counterEvidence: No source refutes the core claim. The only bounding nuance (from Whitespark): the anchor is the ORIGINALLY VERIFIED address, not the currently-displayed one — relevant when a business relocates and hides its new address, in which case proximity reverts to the old verification point. This refines rather than contradicts the claim; it actually strengthens the "anchored to one geographic point" thesis. No source claims the service-area setting carries ranking weight.
verdicts.reasoning: URL health: cited Sterling Sky page is live and directly supports the stat+claim, with the captured snippet present verbatim and supported by their own empirical experiment. Self-consistency across 3 stances all converge: (a) skeptic — this is from independent local-SEO authorities, not a vendor selling the setting, and the conclusion (service area does NOT help rank) cuts against any upsell incentive; (b) literalist — exact wording "the only impact that the service area has is visual" matches the snippet character-for-character; (c) practitioner — replicates across Sterling Sky, Whitespark, Rio SEO, OllyOlly, and others with zero dissent, a supermajority well past the "high" threshold. Snippet faithfulness: faithful, verbatim, not stretched. The King Maker pillar's load-bearing inference — that each office's pack reach is anchored to one geographic point (the verified address), making proximity a ceiling — is sound and directly entailed by the sources. Verdict: survived, High confidence. Minor optional precision: "verified physical address" is more exactly "the address at which the listing was originally verified."

verdicts.claim: Google's November 2021 'Vicinity' update — its largest local algorithm change since 2017 — increased proximity weight and shrank the pack's radius of visibility, making it harder for one location to rank in the 3-pack outside its home city.
verdicts.stat: rolled out Nov 30–Dec 8, 2021; biggest local update since 2017; radius of visibility reduced
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (confirmed algorithm update + observed ranking shifts)
verdicts.externalSignal: Cited source (Sterling Sky / Joy Hawkins, the analyst who first documented and named the update) is LIVE and directly supports every element: rollout "began Nov 30 and ran through Dec 8" (2021); "the biggest change I have seen to the local SERPs since the Hawk update in 2017"; "I believe that this was an update that impacted proximity, making it weight heavier"; "map packs have shrunk, are way more zoomed in." Independently corroborated by BrightLocal (named it "Google's Biggest Local Search Algorithm Update in Five Years"), Search Engine Land (winners/losers analysis; found primary business locations took a greater hit), RioSEO, and Partoo — all describing increased proximity weighting and shrunken/more-zoomed packs.
verdicts.counterEvidence: No source refutes the core claim. The only nuances: (1) one aggregated search result flagged a minor sourcing discrepancy — some commentators frame Possum (2016) as when proximity weighting first spiked — but the cited source itself benchmarks "since the Hawk update in 2017," so the claim is faithful to its citation. (2) BrightLocal's empirical study did NOT directly measure "proximity weight" or "harder to rank outside home city"; it measured the GBP keyword-name-spam dimension (keyword-rich names dropped ~7.9 places). This bounds the claim's mechanism (proximity was one of several rebalanced factors, not the sole lever) but does not contradict it — Google's own confirmation called it "a rebalancing of various factors."
verdicts.reasoning: (a) Skeptic-for-vendor-spin: the cited source is a recognized independent local-SEO authority (Sterling Sky), not the client's own marketing; its claims are echoed by multiple unaffiliated firms and Google's own confirmation tweet — not spin. (b) Literalist: rollout dates (Nov 30–Dec 8, 2021) match verbatim; "biggest local update since 2017" matches the source's Hawk-2017 benchmark verbatim; "shrunk the pack / increased proximity weight" match the source's wording. The captured snippet's specific phrase "much harder to rank in the 3-pack for locations outside their home city" is a faithful synthesis of the source's substance ("businesses... able to rank very far away from their office. That doesn't appear to be the case anymore") rather than a single verbatim line, but does not overstate. (c) Practitioner replication: the effect replicates across BrightLocal, Search Engine Land, RioSEO, Partoo, and Google's confirmation — supermajority agreement, no credible debunking. Verdict: survived at High confidence; measured (real SERP observation + a published empirical study), not modeled.

verdicts.claim: Pack ranking decays exponentially with distance from the anchor, with a sharp first-mile cliff averaging ~8 positions dropped in the first mile across ~1,100 firms sampled in 50 cities.
verdicts.stat: exponential decay (lambda≈2.3); ~-8 positions in the first mile; n≈1,100 across 50 cities; 15x15 grid at 10mi
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (geo-grid study); radius-to-miles is directional, density-dependent
verdicts.externalSignal: The cited Rankings.io proximity data study (https://rankings.io/data-studies/proximity-data-study/) resolves live and verbatim supports every figure: WebFetch confirmed "On average, the drop in ranking in the first mile is -8 positions," "The decay constant λ estimated by the fit is 2.3," n=1,100 (20 firms x 50 cities), and "225 locations on a 15×15 grid" at a 10-mile radius. The same figures are reproduced independently in Rankings.io's companion blog and summarized by third parties (Search Atlas, Search Engine Land, eSEOspace, Digital Harvest).
verdicts.counterEvidence: Bounding, not refuting: (1) Single-study, single-vertical — the dataset is exclusively personal injury LAWYERS, not contractors or "firms" generally; the claim's word "firms" elides this. (2) The -8 and lambda=2.3 are parameters of an exponential curve FIT, and the authors note they assigned an arbitrary value of 25 to all "20+" rankings to make the fit computable, which mechanically shapes DropFinal/lambda. (3) City variance is enormous (27% to 92% of firms dropping out of top 20 by 14mi), so the single averaged lambda hides large heterogeneity — no independent dataset replicates lambda=2.3 specifically. (4) Other studies (Search Atlas via Kayla Rose Hall) put distance at ~72% of ranking variance across all positions but show rating quality (~49%) overtaking proximity inside the top 10, so "proximity ceiling" is real but not monotone-dominant at the top.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: live and directly supportive — not dead, not fabricated. Every quantitative element of the captured snippet (first-mile -8, exponential decay, lambda=2.3, n~1,100, 50 cities, 15x15 grid at 10mi) was independently re-confirmed against the live page via WebFetch. SELF-CONSISTENCY across three stances: (a) Skeptic/vendor-spin — Rankings.io is a vendor with an interest in the proximity narrative, BUT the figures are mechanically transparent (grid method, raw parameters, per-city tables published), and third parties cite the same numbers, so it is not unfalsifiable spin. (b) Literalist — the exact numbers match to the decimal (lambda 2.3, Drop0 -2.1, DropFinal -11.9, -8 first-mile). The one literal slip is "firms" vs the actual cohort "personal injury law firms," and "exponentially" is correctly characterized. (c) Practitioner/replication — the GENERAL phenomenon (sharp first-mile cliff, distance-decay, proximity dominating ranking variance) replicates across multiple independent sources (Search Atlas, SEL, eSEOspace); the SPECIFIC lambda=2.3 does not have an independent reproduction and is a single-vertical model. Supermajority of stances support the claim as stated -> High confidence on the figures as faithfully sourced. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: faithful, not a stretch — the snippet is a near-verbatim transcription of the source's own sentences. COUNTER-SOURCE: the strongest bound is the Search Atlas / Kayla Rose Hall study showing rating quality overtakes proximity inside the top 10 (proximity ~72% of variance overall but not dominant at the very top), which bounds the universality of a "proximity ceiling" without refuting the first-mile decay. NET: claim survives — accurate transcription of a real, live primary source. The honest framing caveat for downstream use: it is ONE modeled study on PI lawyers, so present lambda=2.3/-8-per-mile as "a published proximity study found," not as a universal constant, and consider noting the vertical.

verdicts.claim: The pack captures a large but not dominant share of local clicks — organic out-clicks the pack (~44-51% organic vs ~29-32% pack) in a controlled 5,500-tester study.
verdicts.stat: pack 28.8% (LSAs present) / 32.3% (absent); organic 43.9% / 50.8%; n=5,500
verdicts.externalSignal: Cited BrightLocal "Local Services Ads Click Study" page is live and supports EVERY figure verbatim: Local Pack 28.8% / Organic 43.9% (LSAs present); Local Pack 32.3% / Organic 50.8% (LSAs absent); 5,500+ testers; 5 SAB categories (garage door, painting, locksmith, plumbers, towing) in San Francisco; "organic results receive the most clicks of all SERP types." Independently echoed by onthemap.com and Local Search Forum. COUNTER-SIGNAL: a widely-circulated near-mirror-inverse stat — Local 3-Pack 44% / organic 29% (traced to ~2015 Moz/static-SERP click study) — and the independent iLawyerMarketing first-click study (n=1,001) finding LSAs 42% / Pack 29% / Organic 22%, where the pack OUT-clicks organic.
verdicts.counterEvidence: The "44% local pack / 29% organic" figure (Moz 2015, restated by Locafy/RedLocal/direction.com and many others) is the near-exact inverse of BrightLocal's ordering and is at least as widely cited in the industry. The independent iLawyerMarketing click study (n=1,001 shown a static SERP image, asked for first click) found Pack 29% out-clicking Organic 22%. So "organic out-clicks the pack" does NOT replicate across methodologies — it holds in BrightLocal's live-SERP behavioral test of SAB categories, but reverses in static-image first-click studies and is query-type dependent (pack wins transactional/proximity intent). The numbers cited are accurate; the GENERALIZED inference drawn from them is contested.
verdicts.reasoning: The stat itself is bulletproof: the cited URL resolves and supports every number, the sample size, the geography, and the categories exactly as written — no fabrication, no inflation, faithful snippet, faithful "controlled 5,500-tester" description (real users, live SERPs, first-click). On the literal + URL-health axes this is a clean survive. It is downgraded to FLAGGED (not survived) because the claim does not merely report the figure — it leverages it as a general truth ("the pack captures a large but not dominant share; organic out-clicks the pack"). That generalization rests on a SINGLE vendor study (BrightLocal, ~2018, one city, SAB verticals) and is directly contradicted by an equally-cited body of work (the Moz-2015-lineage "44% pack / 29% organic" figure and the independent iLawyerMarketing first-click study) where the pack out-clicks organic. The divergence is methodological — live behavioral multi-SERP testing vs. static-image first-click — and intent-dependent. Not corrected (the numbers are right and there is no single better replacement figure; the literature genuinely splits), not killed (source is live and supportive). The honest posture: cite this number as "in one controlled BrightLocal study of SAB categories" — do NOT present "organic out-clicks the pack" as a settled, universal finding, because a well-known counter-study inverts it.

verdicts.claim: Google's organic algorithm is materially less proximity-constrained than Maps, so organic pages can rank in a city the business services but is not physically located in; the pack is the more proximity-bound surface.
verdicts.stat: qualitative structural distinction; Sterling Sky 2025: proximity 'less influential than in the past' on organic
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (longitudinal listing study) + directional (datapins corroboration at datapins.com/seo-for-multiple-cities)
verdicts.externalSignal: Independent corroboration of the CORE proposition from multiple reputable local-SEO authorities: BrightLocal ("It's nearly impossible to get into the local pack for a city in which you don't have an office. However, you can rank #1 in the organic results for your surrounding neighborhoods and cities"); Whitespark (dedicated city landing pages rank service-area businesses organically in cities with no physical address); Jurisdigital's 138-zip Houston study ("The closer your firm is to the searcher, the more likely Google will show your business in the local pack") which explicitly recommends organic as the complementary surface for broader geographic reach. The cited Sterling Sky 2025 page (Joy Hawkins, Aug 26 2025) live-verified to contain "Proximity still affects organic rankings, but is less influential than in the past."
verdicts.counterEvidence: The SPECIFIC captured snippet is an imperfect/partially-contradictory support. The cited Sterling Sky page's 2022 key takeaway, verified verbatim, is: "proximity had a stronger impact on rankings in the localized organic results than in the Local Pack results." On the INTENSITY-of-proximity-as-a-rank-ordering-factor axis, that finding runs OPPOSITE to the claim's "the pack is the more proximity-bound surface." The 2025 update also does not provide a direct organic-vs-pack proximity comparison, and the page never states that organic lets you rank in a serviced-but-not-located city more than the pack does — that supporting evidence comes from OTHER sources, not the cited URL.
verdicts.reasoning:
URL HEALTH: live and supports the narrow stat it is cited for — the Sterling Sky 2025 page (Joy Hawkins, Aug 26 2025) does say proximity is "less influential than in the past" on organic. So urlHealth = live-supports, not dead/fabricated.

The claim conflates two distinct axes and the evidence splits on them:
(1) REACH/RADIUS axis — "organic pages can rank in a city the business services but is not located in; the pack is the more proximity-bound surface." This is the claim's operative business proposition and it is SETTLED local-SEO consensus, independently corroborated by BrightLocal, Whitespark, and the Jurisdigital Houston grid study. Strongly TRUE.
(2) INTENSITY axis — proximity's strength as a rank-ordering input WITHIN each surface. Here the exact snippet the claim cites actually reports the REVERSE for 2022 (proximity affected localized-organic MORE than the Local Pack). The 2025 study softened proximity on organic but did not re-run the direct organic-vs-pack comparison.

Three stances: (a) skeptic — no vendor spin; sources are independent authorities, claim is qualitative not a fabricated number. (b) literalist — the headline cited stat is faithful, but the specific 2022 sub-finding in the snippet contradicts the claim on the intensity axis; the snippet does NOT cleanly say "pack is more proximity-bound." (c) practitioner — the reach proposition replicates across multiple independent sources and is the version that matters operationally.

Net: the CONCLUSION holds on independent evidence (would be "survived"), but the cited source + captured snippet are an imperfect support — one of the snippet's own findings runs opposite, and the strongest corroboration lives in sources OTHER than the cited URL. That citation-hygiene gap is exactly what an adversarial pass must surface, so verdict = flagged (not killed: the operative claim is true and well-supported; not corrected: the claim text needs no factual replacement, only a better/added citation). Recommend re-anchoring this pillar to BrightLocal/Whitespark/Jurisdigital for the reach proposition and reserving the Sterling Sky page for the narrower "proximity less influential on organic over time" point. Confidence Medium: high on the core proposition, dragged down by the snippet/source mismatch on the precise wording.

verdicts.claim: Google's own first-party definition of the local-pack Prominence ranking factor explicitly counts inbound website links and reviews as inputs — making web/organic authority a stated Google local-ranking factor.
verdicts.stat: Prominence is 1 of 3 named ranking factors (relevance, distance, prominence); inputs named verbatim: 'how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have.'
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: directional (Google first-party definition; named input, not a measured weight)
verdicts.externalSignal: Google's own first-party help page (support.google.com/business/answer/7091) returned LIVE via WebFetch with the exact verbatim wording: "Prominence means how well-known a business is... This factor's also based on info like how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have. More reviews and positive ratings can help your business's local ranking." verdicts.counterEvidence: No counter-source refutes the existence of the factor. The only bounding point: Google does NOT quantify the weight of links/reviews — the popular "prominence ~= 60% of the algorithm" figures cited by third parties (Local Dominator, devtrios) are MODELED industry estimates, not Google's first-party statement. The claim avoids this trap by only asserting "1 of 3 named factors" and quoting verbatim inputs, which is exactly what the doc says. A pedantic literalist note: the doc says links/reviews are "info like" prominence is "based on" — i.e. illustrative examples, not an exhaustive or weighted list — but it does explicitly name both, so the claim's framing ("explicitly counts inbound website links and reviews as inputs") holds.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: cited source resolves live and contains the captured snippet verbatim — confirmed via WebFetch (firecrawl out of credits). SELF-CONSISTENCY across three stances: (a) Skeptic-assumes-vendor-spin — this is NOT vendor spin; the source IS Google's own first-party documentation, the strongest possible authority for "is this a stated Google factor," so skeptic concern is neutralized. (b) Literalist checking exact wording — the snippet matches the live page word-for-word, and the claim's structure (relevance/distance/prominence as the 3 named factors; links + reviews named as prominence inputs) is exactly Google's text; the claim does not overstate by attaching a weight. (c) Practitioner asking does-it-replicate — yes, replicates across 8+ independent local-SEO sources that uniformly cite the same three pillars and name links/reviews under prominence. Supermajority (effectively unanimous) → High. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: faithful, not a stretch — the snippet directly states links and reviews as prominence inputs. The claim's interpretive leap ("making web/organic authority a stated Google local-ranking factor") is sound: inbound website links and a website-hosted review presence are web/organic-authority signals, and prominence is explicitly one of Google's three stated factors. Verdict: survived at High confidence. The only honesty guardrail to carry forward: do NOT let downstream copy attach the "60%" prominence weight to GOOGLE — that number is modeled, not Google-stated.

verdicts.claim: A more prominent/authoritative business can outrank physically-closer competitors and rank across a WIDER geographic radius — the radius-dilation mechanism, stated mechanistically, not as a measured miles-per-link figure.
verdicts.stat: No numeric radius; directional — specialized/authoritative businesses 'rank across a wider radius' and 'a business slightly farther away but significantly more prominent and relevant can still outrank a closer competitor.'
verdicts.externalSignal: Google's own Google Business Profile Help (support.google.com/business/answer/7091) states the mechanism first-party: "our algorithms might decide that a business that's farther away from your location is more likely to have what you're looking for than a business that's closer, and therefore rank it higher in local results," and defines Prominence as "how well-known a business is. Prominent places are more likely to show up in search results." Independently quoted by Search Engine Journal. The cited Search Engine Land page resolves live and contains the captured snippet verbatim ("If your business has built up stronger signals of relevance and prominence than competitors who are physically nearer to a searcher, you may succeed at outranking them") plus the radius-dilation language ("you may find yourself ranking across a significantly wider radius").
verdicts.counterEvidence: Two bounds, neither refuting the claim: (1) The cited source is vendor content — Search Engine Land is Semrush-owned and the page is authored by a paid contributor (Miriam Ellis), so it is not independent editorial. This is mitigated entirely by Google's first-party corroboration. (2) BrightLocal's ranking-factors guide and multiple practitioner sources still describe proximity/distance as "one of the most crucial factors," and the radius-dilation effect is strongest in low-competition areas or for specialized/hard-to-find offerings — i.e. prominence does not universally erase distance. The claim is stated directionally/mechanistically (no miles-per-link number), so these caveats bound the magnitude but do not contradict the mechanism.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: live-supports. The cited Search Engine Land URL resolves and contains the captured snippet word-for-word, plus the concrete restaurant example (20-min-away with more citations/reviews outranking a 3-min-away competitor) and the explicit "ranking across a significantly wider radius" framing. SELF-CONSISTENCY (3 stances, all confirm): (a) Skeptic — the source IS vendor content (Semrush/Miriam Ellis), a real provenance flag, but the mechanism does not rest on vendor spin because it is independently confirmed; (b) Literalist — the claim is explicitly mechanistic with NO numeric radius/miles-per-link figure, so there is nothing numeric to falsify, and the qualitative wording matches the source and Google verbatim; (c) Practitioner — proximity-relevance-prominence as Google's three local-ranking pillars, with prominence/relevance able to overcome distance, is the bedrock replicated consensus across Google's own docs, SEJ, BrightLocal, and the existing KM rubric. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: faithful — the captured snippet is a direct, in-context quote from the live page and accurately conveys the radius-dilation mechanism; no stretch or misattribution. COUNTER-SOURCE: BrightLocal's guide emphasizing distance as "one of the most crucial factors" is the strongest bounding source, but it endorses the same 3-pillar model and does not deny prominence can overcome proximity — it bounds magnitude, not direction. VERDICT: survived at High confidence. The decisive driver is first-party Google documentation stating the exact mechanism, which is the strongest possible corroborator and elevates this above the vendor-source concern. measured_or_modeled = modeled: this is a stated/documented algorithmic mechanism, not an empirically measured effect size — consistent with the claim's own framing ("stated mechanistically, not as a measured miles-per-link figure").

verdicts.claim: The 2026 Whitespark Local Search Ranking Factors survey quantifies the asymmetry: on-page/website signals are weighted ~2x more in Local Organic than in the Local Pack, and links are a top-tier organic factor but minor for the pack.
verdicts.stat: Local Pack: GBP ~32%, on-page ~15%. Local Organic: on-page ~33%, links ~24%. On-page ~2x heavier organically (47 experts, 187 factors, published Nov 6 2025).
verdicts.externalSignal: Two independent third-party recaps report the EXACT figures verbatim: AdviceLocal ("GBP Signals – 32%", "On-Page Signals – 15%" for Local Pack; "On-Page Signals – 33%", "Link Signals – 24%" for Local Organic) and Sam Bretzmann (same Pack/Organic numbers + "47 of the industry's leading local search experts", "187 different factors"). A third source (Harmo) independently corroborates the 47-expert count. The cited whitespark.ca URL resolves live and self-identifies as the "2026 Local Search Ranking Factors Report, Published November 6, 2025" by Darren Shaw.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Minor: the cited URL's percentage tables are JS-rendered and did not surface raw numbers via WebFetch (verified only through independent recaps, not the primary page's own text in this pass). One date discrepancy in a secondary recap (Harmo listed "18/11/2025") vs whitespark.ca's own "November 6, 2025" — the primary source governs, so the claim's date is correct. Sub-claim "links minor for the pack": link signals still carry ~15% in the Local Pack per the recaps, which is non-trivial, so "minor" slightly understates pack link weight — but the asymmetry direction (links far heavier organically at 24% vs pack) holds. Not material enough to flag.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: cited source resolves live, confirmed as the genuine Whitespark 2026 report (Darren Shaw, Nov 6 2025). Not dead/fabricated. SELF-CONSISTENCY: (a) skeptic — vendor authorship is offset by the 47-expert aggregate methodology and identical figures appearing in multiple unaffiliated recaps, no spin detected; (b) literalist — every load-bearing number matches verbatim (Pack GBP 32%/on-page 15%, Organic on-page 33%/links 24%, 47 experts, 187 factors, Nov 6 2025); on-page 33%÷15% = 2.2x, fully supporting "~2x heavier organically"; (c) practitioner — replicates cleanly across AdviceLocal, Sam Bretzmann, and Harmo, a supermajority of independent sources. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: the captured snippet ("Local Pack weights GBP 32% and on-page 15%; Local organic weights on-page 33% and links 24%") is faithful and directly supported. The claim's framing — on-page ~2x heavier in organic, links top-tier organic but minor for pack — is accurate; the only soft spot is "minor for the pack" (pack links ~15%), too small to downgrade. Supermajority external corroboration → survived at High confidence.

verdicts.claim: Named-authority MEASURED case studies (Joy Hawkins / Sterling Sky) that isolated link building show organic and local-pack rankings respond very differently — establishing the asymmetry causally, not by survey opinion.
verdicts.stat: BrightonSEO San Diego 2024 talk: case studies where 'we did nothing but link building' produced 'very different' organic vs local results; 'Links do not impact the organic + local algorithm the same.'
verdicts.externalSignal: The cited brightonseo.com abstract is LIVE and supports the claim verbatim. All four key phrases confirmed exactly on the live page: "never-before-seen case studies", "did nothing but link building", "the results were very different", and "Links do not impact the organic + local algorithm the same." Speaker/attribution (Joy Hawkins, Owner at Sterling Sky), talk title, and event (BrightonSEO San Diego, Nov 19 2024) all match. verdicts.counterEvidence: The only soft spot is the word "causally." However, "did nothing but link building" is precisely a single-variable isolation/intervention framing (manipulate one input, observe divergent outputs), which is exactly the practitioner-grade causal-isolation the claim describes — materially stronger than the "survey opinion" the claim correctly contrasts against. No source was found that refutes the directional finding; the consensus across independent local-SEO sources is that links impact local-organic far more than the local pack. This bounds the claim's strength, not its truth.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: live-supports. The cited primary source (a neutral third-party conference site, not a vendor page) resolves and contains the captured snippet verbatim, with correct named attribution to Joy Hawkins / Sterling Sky. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: faithful — the claim uses exact quotes plus an accurate paraphrase; no misattribution or stretch in the substance. SELF-CONSISTENCY: 3/3 stances converge. Skeptic finds no vendor spin (finding is sourced to a named external authority on a neutral site). Literalist confirms verbatim wording with one minor caveat on "causally." Practitioner confirms broad independent replication of the link/organic-vs-pack asymmetry. The lone caveat (case study vs. formal causal experiment) bounds but does not refute, and notably the claim's core contrast — measured isolation vs. survey opinion — is itself correct, since "did nothing but link building" is an intervention design. Per protocol, a correction requires a named signal proposing a replacement; here no signal contradicts the claim, so it is not corrected. Verdict: survived, High confidence, measured (observational isolation case studies, not modeled).

verdicts.claim: Proximity still gates the pack — the mandatory not-oversell counterweight. The best independent measurement found on-page content correlates only slightly with pack rank, results cluster in a tight radius, and removing the address anchor erases the pack.
verdicts.stat: Sterling Sky: 8,186 businesses / 200 cities; on-page content has only a 'slight correlation' with pack rank; review recency + visible address dominate; hiding the address tanked rankings and made the pack disappear for a keyword.
verdicts.externalSignal: Cited Sterling Sky 2025 "near me" study (Joy Hawkins, w/ Places Scout) resolves live and verbatim supports 3 of the 4 components: "there's a slight correlation between having more substantive words on your page and better local rankings"; "The number of reviews you've gotten this month matters more than your total number of reviews"; "a negative correlation between hiding your address and ranking well in the local pack" (address-hide test: rankings "tanked... freefall," restored on re-add). The two remaining specifics are genuine Sterling Sky findings sourced from two SIBLING articles: (1) pack-disappear — the hidden-address study found "Google showed a local pack when the address was showing, but when the address was hidden, the local pack went away and the entire SERP was organic"; (2) tight-radius clustering — Sterling Sky's 2023 "Local Pack Clustering" (Erin Jones): "Regardless of the size or density of a location, Google consistently clusters map results in this 2:1 pattern... within several miles of each other... isosceles triangle pattern." Independent corroboration: Whitespark 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey (47 experts, vendor-neutral) ranks proximity the #1 local-pack factor and on-page signals only ~19% of pack weight — both consistent with the claim's "proximity gates / on-page is minor" thesis.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Bounding nuances, not refutations: (1) Citation-granularity — the "tight radius clustering" and "pack disappeared for a keyword" specifics do NOT live in the single cited 2025 URL; they trace to two sibling Sterling Sky articles (hiding-address-google-business-ranking and local-pack-clustering-making-sense-of-googles-ranking-patterns). The cited URL alone supports only the content/reviews/address-tanking pieces. (2) Whitespark frames proximity as the strongest factor WITHIN the GBP-signals bucket, not literally the sole gate; the often-cited "proximity ~55%" weight is disputed (the project's own claim library already corrected that figure), so "gates the pack" should be read directionally, not as a fixed percentage. (3) Sterling Sky's own data shows hidden-address effects are inconsistent — some listings unaffected, others vanish — so "removing the address erases the pack" is a representative case, not a universal law.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: cited source is live and directly supports the on-page "slight correlation," review-recency-over-total, and hidden-address negative-correlation components verbatim (confirmed via two independent WebFetch reads; raw curl was 403-walled, WebFetch was the reliable reader). Not dead, not fabricated. SELF-CONSISTENCY (3 stances): (a) skeptic — vendor-authored content study, but named, methodologically explicit (8,186 businesses/200 cities/Places Scout), and directionally matches vendor-neutral consensus, so spin doesn't sink it; (b) literalist — three of four sub-claims are verbatim from the cited page; the other two are verbatim from two sibling Sterling Sky articles, a sourcing-granularity imprecision, not a factual error; (c) practitioner — replicates strongly across independent sources (Whitespark, BrightLocal): proximity = dominant local-pack lever, on-page = minor (~19%). Supermajority -> High. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: the captured snippet is faithful and accurate to the live cited page. COUNTER-SOURCE: best bound is that the claim bundles findings from three related Sterling Sky articles under one URL and that proximity's exact weight is contested — but no source refutes the core thesis that proximity gates the pack while on-page content is a minor local-pack factor. No external signal contradicts the claim, so no correction is warranted; verdict = survived. Note for the corpus (optional, non-blocking): if precise attribution matters, cite all three Sterling Sky URLs — the 2025 "near me" study for content/reviews/address, the hidden-address study for the pack-disappear case, and the 2023 Local Pack Clustering article (Erin Jones) for the tight-radius 2:1 pattern.

verdicts.claim: Increasing internal linking causally lifts organic traffic — a controlled SEO split-test produced a 25% organic uplift across category pages, with both linked-to and linked-from page groups gaining 20%+.
verdicts.stat: 25% organic uplift; both page groups 20%+
verdicts.externalSignal: SearchPilot case study (live, fetched verbatim) confirms the exact figures: "one of our most positive tests to date resulting in a 25% uplift to organic traffic across level two and level three category pages — an additional estimated 9,200 organic sessions a month" and "Both page groups alone also had estimated uplifts in the 20%+ range, which means the increased internal linking also benefited the pages being linked from." Methodology is genuine controlled split-testing (control vs variant pages), which SearchPilot states isolates the effect from seasonality, sitewide changes, Google algorithm updates, and competitor changes. Independent corroboration of the causal direction exists from other studies (InLinks "Do Internal Links Improve Organic Search Traffic?" case study; Zyppy 23M-internal-link study).
verdicts.counterEvidence: The 25% is explicitly framed by the vendor as an outlier ("one of our most positive tests to date"), not a typical result — so it should not be generalized as the expected uplift. Effect sizes vary widely across the same vendor's internal-linking tests: a nearby-location-links test produced only ~7%, and a related-article-links test found "no detectable impact on the recipient pages" (the linked-TO group showed null at adequate sample size; only the donor/linked-FROM pages gained 16% at 95% confidence). Source is the testing vendor itself (commercial interest in showing internal-linking works), and the figures are "estimated" model outputs of their split-test platform, not directly observed session counts. Net: the causal mechanism replicates, but the specific 25% magnitude is a single best-case data point and is not representative of internal-linking lift in general.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: Live; WebFetch returned the cited snippet word-for-word, so the source resolves and directly supports the stat (25% overall, both groups 20%+). SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: Faithful — the captured snippet matches the live page exactly, no misattribution or stretch. SELF-CONSISTENCY across three stances: (a) Skeptic — vendor has commercial bias and labels this its best test ever; numbers are "estimated," so treat 25% as a ceiling not a norm. (b) Literalist — every figure (25%, 9,200 sessions, both groups 20%+) matches verbatim; wording is accurate. (c) Practitioner — SearchPilot uses controlled A/B split-testing, the gold standard for SEO causality (rules out seasonality/algo/competitor noise); the causal direction (more internal links → more organic traffic, benefiting both linked-to and linked-from pages) replicates across independent sources (InLinks, Zyppy). Supermajority (literalist + practitioner strongly affirm; skeptic only bounds magnitude, doesn't refute) → High confidence the claim as stated is true. The claim presents the figure as a specific split-test result (which it accurately is) rather than as a universal expected lift, so it survives as written. The only correction-worthy risk would be if the offer copy generalized 25% as typical — which it does not — hence survived, not corrected. Caveat for downstream use: cite it as a best-case controlled result, and pair with the broader "20%+ for both linked-to and linked-from groups" mechanism rather than leaning on the headline 25% as a promise.

verdicts.claim: Internal links to nearby location pages causally lift the linked-to location pages — directly relevant to a multi-city roofing silo cascade.
verdicts.stat: 7% organic uplift on location pages
verdicts.externalSignal: SearchPilot case study page resolves live and verbatim states "This corresponded to a 7% uplift in organic traffic." It describes a controlled SEO split test: a customer with ~8,000 regional USA pages added internal links to the 6 nearest geographic regions in a variant group (avg +12 internal links/page); the variant pages that received new links showed a statistically-tested ~7% organic-traffic improvement vs control/forecast (confidence-interval methodology), prompting them to roll the link blocks out to all location pages. Independent secondary write-up (digitalmarketingsupermarket.com) reproduces the same 7% finding and test description.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Bounding caveats, not refutations: (1) This is a SINGLE vendor's SINGLE test on one client site — n=1, and the same vendor (SearchPilot) publishes internal-linking tests with mixed/null/negative results (e.g. "does reducing the height of an internal linking block improve organic traffic", "can displaying links to popular destinations improve SEO"), so 7% is not a universal constant. (2) The tested corpus was ~8,000 regional/listing-type pages (real-estate/jobs archetype), NOT roofing service-area pages; the 7% magnitude is context-specific. The transfer to a "multi-city roofing silo" rests on the shared MECHANISM (delivering link equity to equity-starved location pages), which is sound, but the specific number should not be promised for a roofing site. No source was found that refutes the directional/causal finding itself.
verdicts.reasoning: Skeptic (vendor-spin): SearchPilot sells SEO split-testing software, so it self-selects publishable wins — but the page transparently documents methodology (control vs variant, forecast + confidence interval) and the same vendor publishes losing tests, which cuts against pure cherry-picking. Literalist: the captured snippet "This corresponded to a 7% uplift in organic traffic" matches the live page word-for-word; "7% uplift on location pages" is accurate. Practitioner/replication: the causal direction (internal links lift equity-starved location pages) is mainstream, well-replicated SEO consensus and a logical fit for a multi-city roofing silo cascade; only the exact 7% is single-source. Supermajority of stances support the claim AS WORDED (it says "directly relevant," not "yields 7% on roofing"). Snippet is faithful, not a stretch. Verdict: survived, High confidence — with the honest framing that 7% is a measured single-test result whose magnitude is illustrative, not a guaranteed roofing outcome.

Self-consistency: literalist confirms every number; practitioner finds directional replication in BrightLocal (reviews heavily drive local-pack clicks); skeptic correctly flags it as a narrow, vendor-run, single-query click-test. Supermajority supports the claim, so it survives — but confidence is Medium not High because it rests primarily on one vendor click-test in one vertical, and the best independent corroborator (BrightLocal) cautions that position still dominates rather than endorsing a blanket "position doesn't determine clicks." Use the claim as measured-from-a-study evidence that reviews can override position within the local pack, not as a universal rule. No correction needed: figures and mechanism are accurate as stated.

verdicts.claim: Proximity to the searcher is the dominant pack factor and the one a business cannot directly improve — a closer competitor wins at a given location, structurally capping a fresh profile's pack reach to a bubble around its office.
verdicts.stat: Proximity = top/dominant pack factor; 'not much a business can do to target this pillar'
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: directional (authority guidance, consistent with Google's distance/relevance/prominence framework)

verdicts.counterEvidence: The single best bounding source — Search Engine Land's "proximity paradox" guide — and the Search Atlas top-10 breakdown both show the claim's edge is softer than a hard cap: (a) at competitive top-10 positions proximity's share drops to ~36.2% while review count rises to ~26%, so proximity is "dominant overall" but not uniformly dominant at the contested top; (b) stronger relevance/prominence "may" expand the ranking radius ~3-5 miles and beat a nearer competitor in low-competition or specialized cases. None of this refutes the core — every counter-source still affirms proximity is fixed/cannot be directly improved and imposes a real geographic ceiling — it only bounds "dominant" and confirms the offset is partial, which the claim already concedes ("bubble," "structurally capping").
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: The cited Whitespark guide resolves and genuinely supports the snippet and claim — it names relevance/distance/prominence as the three pillars, states a business "even a little outside that border" may not be deemed relevant to inside searchers, and explicitly says moving or opening a second location "is the only option that will make this disadvantage completely disappear; everything else is an attempt to work around Google's bias" — i.e., proximity cannot be directly improved. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: faithful, not a stretch; the captured snippet maps directly onto "a closer competitor wins at a given location" and "cannot directly improve." SELF-CONSISTENCY across 3 stances: (a) Skeptic — the 55% is Whitespark's own survey, but the independent Search Atlas ML study lands on proximity = 55.2% and "strongest driver of visibility," defeating the vendor-spin objection via methodological convergence; (b) Literalist — "cannot directly improve" is literally accurate; "dominant" is supported for OVERALL visibility (top feature globally) though it softens to ~36% at top-10 positions — a nuance, not a falsification; (c) Practitioner — replicates across Whitespark, Search Atlas, BrightLocal, Local Falcon, Search Engine Land, Rankings.io (supermajority). COUNTER-SOURCE: the strongest refutation attempt (SEL proximity paradox) still concedes location is fixed and only "partially" offsettable with a real ceiling. Net: supermajority + independent measured corroboration + a faithful live source = survived at High confidence. The claim's hedged framing ("bubble," "structurally capping," "directly improve") is exactly the calibration the evidence supports.

verdicts.claim: Organic results out-click the local pack and organic #1 alone out-pulls the entire pack #1 slot — organic is the larger, distance-unconstrained reach surface.
verdicts.stat: Organic 50.8% / Pack 32.3% (no LSAs); Organic 43.9% / Pack 28.8% (with LSAs); Organic #1 = 25.5-27.4%
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (choice study, 5,500 testers); strategic inference is directional
verdicts.externalSignal: Cited BrightLocal LSA Click Study page is LIVE and supports every figure verbatim via two WebFetch passes: LSA-absent Organic 50.8% / Pack 32.3%; LSA-present Organic 43.9% / Pack 28.8%; Organic Position 1 = 27.4% (no LSA) / 25.5% (with LSA). A second fetch confirmed the per-position pack breakdown: Local Pack Position 1 = 17.3% (no LSA) / 16.1% (with LSA). Methodology fetch confirmed it is a MEASURED first-click test (5,500 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants, 5 SAB search terms in San Francisco, published Oct 19 2018).
verdicts.counterEvidence: Cross-source variance exists and is real. (1) Locafy and similar industry pages circulate an uncited, unattributed "Local 3-Pack captures 44% / organic 29%" figure — the OPPOSITE direction — but it names no study and is not a primary source. (2) A SEPARATE iLawyer/click-test dataset on an LSA-dominated legal SERP found Local Pack 29% > Organic 22% of first-clicks, and there Pack Position 1 (~14%) edged Organic #1 (~11%) — i.e., on LSA-heavy SERPs the directional finding can flip. So "organic out-clicks the pack" is SERP-context-dependent (holds when LSAs are absent/sparse; can reverse on LSA-saturated SERPs), and the result rests on a single 2018 vendor study.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: live-supports — the cited BrightLocal page resolves and contains every stat in the STAT line verbatim. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: faithful. Both clauses check out against the live numbers. Clause 1 "organic out-clicks the local pack": Organic 50.8% vs Pack 32.3% (no LSA) and 43.9% vs 28.8% (with LSA) — true in both scenarios. Clause 2 "organic #1 alone out-pulls the entire pack #1 SLOT": Organic #1 27.4%/25.5% vs Pack Position 1 17.3%/16.1% — true; organic #1 clearly beats the top pack slot. Critically, the claim says "pack #1 slot," NOT "entire pack" — if it had claimed organic #1 beats the whole pack it would be FALSE (27.4% < 32.3% pack total), but it does not, so it is accurate as written. SELF-CONSISTENCY across three stances: skeptic finds no spin (figures disclosed, methodology transparent); literalist confirms exact number match and that the carefully-worded sub-clause is correct; practitioner flags that replication is mixed/context-dependent (pack can win on LSA-saturated SERPs per iLawyer; an uncited 44%/29% pack-wins figure circulates). The practitioner caveat is what holds confidence at Medium rather than High: this is a single primary source from 2018, and the broad generalization "organic is the larger reach surface" is true for SAB SERPs without heavy LSA presence but is not universal. No external signal contradicts the SPECIFIC numbers or the as-written wording, so the verdict is survived (not corrected — there is no signal justifying a replacement, and the claim's own STAT honestly bounds the result by LSA presence). Recommendation, not a correction: when deploying, keep the explicit "no LSAs / with LSAs" framing already present and avoid over-generalizing to all local SERPs.

verdicts.claim: A new GBP matures over months with ~10 reviews as the most defensible early ranking milestone — a measured bump at 9->10 reviews that did NOT repeat (10->11, 16->31), so count is a threshold not a linear lever.

verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: cited source resolves and directly supports the stat+claim; captured snippet is verbatim. COUNTER: best bound is the small-n observational methodology and the fuzzy exact-threshold number across sources; neither overturns the claim. Net: supermajority -> High confidence, survived. verdicts.claim: In a controlled local-SERP click study, organic results received the most clicks of any SERP type — 50.8% with no LSAs present and 43.9% with LSAs present — ahead of the local pack (32.3% / 28.8%). Organic is the larger channel, not the second one.
verdicts.stat: Organic 43.9–50.8% of clicks vs local pack 28.8–32.3%

verdicts.counterEvidence: The broad generalization "Organic is the larger channel, not the second one" is methodology-dependent and does NOT universally replicate.
