Other widely cited local-SERP stats also put the 3-pack ahead of organic (e.g. 44% local-pack vs 29% organic). The discrepancy is structural: BrightLocal aggregates ALL ~10 organic positions into one bucket vs. the 3-slot local pack as a block, so organic-bucket > pack-block is partly an artifact of bucket size and measurement method (heatmap click distribution vs. forced single first-click). Minor literal note: 50.8→43.9 is a 6.9pp drop, but BrightLocal's own copy says "6.8%" and the claim faithfully carries the source's stated figure.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: live and directly supporting. WebFetch of the cited BrightLocal study returned an exact data table matching all four numbers in the claim (organic 50.8%/43.9%, local pack 32.3%/28.8%) and the page explicitly states "Organic results receive the most clicks of all SERP types." SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: the captured snippet ("Organic results receive the most clicks of all SERP types, though they see a drop of 6.8% when LSAs are present") is confirmed verbatim against the live page — faithful, not a stretch. SELF-CONSISTENCY: (a) skeptic — BrightLocal is a vendor but the figures are transparently tabled and the study cuts against pure self-interest by quantifying paid/LSA click capture; not spin. (b) literalist — every number and the key sentence match the source exactly; the only nit is 6.8% vs a computed 6.9pp, but the claim correctly reproduces BrightLocal's own wording. (c) practitioner/replication — the BrightLocal finding itself is genuine and unrefuted as a study, BUT the claim's editorializing generalization ("the larger channel, not the second one") is methodology-bounded: under first-click attention tests (iLawyer) and several other cited datasets the local pack actually outranks organic. So the cited study fully supports the stated claim, while the universalizing gloss is contestable. VERDICT: SURVIVED — the claim is exactly and faithfully attributed to a live, supporting primary source; no external signal refutes the BrightLocal numbers or the "organic receives the most clicks" statement within that study. Confidence High on the cited figures; the caveat (organic-bucket vs pack-block; result is method-dependent and reverses in first-click studies) should be carried so the claim is not overstated as a universal law.

verdicts.claim: City-intent organic rankings are location-stable while the local pack fractures block-by-block. Once a city modifier is added the top-5 organic positions hold constant across every test pin; the pack reshuffles because every geo-grid pin is a separate request from a distinct lat/long (same business can sit #1 at its office and ~#7–#10 a few blocks away).
verdicts.stat: 549 searches / 61 pins — city-modified queries showed 'little to no fluctuation' in the top 5; pack rankings shift #1→~#7–#10 within a few blocks
verdicts.externalSignal: (1) Cited Sterling Sky 2025 page IS live and DOES support the organic half verbatim: "When we added the city modifier... the top 5 positions remained constant with little to no fluctuation across all 3 keywords" (549 searches / 9 keyword variations / 61 pins). (2) The SAME page does NOT cover the local pack at all — it "focuses exclusively on organic results." (3) Independent geo-grid sources (BrightLocal, LocalViking, geogrid.dev, GMBMantra) confirm the pack-fracture half as textbook fact: each grid pin is a separate request from a distinct lat/long, and a business can sit #1 at its office and ~#7 a few blocks/across town away.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Sterling Sky's OWN prior (2022) study — referenced on the cited page — found the directional OPPOSITE of the claim's causal contrast: "proximity had a stronger impact on rankings in the localized organic results than in the Local Pack results." The claim's rhetorical engine is "organic holds stable WHILE the pack fractures because proximity hits the pack harder," but the cited authority found proximity moving ORGANIC more than the pack. This does not make the claim false (the 2025 finding is specifically about CITY-MODIFIED organic, which stabilizes, vs the pack which is inherently per-pin), but it means the single cited source does not support the contrast as framed and partially undercuts it.
verdicts.reasoning: The claim is a COMPOUND of two assertions. Half A (city-modified organic top-5 holds constant across pins) is fully and verbatim supported by the cited URL — snippet is faithful, methodology (549/61) matches. Half B (the local pack fractures block-by-block; geo-grid pins are distinct lat/long requests; same business #1 at office, ~#7-10 a few blocks away) is TRUE on its own merits per multiple independent geo-grid sources, but is NOT supported by the cited Sterling Sky page, which never analyzes the pack. Worse for the framing: Sterling Sky's 2022 finding (quoted on the same page) says proximity hits localized ORGANIC harder than the pack — the inverse of the claim's "pack fractures more" contrast. Skeptic stance: vendor framing welds two real facts into one citation, over-attributing the pack half to a source that doesn't carry it. Literalist stance: every number in the organic half checks out; the pack half's numbers are unsourced-from-this-URL but verifiable elsewhere. Practitioner stance: both phenomena replicate independently — the claim is not false, it is mis-cited and its causal "because proximity hits the pack harder" link is not what this source measured. Net: not killable (both halves are real, externally corroborated), not clean-survived (the cited source supports only ~half the claim and its prior study cuts against the contrast). Fix is sourcing, not facts: split the citation — keep Sterling Sky 2025 for the organic-stability half, add an independent geo-grid source (BrightLocal/LocalViking) for the pack-fracture half, and soften the causal "because" to a parallel-observation rather than a same-study contrast. No single replacement text resolves it cleanly, so verdict is flagged rather than corrected.

verdicts.claim: The website is the dominant lever for organic, and a weaker lever for the pack — the two channels run on different ranking-factor weights. Local Organic: On-page 33% / Links 24% / Behavioral 10%. Local Pack: GBP 32% / Reviews 20% / On-page 15%. A well-built site moves organic directly; the pack is gated on GBP completeness + review accumulation.
verdicts.stat: Local Organic: On-page 33%, Links 24%, Behavioral 10%. Local Pack: GBP 32%, Reviews 20%, On-page 15%.
verdicts.externalSignal: The cited BrightLocal page live-resolves and reproduces the exact figures verbatim (Local Organic: On-page 33% / Links 24% / Behavioral 10%; Local Pack: GBP 32% / Reviews 20% / On-page 15%) — confirmed by WebFetch. These numbers originate from the Whitespark Local Search Ranking Factors survey (2026 edition, released Nov 2025, ~50 expert respondents) that BrightLocal republishes, and replicate identically across at least three independent republishers (RocksDigital/LissaDuty full Local Organic table verbatim: 33/24/10/8/7/7/6/5; advicelocal; digitalapplied). An older 2023 edition carried different numbers (Local Pack On-page 19% / Reviews 16%; Local Organic On-page 36%), so the claim is correctly citing the current edition.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Three bounding caveats, none of which refute the cited percentages: (1) These are an opinion-survey aggregate (modeled expert weights), not Google-measured signal weights. (2) They are weights among CONTROLLABLE/thematic factors; Whitespark separately treats proximity as the single largest pack factor (~55% in some readings) and it is uncontrollable — so the claim's "pack is gated on GBP completeness + review accumulation" understates proximity's role. (3) A competing survey lineage (Moz, cited via searchlab.nl) weights Local Pack On-page ~16% and Reviews ~15%, differing from Whitespark's 15%/20% — i.e., the exact split is methodology-dependent, though the directional ordering (GBP > Reviews > On-page for the pack; On-page > Links for organic) is stable across both.
verdicts.reasoning: All six numbers match the cited source exactly with zero drift, and the source is a genuine independent expert survey (Whitespark, republished by BrightLocal), not vendor self-promotion. Numbers replicate across the primary survey and 3+ independent republishers (supermajority across all three stances). The qualitative thesis — site is the dominant lever for organic (On-page + Links = 57%) and a weaker lever for the pack (On-page only 15%, while GBP + Reviews = 52%) — is a faithful, defensible reading of the data. The "different ranking-factor weights per channel" framing is precisely what the survey reports. The only honest limitation is that these are modeled opinion weights and the pack interpretation soft-pedals proximity (the dominant but uncontrollable pack factor), which is a framing nuance rather than a factual error in the cited stat. Stat is verbatim-accurate and current; verdict survived at High confidence. No signal warrants correction.

verdicts.claim: Organic compounds, it is not instant — the honest floor. So slow-average and fast-mover facts coexist: low-competition long-tail / city pages rank in weeks-to-months while head terms compound over 6–18mo.
verdicts.stat: 1.74% of new pages reach top 10 within a year; average #1 page is 5 years old; 40.82% of top-10 rankers ranked within 1 month

verdicts.counterEvidence: No source refutes the figures. The only genuine bounding nuance: Ahrefs attributes fast (month-1) ranking to HIGHER-SEARCH-VOLUME terms (lower-volume terms distribute more evenly over the year), whereas the claim attributes fast ranking to "low-competition long-tail / city pages." That is a reasonable but not perfectly literal mapping of Ahrefs' own framing (volume != competition). It is interpretive color, not a misstatement of the cited stat, and does not undermine the load-bearing point (slow-average + fast-mover facts coexist). Also note the 40.82% is a CONDITIONAL stat (of pages that did reach top 10), which the claim states correctly.
verdicts.reasoning: Three-stance check. (a) Skeptic: Ahrefs is a vendor, but the figures cut AGAINST any vendor incentive to oversell quick SEO wins — they emphasize how HARD/slow ranking is (1.74%, 5-year-old #1 pages). No spin detected; if anything the honest-floor framing is conservative. (b) Literalist: all three numbers match the live page to the decimal (1.74%, 5 years, 40.82%) with no rounding or alteration; the claim quotes them accurately and correctly preserves the conditional nature of the 40.82% ("pages that DO reach top-10"). (c) Practitioner: the study replicates across ~6 independent third-party citations, all reproducing identical figures; it is the canonical industry-cited dataset on time-to-rank. Supermajority across all three stances. The only soft spot is the claim's competition-vs-volume gloss in the final clause, which is interpretive framing layered on top of the verified stat, not a corruption of it — insufficient to flag the core claim. Stat is measured from a real Ahrefs dataset, current as of the May 2025 study update. Verdict: survived, High confidence.

verdicts.claim: Google first-party: a business's position in ordinary web (organic) results is itself a stated local-pack factor, and prominence is built from links, articles, and directories. Organic authority feeds the pack — the channels are entangled, organic is the leading edge that drags the pack up over time, not a wholly separate track.
verdicts.stat: Qualitative — Google states position in web results is a local-ranking factor

Prominent places are more likely to show up in search results. This factor's also based on info like how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have." (2) Search Engine Land's canonical documentation of this exact page confirms the captured snippet IS the page's prior verbatim wording: "Your position in web results is also a factor, so SEO best practices also apply to local search optimization" and "Prominence is also based on information that Google has about a business from across the web (like links, articles and directories)."
verdicts.counterEvidence: The current live version of the cited page has been CONDENSED and no longer contains the captured snippet's exact sentences ("Your position in web results is also a factor, so search engine optimization (SEO) best practices apply") — that phrasing now exists only in archived/secondary records of the older version. Google has also publicly cautioned (Sterling Sky / John Mueller commentary, broadly noted in the local-SEO literature) that the three-factor framing is high-level guidance, not a weighted algorithm — so "organic drags the pack up over time" is a defensible directional inference, not a quantified Google statement. The causal/temporal layer of the claim (organic as "the leading edge that drags the pack up over time, not a wholly separate track") is the practitioner's interpretation, not Google's literal words; Google states entanglement (web results are a factor) but not the lead/lag sequencing.
verdicts.correctedText: Google first-party: in its official "Tips to improve your local ranking" help page, Google states that local-pack prominence is "based on info like how many websites link to your business" — i.e., the same off-/on-site web-authority signals (links, cross-web information, reviews) that drive organic ranking also feed the local pack. Google's documented wording historically read "Your position in web results is also a factor, so SEO best practices also apply" (current page condenses this to the links/reviews phrasing); SEO best practices therefore apply to local. The channels are entangled — organic authority feeds the pack — though the specific framing that organic is "the leading edge that drags the pack up over time" is a defensible practitioner inference, not a Google-stated sequencing. Source: support.google.com/business/answer/7091 (current); prior verbatim wording documented by Search Engine Land (searchengineland.com/google-documents-google-business-local-ranking-factors-246428).
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: cited source is live and Google first-party. The captured snippet ("Your position in web results is also a factor, so search engine optimization (SEO) best practices apply" + "links, articles, and directories") does NOT appear verbatim on the current 2026 page — Google condensed the prominence paragraph to "based on info like how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have." So the snippet is STALE, not fabricated: it is the page's documented prior wording, confirmed verbatim by Search Engine Land's canonical write-up of this exact help doc. SELF-CONSISTENCY across 3 stances: (a) Skeptic — this is Google's own documentation, not vendor spin; passes. (b) Literalist — the exact captured sentence fails against the live page today but matches the historical version verbatim per an independent record; partial. (c) Practitioner — the substance (web/organic authority + links feed local-pack prominence; SEO applies to local) is near-universally replicated across independent local-SEO sources (SEJ, Sterling Sky, Whitespark) and remains on the live page via the links signal; passes strongly. Supermajority supports the SUBSTANCE; the defect is purely that the captured snippet text is outdated relative to the live URL. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: the snippet faithfully supports the entanglement core of the claim, but quotes a version Google has since edited. COUNTER-SOURCE: the live page itself, which omits the SEO sentence, bounds the claim — Google still affirms web-link authority feeds prominence but no longer spells out the "position in web results / SEO applies" framing, and never literally states the lead/lag "drags up over time" sequencing (that is a sound inference, not a Google quote). Net: substance verified High-confidence, snippet corrected to match the current live page + cite its documented prior wording. Verdict corrected (named external signal + replacement provided).

verdicts.claim: At the session level, organic and paid search convert at nearly identical rates — so the organic advantage is NOT a higher raw conversion rate. The edge is intent-mix, ticket size, owned environment, and de-risking.
verdicts.stat: Organic search 4.9% vs paid 5.4% conversion overall; Construction & Engineering organic 4.8% vs paid 5.1% (110M+ sessions, 5M+ conversions)
verdicts.externalSignal: WebFetch of the cited Ruler Analytics page (now titled "Conversion Rate Benchmarks 2026: Based on 5+ Million Conversions Tracked Across 13 Industries") returned every figure verbatim: Organic search avg 4.9%, Paid search avg 5.4% ("highest-converting channel"); Construction & Engineering Organic 4.8% / Paid 5.1%; scope "110M+ Sessions recorded, 5M+ Conversions captured, £33.8M+ Spend across 13 industries." BUT this is a denominator/methodology mismatch, not a session-level comparison: Google Ads platform benchmarks (WordStream-lineage) count conversions per ad click inside the ad platform's own attribution, whereas Ruler measures conversions per session in one unified analytics dataset. The claim is explicitly scoped to "the session level," which neutralizes this counter-source rather than being refuted by it. Secondary caveat: Ruler is an attribution VENDOR (self-reported data, not independently audited), and some legacy studies (e.g. MarketingProfs 2013) historically showed paid out-converting organic — but those too compare across platforms, not session-level.
verdicts.reasoning: The cited URL is live and supports the stat verbatim (4.9% vs 5.4% overall; 4.8% vs 5.1% Construction & Engineering; 110M+ sessions / 5M+ conversions). Literalist stance: numbers are exact, no fabrication. Skeptic stance: vendor self-reported data, but figures are internally consistent and the conservative direction (paid slightly HIGHER) is the opposite of self-serving spin for an SEO pitch — the claim concedes organic does NOT win on raw conversion rate, which is the honest reading. Practitioner stance: the small-gap finding replicates across independent channel datasets (B2B, e-commerce, local all show <1pt session-level gaps). The one large-gap counter-source (organic 2-4% vs Google Ads 7.52%) is a cross-platform denominator mismatch, not session-level — and the claim's deliberate "at the session level" scoping is precisely what defuses it. The interpretive layer (edge = intent-mix, ticket size, owned environment, de-risking — not conversion rate) is an analyst framing, not a statistic, and is internally non-contradictory. Supermajority of stances support: survived. Note "nearly identical" is slightly generous (paid is ~10% relatively higher overall, ~6% in Construction), but the claim's own load-bearing assertion — "the organic advantage is NOT a higher raw conversion rate" — is fully supported and conservative. Measured (real session/conversion data), not modeled.

verdicts.claim: Considered high-ticket buyers run a multi-bid bake-off and are price-aware; the owned site improves win probability by framing value first, but does not eliminate the comparison.
verdicts.stat: 42.02% compare 2 quotes, 27.90% compare 3, 15.64% compare 4+ (~85% compare three or fewer); 64.81% say pricing is 'very important'
verdicts.externalSignal: (1) The cited Modernize page is live and reproduces the stat verbatim: "42.02% of homeowners compare 2 quotes; 27.90% compare 3; Only 15.64% compare 4 or more" and "64.81% of homeowners say pricing is 'very important'" (confirmed via WebFetch). (2) Independent corroboration of the multi-bid bake-off behavior: McKinley Construction Management and GreatBuildz both report homeowners/experts converge on getting 3 quotes; a widely-cited figure shows ~94% plan to get multiple quotes and ~67% actually do — consistent with the ~85%-compare-three-or-fewer pattern. (3) Independent corroboration that price is a major-but-not-sole driver: Pro Builder reports "43% of homeowners choose contractors based on price" (leading factor, vs 28% reviews/ratings); ServiceDirect/Service Business Mastery surveys report reputation/experience rank at/above price for many homeowners. The qualitative claim — buyers run a price-aware multi-bid comparison, value-framing improves but does not eliminate the comparison — is supported across all of these.
verdicts.counterEvidence: The strongest bounding source is the ServiceDirect / Service Business Mastery survey line that "nearly 70% of homeowners say price is NOT the most important factor," with experience/reputation cited as the chief factor (~34% most-important) and online reviews "very/extremely important" for ~67%. This BOUNDS, but does not refute, the claim: it shows pricing being labeled "very important" (64.81%) is not the same as price being decisive — which is precisely why the claim is correctly hedged ("frames value first, but does not eliminate the comparison"). A secondary weakness: the headline stat originates from a single vendor (Modernize, a lead-gen company), and several apparent corroborators (e.g., the Pro Builder 43% figure) trace back to Modernize's own survey data rather than being fully independent — so the exact decimals rest on one primary source even though the directional behavior is multiply corroborated.
verdicts.reasoning: Adversarial default was to refute. URL health: PASS — the cited page resolves and reproduces both stats verbatim (no fabrication, no misattribution; snippet faithfulness is exact). Self-consistency across three stances: (a) Skeptic — flags Modernize as a price-shopping-incentivized lead-gen vendor and notes single-source origin; legitimate, but lowers confidence rather than killing, since the behavioral pattern replicates. (b) Literalist — the exact figures (42.02/27.90/15.64; 64.81) match the live page word-for-word; the claim text does not misstate them and correctly summarizes "~85% compare three or fewer." (c) Practitioner — the underlying behavior (small 2-3 quote bake-off, price salient but reputation/reviews co-decisive) replicates across independent sources (McKinley, GreatBuildz, ServiceDirect, Pro Builder), a supermajority of which agree directionally. The claim is also notably well-scoped: it explicitly states framing "does not eliminate the comparison," so the reputation/review counter-evidence reinforces rather than contradicts it. Measured (specific survey decimals, not round-number modeling). Net: supermajority agreement on the qualitative claim → survives; single-vendor dependency for the exact decimals → Medium not High. No named external signal justifies a correction, so no correctedText.

verdicts.claim: A map pin is a rented asset exposed to GBP suspension, a real and rising risk with a multi-week, non-guaranteed appeal; an owned domain carries no such exposure. (Do NOT assert a precise annual suspension base rate.)
verdicts.stat: GBP suspension reports up 80%+ since 2023; appeal wait times ~5-6 weeks in early 2025
verdicts.externalSignal: Cited Sterling Sky page is live and supports the appeal-wait stat verbatim ("In the last half of 2022, wait times were 3-5 weeks. In early 2025, they were 5-6 weeks!"). Independently, Search Engine Journal (Mar 2025, "Google Business Profile Suspensions Rise, But Appeals Are Delayed") corroborates BOTH legs structurally: suspension surge tracked via Mike Blumenthal's forum-volume data ("forum complaints about suspensions reached their highest level since last August... it's accelerating") AND appeal delay ("Appeal resolution times have grown significantly – from about five days to nearly five weeks"; "the appeal process is taking somewhere on the order of 4 weeks or more, not the ~5 days noted by Google"). Multiple reputable secondary outlets (SE Roundtable, Search Engine Journal, Proceed Innovative) independently report the rising-suspension trend. The structural premise (pin = revocable/rented asset with multi-week non-guaranteed appeal; owned domain carries no equivalent platform-suspension exposure) is uncontested and self-evidently true of the GBP vs. owned-domain ownership model.
verdicts.counterEvidence: No source refutes the structural claim or the rising-risk direction. The one soft spot is the secondary STAT "suspension reports up 80%+ since 2023": it is NOT on the cited Sterling Sky page, and traces only to marketing blogs (e.g. assetdigitalcom.com) that attribute it to "BrightLocal, 2024" — a primary BrightLocal study with that exact figure could not be located (BrightLocal research search returned no matching 80% statistic). So the 80% magnitude is a propagated, weakly-sourced number, not a verified primary measurement. This bounds the precision of the magnitude only; it does not bound the directional/structural claim, which the claim text already protects by explicitly NOT asserting a precise base rate.
verdicts.reasoning: Three-stance review. (a) Skeptic: the "80%+" figure is exactly the kind of round, viral, vendor-friendly number that propagates through SEO marketing blogs without a locatable primary — treat it as unverified. But the claim's CORE does not depend on it; the claim wisely caveats "Do NOT assert a precise annual suspension base rate." (b) Literalist: the captured snippet is reproduced verbatim on the live cited page (5-6 weeks early 2025) — faithful, no misattribution. The "80%+" portion of the STAT line is NOT on the cited page, so that specific number is not supported by the named source. (c) Practitioner: the rising-suspension + delayed-appeal phenomenon replicates across independent reputable sources (Sterling Sky, Mike Blumenthal/Near Media forum tracking, Search Engine Journal, SE Roundtable) — supermajority, high confidence. Net: the load-bearing assertion (rented/revocable pin with multi-week non-guaranteed appeal vs. owned-domain with no such exposure) is true and well-corroborated; survives at High. Recommendation (not a correction, since the claim text itself doesn't carry the 80% number — that lives in the STAT line): drop or re-source the "80%+ since 2023" figure to a verifiable primary, and lead the supporting stat with the verbatim Sterling Sky wait-time data, which is rock-solid. Verdict survived because the claim as written holds; the weak 80% is a citation-hygiene flag on the auxiliary stat, not a defect in the claim.

verdicts.claim: The quality differential is conditional on actually ranking for commercial/buying-intent terms — it is a consequence of ranking, never automatic from having a good site. This is why the offer must be tied to a ranking outcome, not site-build delivery.
verdicts.stat: ~90% of pages get zero organic traffic from Google; most SEO campaigns fail to generate expected leads, usually by targeting informational not commercial terms
verdicts.externalSignal: Cited marketingeye.com page is LIVE and explicitly supports all three stat components: (1) "approximately 90% of pages get no organic traffic from Google," (2) "many organizations find that their SEO strategies do not result in the level of lead generation they expect," (3) the gap between traffic/informational keywords vs "buyer intent keywords, which attract those ready to buy or inquire." The 90% figure traces to a PRIMARY Ahrefs study (90.63% original / 96.55% in 2023 update over ~14B pages), so ~90% is conservative and accurate. The logical inference — that lead quality follows from ranking for COMMERCIAL/buyer-intent terms rather than from having a good site or ranking for informational terms — is independently corroborated by Semrush, Backlinko, AIOSEO, WhatConverts, GA Connector: "Rankings alone don't generate leads... A keyword can bring a ton of clicks and still be useless"; "Sites that get the highest ROI from SEO tend to focus almost 100% on keywords with lots of buyer intent"; intent-driven leads convert at 2-3x.
verdicts.counterEvidence: No source refutes the core claim. The only bounding nuance: independent sources frame the lever as "rank for the RIGHT (commercial-intent) keywords," which is slightly broader than the claim's tighter phrasing "consequence of ranking." A pedant could note that ranking for commercial terms is necessary but not sufficient — page/offer conversion quality also matters (a good landing page still converts the commercial-intent visitor). But this strengthens rather than refutes T7-4's central logic: a good site that does NOT rank for commercial terms produces no quality differential, which is exactly the claim. No counter-source argues that a good unranked site automatically yields qualified leads.
verdicts.reasoning: Three-pass adversarial check. (1) URL HEALTH: cited page resolves and verbatim supports the 90%-zero-traffic stat, the SEO-fails-to-generate-leads claim, and the informational-vs-buyer-intent keyword distinction — not fabricated, not a stretch. (2) SELF-CONSISTENCY across three stances: the skeptic's "vendor spin" worry is defused because the load-bearing number is a primary Ahrefs study, not the vendor blog's own figure; the literalist confirms ~90% is faithful (Ahrefs reported 90.63%, later 96.55% — claim rounds down, conservative); the practitioner finds the commercial-vs-informational intent principle is settled SEO consensus replicated across Semrush, Backlinko, AIOSEO, WhatConverts, GA Connector. Supermajority concurrence → High. (3) SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: captured snippet matches live page wording closely; no misattribution. (4) COUNTER-SOURCE: the strongest bound is "ranking for commercial terms is necessary but not alone sufficient" — but that does not contradict the claim, which only asserts the differential is a CONSEQUENCE of ranking (and conditional on it), not that ranking is the sole input. The offer-design conclusion (tie to ranking outcome, not site-build delivery) follows soundly from the evidence that a good site absent commercial-term ranking yields no lead-quality differential. Verdict: survived, High confidence, measured (rooted in an empirical Ahrefs index study + observed conversion-rate differentials).

verdicts.claim: Exclusive, high-intent contractor leads close far above commodity/shared leads, supporting the general principle organic-owned leads exploit (exclusive + high-intent + bigger ticket beats commodity/shared). NOT a direct organic-vs-pack measurement.
verdicts.stat: Roofing 23% close @ $8,400 avg; windows 31% close @ $22,000 avg (exclusive paid leads); shared paid leads ~6-10%
verdicts.externalSignal: The cited leadgenjay page is live and contains both stat figures VERBATIM ("My roofing client averages 23% close rate with $8,400 average job value... My window contractor client closes 31% of Modernize leads with $22,000 average job value"). BUT the same page explicitly labels the services differently than the claim does: Angi Pro (the roofing 23%/$8,400 figure) = "Up to 4 contractors per lead" i.e. SHARED; Modernize (windows 31%/$22,000) = "Exclusive leads only." The claim's parenthetical "(exclusive paid leads)" applied to BOTH figures is contradicted by the source for the roofing number. The general principle is independently corroborated: shared leads close ~5-15% / exclusive ~30-60%, exclusive 2-5x shared (constructionleadpro, minyona, baadigi, 99calls), and minyona's table gives shared overall close 6% vs exclusive 26% — directly supporting both the "shared ~6-10%" figure and the exclusive-beats-shared principle.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Two issues bound the claim. (1) Misattribution: the cited source itself classifies Angi Pro as a shared service (up to 4 contractors), so the roofing 23%/$8,400 stat is NOT an "exclusive" lead datapoint as the claim's "(exclusive paid leads)" framing asserts — only the windows/Modernize figure is exclusive per the source. (2) Unsourced addition: the "shared paid leads ~6-10%" comparator does NOT appear anywhere on the cited leadgenjay page (confirmed via two targeted fetches); it is supplied from elsewhere. It happens to be roughly correct (minyona puts shared overall close at 6%), but it is not supported by the cited URL. Skeptic note: the 23%/31% are single-client anecdotes from a lead-gen marketer's blog ("my client"), not a controlled study — directional, not a measured population statistic.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: live-supports. The cited page resolves and carries both headline stats verbatim, so the claim is not fabricated or dead. SELF-CONSISTENCY (3 stances): (a) Skeptic — these are single-client anecdotes on a lead-vendor blog, vendor-spin and selection risk are real; treat as illustrative not measured. (b) Literalist — the numbers match exactly, but the claim's "(exclusive paid leads)" label is wrong for the roofing figure: the source ties 23%/$8,400 to Angi Pro, which it defines as SHARED (up to 4 contractors); only the 31%/$22,000 Modernize figure is exclusive. Also the "shared ~6-10%" comparator is absent from the cited page. (c) Practitioner/replication — the underlying PRINCIPLE (exclusive + high-intent + bigger ticket beats commodity/shared) replicates across many independent sources: shared ~5-15%, exclusive ~30-60%, 2-5x lift; minyona's table reads shared overall close 6% vs exclusive 26% (4x). SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: the captured snippet is faithful to the page, but the STAT line wrapping it overreaches by calling both figures "exclusive" — the source contradicts that for roofing. COUNTER-SOURCE: the cited page itself is the best bounding source (it labels Angi shared), and minyona/baadigi independently set the comparator ranges. NET: the load-bearing claim — which is explicitly scoped as "the general principle... NOT a direct organic-vs-pack measurement" — survives on independent replication, so this is not a kill. But the specific framing has a source-contradicted misattribution (roofing stat is shared, not exclusive) plus an unsourced comparator, which is why this is flagged rather than survived. Recommended tightening (not a forced correction since the principle holds): attribute the 23%/$8,400 to a SHARED service (Angi) and only the 31%/$22,000 to exclusive (Modernize), and source the "shared ~6-10%" line to minyona's 6% overall-close figure rather than to leadgenjay. Confidence Medium: principle robust, specific datapoints are single-client/modeled with a labeling error.

verdicts.claim: Business websites appear in 61% of top-10 organic results for transactional queries but only 32% for informational queries, where directories (37%) outrank them — so a thin transactional/pack-optimized site has structurally less eligibility to rank on research queries.
verdicts.stat: Business sites: 61% top-10 organic (transactional) vs 32% (informational); directories take 37% on informational
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (8,000 results / 800 manual searches; 1 transactional + 1 informational keyword across 20 verticals x 20 US cities)
verdicts.externalSignal: Primary source confirmed live and supporting: BrightLocal "Business Listings Visibility Study" (published Oct 15, 2024) at the cited URL contains the exact figures. WebFetch verbatim quote from the page: "The difference between how often business websites are shown in results for transactional searches (61%) and informational searches (32%)..." and "For informational searches... directories take the larger share (37%) over business sites (32%)." Methodology is real measured data, not modeled: 800 manual Google searches recording the first 10 organic results each = 8,000 results, across 20 verticals x 20 US cities, using one transactional + one informational keyword per vertical. WebSearch independently surfaced BrightLocal as the canonical source plus a third-party reproduction (freeoseocheck.com) repeating the figures.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Boundaries on weight, not a refutation: (1) Single-vendor source — BrightLocal is the sole originator; no fully independent dataset (e.g., a SISTRIX/Semrush/Ahrefs SERP study) was found reproducing the exact 61/32/37 split, so corroboration is the same study echoed by third parties rather than methodologically independent replication. (2) Snapshot/recency — figures reflect Oct-2024 Google SERPs; the SERP landscape (AI Overviews, SGE expansion through 2025-2026) is shifting and could move these shares. (3) Operationalization — "transactional vs informational" was proxied by one keyword each per vertical (e.g., "coffee shop" vs "best coffee shop"), a coarse intent split; the headline overall figure is 47% business sites, with the 61/32 being the intent breakdown. None of these contradict the numbers as cited.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: The cited brightlocal.com URL resolves and is the genuine primary source. WebFetch returned the exact figures verbatim (61% transactional, 32% informational for business sites; 37% directories on informational), with a direct supporting quote and a confirmed measured methodology (8,000 results from 800 manual searches). Not dead, not fabricated. SELF-CONSISTENCY across three stances: (a) Skeptic — yes BrightLocal is a vendor that sells citation/listing services and has an incentive to elevate directories' importance, but the methodology is transparent, reproducible, and the directional finding (directories rank better on informational/research queries) is mundane and consistent with how aggregator/"best of" listicle pages behave on Google; no spin detected in the numbers themselves. (b) Literalist — every number in the claim matches the page exactly: 61, 32, 37, and the "directories take the larger share over business sites" phrasing maps cleanly onto "outrank (37% vs 32%)." (c) Practitioner — the pattern replicates against lived SERP experience: informational/"best X" queries surface directories, listicles, and aggregators above individual business sites; this is uncontroversial in local SEO. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: The captured snippet is faithful, not a stretch. The factual half (the percentages and which type outranks which) is a direct match. The interpretive half of the CLAIM — "a thin transactional/pack-optimized site has structurally less eligibility to rank on research queries" — is a defensible inference the study supports directionally (it explicitly frames the split as Google measuring user intent), though it is the claim's own extrapolation rather than a BrightLocal conclusion; it does not overstate the data. COUNTER-SOURCE: Best bounding source is the absence of independent replication — the figures trace to a single Oct-2024 BrightLocal study; no contradicting study was found, but also no methodologically independent confirmation, so confidence rests on one well-documented measurement. VERDICT: survived at High confidence — primary source live and exact-match, measured methodology, faithful snippet; the only caveats are single-vendor provenance and SERP recency, which bound the weight without refuting the stat.

verdicts.claim: In a June 2026 SERP study of UK trades, the roofing vertical showed a local pack on 97.4% of genuine hire-intent queries — but only after research/cost/comparison/jobs/training/brand noise was filtered out, confirming the pack owns the transactional slice while the research slice the silos target is a categorically separate demand pool.
verdicts.stat: 97.4% local pack presence on roofing hire-intent queries (979 local-intent keywords, June 2026)
verdicts.externalSignal: Studio36 page (live, dated June 11 2026) reproduces the stat verbatim: "After filtering out non-local noise such as jobs, salaries, training, software and brand terms, we analysed 979 genuine local-intent keywords... 95.6% of trades queries" with roofing at 97.4% in the sector league table. Methodology is the Ahrefs API keyword database (NOT live SERP scraping), authored by an SEO agency that sells roofer-SEO services. Independent corroboration is directional only: BrightLocal/aggregators report "at least 93% of local-intent searches include a Local Pack" — same band, but the exact 97.4% roofing figure is single-source and uncorroborated.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Two distinct problems bound the claim. (1) Single-vendor + modeled: the 97.4% comes from one Blackpool SEO agency's Ahrefs-derived dataset (a June-2026 snapshot the authors themselves caveat as location-variable), not independent live SERP observation; no second source reproduces the roofing-specific figure. (2) The interpretive leap is unsupported: the source filtered out "jobs, salaries, training, software, brand" as methodological NOISE removal — it did NOT study cost/comparison/research queries as a separate non-pack demand pool, and the page "doesn't develop a framework distinguishing how research-focused searches operate separately." The claim's own paraphrase inserts "research/cost/comparison" into the source's filter list (a misattribution — those terms are not in it). Search evidence further notes roofing COST queries often still trigger local packs ("location-specific cost inquiries like how much does roof repair cost near me"), which directly undercuts the "categorically separate demand pool" conclusion.
verdicts.reasoning: DEFAULT-REFUTE posture. The raw STAT survives: the cited URL is live, correctly dated June 2026, and supports the number (95.6% trades / 97.4% roofing / 979 keywords / the filter list) word-for-word, with directional independent backing (~93%+ local-pack presence on local-intent queries is a well-replicated figure). What does NOT survive is the load-bearing strategic FRAMING the stat is deployed to prove. The pillar uses 97.4% to "confirm... the research slice the silos target is a categorically separate demand pool." The source establishes only that hire-intent trades queries overwhelmingly show a local pack — it does not measure, and the authors explicitly do not theorize, a separate research/cost/comparison pool that fails to trigger the pack. Skeptic stance: vendor with a direct sales incentive (sells roofer SEO), modeled keyword data, exactly the spin profile to discount a sole-source figure. Literalist stance: the number is faithful, but the claim's restatement of the filter set ("research/cost/comparison/jobs/training/brand") inserts terms not in the source — a real misattribution. Practitioner stance: replicates directionally (BrightLocal ~93%) but the exact 97.4% does not, and the practitioner counter-note is that roofing cost/near-me queries frequently DO carry local packs, contradicting the strict bifurcation. Net: stat accurate + faithfully cited, but single-source/modeled and over-extended into a conclusion the evidence does not license. Not killed (the number is real and corroborated in-band), not corrected (no external signal contradicts the number itself, only its interpretation). FLAGGED: cite it as a single-vendor directional indicator, drop the "categorically separate demand pool" certainty and the inflated filter-list paraphrase.

verdicts.claim: Roughly 70% of searches return no map pack at all — only 29.7% of searches trigger a Local Pack across a large keyword panel — so the pack-free research/comparison territory is a large demand pool, not a niche.
verdicts.stat: 29.7% of searches trigger a Local Pack (=> ~70% return none)
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (Ahrefs API, 1,000 high-volume keywords, 22 industries, ~404M monthly searches, Oct 2025; UK market — directional for US)
verdicts.externalSignal: Three independent measurements bracket the claim's directional core (most searches return no Local Pack): (1) SEMrush Sensor reports Local Pack appears on ~17.62% of all SERPs; (2) SOCi benchmark data shows ~33.4% Local Pack presence even for competitive multi-location keywords; (3) the cited Studio36 Digital study (live, Ahrefs UK API, 1,000 high-volume keywords across 22 industries, Oct 2025) states "29.7% of all UK searches trigger a Local Pack." All three cluster in the ~17-33% range, none contradicting that a clear majority of searches show no pack.
verdicts.counterEvidence: The most-cited "93%" figure (SearchEngineLand/various local-SEO stat roundups) and the "Local 3-pack appears in 93% of searches with local intent" stat use a DIFFERENT denominator — local-intent searches only, not all searches — so they do not refute the claim; they answer a different question. The genuine bounding caveat is methodological: 29.7% is UK-specific, single-vendor (Ahrefs panel), and derived from only 1,000 high-volume keywords, so it is a panel estimate, not a census of "all searches." The exact figure could shift with a US panel or a different keyword universe.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: The cited source resolves and WebFetch confirms it states verbatim "29.7% of all UK searches trigger a Local Pack," with methodology disclosed (Ahrefs UK API, 1,000 keywords / 22 industries / 404M monthly searches, Oct 2025). Live-supports. SELF-CONSISTENCY across three stances: (a) Skeptic — Studio36 is a vendor blog, but the figure is conservative for their own selling interest (a higher pack % would better justify local-SEO services), and it aligns with non-affiliated SEMrush Sensor data, so vendor-spin risk is low. (b) Literalist — the exact number 29.7% is faithfully reproduced; the claim's derived "~70% return none" is the correct arithmetic complement; the only stretch is generalizing a UK/1,000-keyword panel to "searches" globally. (c) Practitioner — replicates across independent sources: SEMrush ~17.6%, SOCi ~33.4% for competitive keywords; the broad zone is consistent, so the directional claim ("pack-free territory is a large pool, not a niche") holds robustly. Supermajority of independent stances support the directional claim. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: the captured snippet "29.7% of all UK searches trigger a Local Pack" matches the live page exactly and genuinely supports the stat. The claim's framing ("roughly 70%") is a fair rounding. VERDICT: survived, but Medium (not High) confidence because the precise 29.7% rests on a single UK vendor panel; the underlying directional thesis is what is strongly corroborated. The KM-relevant assertion (large pack-free research/comparison demand pool) is sound under every independent source examined — SEMrush's lower 17.6% would make it even larger.

verdicts.claim: Firsthand SERP inspection confirms roofing research queries return organic guides, calculators, manufacturer and .gov pages with NO map pack — exactly the resources/cost-guide silo territory a thin site cannot reach.
verdicts.stat: 0 map pack on 'roof replacement cost' / 'metal vs asphalt roof' / 'how to file a roof insurance claim' — organic content only
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (firsthand SERP observation this session; single-pass, not a large-N panel)
verdicts.externalSignal: Live WebSearch on all three named queries returned purely organic/informational result sets with no local-pack/GBP listings: 'roof replacement cost' -> roofingcalculator.com, NerdWallet, Angi, Homewyse, drroof calculator; 'metal vs asphalt roof' -> Roof Maxx, MetalCon, This Old House, State Farm; 'how to file a roof insurance claim' -> GAF, IKO, TDI Texas (.gov), state roofing associations, attorney/contractor guides, State Farm. Independent SEO corroboration (seranking.com, localfalcon.com, link-assistant.com via search) confirms the mechanism: informational-intent queries (how-tos, comparisons, definitions) do NOT trigger the local pack; packs fire on local/transactional 'near me' intent. Cited source thisoldhouse.com/roofing/shingles-vs-metal-roof-cost resolves live ('Shingles vs. Metal Roof Cost (2026 Guide)', updated 04/03/2026) and is an organic cost guide -> exactly the silo the claim describes.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Two bounding caveats, neither fatal. (1) The CITED-SOURCE captured snippet is now stale/mismatched: it quotes a steel standing-seam average of $51,865 and asphalt $31,871 attributed to a 'JLC 2025 Cost vs Value Report,' but the live page (updated 04/03/2026, post-capture) shows $53,811 metal / $14,182 asphalt and uses JLC's 2025 report only for a resale-value stat (68% asphalt vs 50% metal), not those cost figures. So the snippet is weak as a faithful quote even though the page validly supports the broader 'organic guide' point. (2) WebSearch returns organic links only and does not render Google's local-pack widget, so 'zero pack' is inferred from result composition + SEO doctrine rather than pixel-confirmed; 'roof replacement cost' can occasionally surface a pack if Google reads local-commercial intent, but it did not in this test and the dominant pattern is organic. Neither caveat refutes the load-bearing thesis (informational roofing research queries = organic silo a thin site cannot reach).
verdicts.reasoning: The load-bearing claim is the SERP-composition thesis: roofing research queries return organic guides/calculators/manufacturer/.gov pages with no map pack — territory a thin site cannot reach. That thesis replicated across all three named queries live and is independently corroborated by established search-intent doctrine (informational intent does not fire the local pack). Three-stance review converges: skeptic finds no spin (structurally true SEO mechanics), literalist confirms organic-only composition though cannot pixel-verify the pack widget, practitioner confirms replication and consistency with local-pack-fires-on-local-intent doctrine. The cited source is live and on-topic, so urlHealth is live-supports and the verdict is survived. I did NOT downgrade to corrected because no external signal warrants rewriting the claim's load-bearing assertion — the only mismatch is in the captured cost-figure snippet (stale after a 04/03/2026 page update), which is a source-snippet faithfulness weakness, not a defect in the claim. Confidence High on the thesis; the stat ('0 map pack' on the three queries) is measured via live search composition with the noted widget-rendering caveat.

verdicts.claim: AI Overviews are eroding the informational/research lane the silos target — coverage ~6.5% (Jan) to ~25% peak (Jul) to ~16% (Nov) 2025, ~91% informational-intent early-year — cutting informational organic CTR an estimated 38-61%, so the silo must be sold as qualified-coverage + AI-citation surface, not a guaranteed click windfall.
verdicts.stat: AIO coverage ~6.5% -> ~25% peak -> ~16% (2025); ~91% informational; informational organic CTR down 38-61%
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (Search Engine Land reporting on Semrush 10M+ keyword dataset, Jan-Nov 2025)
verdicts.externalSignal: Two concrete signals. (1) The cited Search Engine Land URL (Danny Goodwin, citing Semrush's 10M-keyword Jan-Nov 2025 analysis) is live and SUPPORTS the coverage curve (Jan 6.5% -> Jul "just under 25%" peak -> Nov "less than 16%") and the 91% informational-intent figure (Jan 91% -> Oct 57%). (2) The SAME URL CONTRADICTS the CTR portion: it states "click-through rates for keywords with AI Overviews have steadily risen since January" and zero-click rates FELL 33.75%->31.53%. The "38-61% CTR decline" does not appear on the cited page at all. That CTR range is instead corroborated by INDEPENDENT sources: Ahrefs (Dec 2025, 300K keywords matched for informational intent, GSC data: "58% lower average clickthrough rate for the top-ranking page"), Amsive (700K keywords: -37% when AIO + Featured Snippet co-occur, -19.98% non-branded), Mersel (61%).
verdicts.counterEvidence: The cited source itself is the strongest counter-source to the CTR sub-claim: Semrush's data argues AIO does NOT suppress clicks and CTR for AIO keywords ROSE through 2025 — the opposite of a 38-61% decline. This is a genuine methodological dispute in the field: Semrush (impression-weighted, same-keyword before/after) shows rising CTR, while Ahrefs/Amsive (GSC top-position CTR, pre-AIO vs post-AIO baseline) show steep decline. The 38-61% figure is real but is NOT a settled consensus and is contested by the very citation attached to it.
verdicts.correctedText: AI Overviews coverage swung from ~6.5% of queries (Jan 2025) to a ~25% peak (Jul) and pulled back to under 16% (Nov), with informational-intent queries falling from ~91% (Jan) to ~57% (Oct) [Semrush 10M-keyword analysis, via Search Engine Land]. verdicts.claim: Backlinks have a demonstrated causal effect on organic traffic, not just correlation: Ahrefs disavowed 3,476 links to three of its own pages, traffic dropped 13.3%-18%, then recovered to ~99% when the disavow was removed.
verdicts.stat: Disavow of 3,476 links -> -13.3% to -18% traffic; recovery to ~99% on restoration
verdicts.measured_or_modeled: measured (controlled before/after on real pages — strong causal evidence)
verdicts.externalSignal: Cited source (ahrefs.com/blog/impact-of-links/, Patrick Stox's "Do Links Still Matter for Rankings? A Study by Ahrefs") resolves live and contains the exact figures verbatim: "We disavowed 3,476 links across three blog posts"; "While the links were disavowed, this page [SEO Pricing] lost 13.3% of its traffic. But when we removed the file, the page got back to 99% of the previous traffic"; the YouTube page "lost about 18% of its search traffic in the first month"; conclusion "Links still matter." Independently referenced/described by Ahrefs' own later follow-up (ahrefs.com/blog/toxic-backlink-disavowal/) and third-party SEO write-ups (editorial.link, contentpowered.com) confirming the 2021 experiment and that "traffic fell off a cliff" when links were disavowed.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Two bounding caveats, neither of which falsifies the claim as worded. (1) Cherry-pick risk: the experiment's three pages were MIXED, not uniformly clean. The third (Bing) page barely moved while disavowed and then ROSE ~44%, and the author conceded "The pages tested are still down from where they started" — i.e., recovery was incomplete in aggregate. The claim quotes the cleanest page's 99% recovery as the headline recovery figure, which is literally accurate for THAT page but is the most favorable of the three outcomes. (2) Causal-strength bound: it is a single n=3 quasi-experiment on one site with no control group, so confounds (algorithm updates, seasonality over the Aug–Sep 2021 window) cannot be fully excluded; John Mueller (per SearchEngineJournal) has separately cautioned that traffic drops are often unrelated to specific links. This is a strong before/after intervention, not a randomized trial.
verdicts.reasoning: URL HEALTH: live and directly supportive — every numeric in the claim (3,476 links; 13.3%–18% drop; ~99% recovery) is quoted verbatim on the cited Ahrefs page, and the author's stated conclusion is "Links still matter." SELF-CONSISTENCY across three stances: (a) Skeptic — would expect vendor spin, but Ahrefs publishing a result that UNDERMINES the toxic-backlink/disavow-tool industry is anti-self-serving, reducing spin risk; passes. (b) Literalist — the claim's wording gives a RANGE ("13.3%-18%") and a single recovery figure ("~99%"), which matches the source exactly; it does not assert uniform recovery across all pages, so it is not technically overstated; passes. (c) Practitioner — the result is corroborated by Ahrefs' own 2024 follow-up and independent SEO outlets, and the before/after disavow-ON/disavow-OFF design is the strongest causal evidence short of an RCT; the "causal not just correlation" framing is the experiment's explicit point; passes. Supermajority (3/3) supports. SNIPPET FAITHFULNESS: the captured snippet is faithful — it is a near-verbatim paraphrase of the SEO Pricing page sentences. The only honesty note is that the claim foregrounds the cleanest page; a maximally rigorous restatement would note the aggregate was mixed and recovery incomplete. But as literally worded the claim is accurate and well-sourced, so it SURVIVES rather than requiring correction (no contradicting external signal exists — the caveats bound, not refute). Confidence High because the primary source is the experiment itself and it is quoted exactly.

verdicts.claim: The one-time, in-scope on-site link architecture King Maker ships produces causal organic uplift: SearchPilot A/B tests show +5% to +25% organic uplift, and a roofing-relevant test adding links to the 6 nearest geographic regions across ~8,000 location pages produced a +7% organic uplift on the linked pages.

verdicts.claim: The review mandate must be universal and unscreened to be legal: the FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect Oct 21, 2024, carries civil penalties up to $51,744 per violation, and bans review suppression, incentivizing reviews of a particular sentiment, and review gating.
verdicts.stat: Effective Oct 21, 2024; up to $51,744 per violation; bans suppression + incentivized/gated reviews

verdicts.counterEvidence: No source refuting the date, penalty figure, or banned-conduct categories was found. Only bounding nuances: (1) "$51,744 per violation" is the inflation-adjusted FTC Act civil-penalty maximum (an annually-updated ceiling, not a fixed/guaranteed amount); the claim's "up to ... currently" framing is accurate. (2) "Review gating" is a practitioner/industry term, NOT statutory language — the FTC rule does not use the word "gating." The rule reaches gating behavior via its sentiment-conditioned-incentive ban (465.4) and suppression ban (465.7), so the substance is covered, but a strict literalist would note the FTC text says "particular sentiment" and "suppression," not "gating."
verdicts.reasoning: URL health: cited FTC press-release URL is live and substantive — WebFetch hit a 403 (FTC.gov bot-blocking), not a dead/fabricated page; WebSearch returned the page's actual content (5-0 vote, the exact banned-conduct list, "currently $51,744 per violation"), and the URL appears as a returned search result, confirming it resolves. Self-consistency across 3 stances: (a) skeptic — this is a govt-regulation citation, not vendor spin; corroborated by the primary Federal Register text, removing spin risk; (b) literalist — effective date "Oct 21, 2024" matches exactly; "$51,744 per violation" matches verbatim; "suppression" and "particular sentiment" match the actual rule sections (465.7, 465.4); only "review gating" is non-statutory shorthand but substantively accurate; (c) practitioner replication — replicates across primary (FTC, Fed Register, eCFR) AND independent secondary (5+ law firms) sources, a clear supermajority. Snippet faithfulness: the captured snippet ("addresses the suppression of negative reviews and the purchase or incentivizing of reviews expressing a particular sentiment. Civil penalties currently $51,744 per violation") is genuine FTC press-release language and directly supports the claim — no stretch or misattribution. Verdict survived at High confidence: every load-bearing figure (date, penalty, banned conduct) is confirmed by primary government sources plus independent corroboration. The "review gating" wording is the only soft spot and is a defensible plain-English label for the rule's sentiment/suppression bans — not a factual error warranting correction.

verdicts.claim: $5-10k/mo off-page budget is enterprise-tier, not typical: SE Ranking's survey of 260 agencies found 64% charge under $1k/mo, 20% $1-2k, 13% $2-5k, and only ~2% above $5k/mo. The honest framing is a floor of typical $1-2k/mo scaling to a $5-10k ceiling for enterprise domination.

verdicts.reasoning: All four cited percentages (64/20/13/2) and the n=260 sample match the live page exactly, confirmed via WebFetch (firecrawl was out of credits). The snippet is faithful, not a stretch. Across three adversarial stances — skeptic, literalist, practitioner — the claim holds: the vendor figure is sober and independently replicated (Ahrefs n=439 avg $2,917/mo, ~31% over $2k; GoodFirms n=150). The load-bearing point the claim uses this stat for — that a $5-10k/mo off-page budget is enterprise-tier and atypical, with typical spend an order lower — is well-supported; Ahrefs even shows a long tail to $25k-50k/mo, making $5-10k a reasonable "enterprise ceiling" rather than an exaggeration. The "$1-2k typical floor" is framing/interpretation but does not break the underlying data. Supermajority of independent evidence supports → survived, High confidence.

verdicts.claim: Owned citation builds are one-time (no subscription, ownership transferred), whereas Yext is a rental whose listings degrade on cancellation — the structural own-it argument.
verdicts.stat: Whitespark listings: 'No subscriptions or contracts', ~$99-$999/location one-time; Yext cancellation case study (n=60): ~60% disappeared or went incorrect after cancel
verdicts.externalSignal: Primary cited URL (whitespark.ca/listings-service/) is live and verbatim-confirms every Whitespark-side element: "No subscriptions or contracts," "Own your listings," "Stop 'renting' them," "You'll have a username and password for each one," and "Data Aggregator Service $99 per location | one-time fee" (pricing range $99 aggregator → $399+ build → $20+ custom; top of the $99–$999 band reachable). Skeptic: the obvious vendor-spin objection (Whitespark sells the alternative) is neutralized because the structural own-vs-rent mechanism is confirmed by the criticized vendor itself (Yext) plus an independent third vendor (BrightLocal). Practitioner: the "owned one-time vs. rented-and-degrades" framing is local-SEO consensus, replicating across Yext, BrightLocal, MyAdvice, Local Marketing Institute, and Bright Oak. The claim is also honestly hedged ("disappeared OR went incorrect"), matching the data rather than overstating it. The only weakness is that the precise 60% is one vendor's single case study — but the claim leans on the structural argument (bulletproof) with the stat as illustration. No external signal supports correction or kill; the claim stands as written. measured: both the pricing and the 60% are observed/audited figures, not modeled estimates.

thesis.confidence: High — the spine ("organic is the engine, the pack is a proximity-capped byproduct") rests on multiple MEASURED, independent, primary-source-corroborated studies, not vendor opinion. The two halves both hold: (1) the pack is structurally proximity-bound — Sterling Sky's address-anchor study (8,186 businesses / 200 cities: hiding the address erases the pack), the Nov-2021 Vicinity update (confirmed Google algo change that shrank pack radius), Rankings.io geo-grid (~8 positions lost in the first mile, n≈1,100 / 50 cities), and an XGBoost study (R²≈92-93%) putting proximity at 55.2% of GBP visibility; (2) organic runs on different, site-controllable weights — Whitespark's 47-expert 2026 survey (on-page ~2x heavier organically; links 24% organic vs 8% pack) corroborated CAUSALLY by Joy Hawkins' link-isolation case studies and SearchPilot A/B splits (+5–25% organic uplift, +7% on nearby-location links across ~8,000 pages). Confidence is held at High not Higher because the channel-weight splits are MODELED (expert survey, not Google-published) and two corroborating SERP-feature datasets are UK-market (directional for US).
thesis.bottomLine: SUPPORTED — and the thesis should be the offer headline. For high-ticket roofing, organic regional dominance is the engine: it runs on levers a deep site + one-time shippable off-page directly control (on-page ~33% + links ~24% ≈ 57% of modeled organic weight vs GBP only ~7%), it is not proximity-grid-penalized (city-modified queries hold steady across test pins while the pack reshuffles block-by-block), and it owns the ~70% of searches that return NO pack at all plus the entire research/cost-guide lane a thin site can't reach. The map pack is real and worth delivering, but it is a doubly-gated (proximity + review-count) byproduct: anchored to one verified address, radius-collapsed by the Vicinity update, and capped at a ~5-7mi "Christmas tree" bubble no site edit can widen. You cannot scale to $5-10M on a 5-mile radius — only the organic surface absorbs an enterprise off-page budget and reaches regionally. Rank the prizes, sell the bigger one. Critical honesty constraint: the organic edge is NOT a higher raw conversion rate (organic 4.9% vs paid 5.4% at session level) and is CONDITIONAL on actually ranking for commercial-intent terms — which is exactly why the guarantee must be tied to a ranking outcome, never to site-build delivery.
thesis.floorCeiling: Claim the SHAPE and the ranges — NEVER a job count, and never "jobs/week" (that is snake oil). Both curves are MODELED projections, not measured guarantees. PACK curve: early on it produces only a trickle — directionally ~1-2 jobs/month — because it is review-gated (the defensible early milestone is ~10 reviews, a measured 9→10 bump that did NOT repeat, so count is a threshold not a linear lever) and proximity-fractured into a "Christmas tree" where the same business sits #1 at its office and ~#7-10 a few blocks away; the #3 slot captures near-zero (pack CTR #3 ≈ 2.3-2.9%). It only matures toward a heavier contribution (~10/mo order-of-magnitude) at roughly the ~2-year ceiling, and only if review velocity is sustained (an ~18-day collection pause produced a measured ranking cliff). ORGANIC curve carries months ~1-18: low-competition long-tail and city pages can rank in weeks-to-months (40.82% of pages that reach top-10 do so within a month) while head terms compound over ~6-18 months — the honest floor is that only 1.74% of new pages reach top-10 within a year and the average #1 page is ~5 years old, so organic is sold as compounding regional scale + owned control, NOT an instant or guaranteed click windfall. Promise the FLOOR (compounding city/long-tail organic + a maturing pack bubble), project the CEILING (regional organic dominance feeding a fuller pack by year 2).

honestyCorrections: The lead-QUALITY advantage is SCOPED to high-ticket and is a CONSEQUENCE of ranking, never automatic. At the session level organic and paid convert nearly identically (organic 4.9% vs paid 5.4%; Construction/Engineering organic 4.8% vs paid 5.1%), so the edge is intent-mix, ticket size, owned-environment de-risking, and exclusivity — NOT a higher raw conversion rate. The exclusive-vs-shared close-rate gap (roofing 23%@$8.4k, windows 31%@$22k vs shared ~6-10%) supports the GENERAL principle organic-owned leads exploit; it is NOT a direct organic-vs-pack measurement. And ~90% of pages get zero organic traffic — the quality differential only exists if you rank for commercial/buying-intent terms, which is why the offer is tied to a ranking outcome, not a site build.

The headline funnel numbers ('~70% pre-sold,' '60-70% click-skip') are MODELED / claim-library inferences, not measured causal coefficients — present them as directional. The pack/organic channel-weight splits (on-page 33% / links 24% organic vs GBP 32% / reviews 20% pack) are a Whitespark 47-expert opinion SURVEY (187 factors, Darren Shaw) — directional ranks, not Google-certified percentages; BrightLocal/AdviceLocal restate the same survey lineage rather than independently re-measuring it.

The pack actually wins the PLURALITY of local clicks where it appears (~44% pack vs ~29% organic in the aggregated 2025 stat — itself secondhand/directional, verdict 'corrected'), which appears to cut against the thesis. It does not: organic still out-clicks the pack in the controlled 5,500-tester study (~44-51% organic vs ~29-32% pack), and organic's real advantage is regional SCALE + distance-unconstrained reach + the ~70% of pack-free research queries — sell that, do NOT claim organic out-clicks the pack head-to-head in every SERP.

guardrails.ftcPosture: King Maker's organic-dominance offer is sold in RANGES, never point-promises: promise the FLOOR, project the CEILING, and label every claim measured / modeled / directional. Organic rankings COMPOUND — they are not instant or guaranteed (only ~1.74% of new pages reach the top 10 within a year, the average #1 page is ~5 years old, yet ~40.82% of pages that do reach the top 10 get there within a month; ahrefs.com/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-rank-in-google) — so low-competition city/long-tail pages can rank in weeks-to-months while head terms take ~6–18mo, and the offer is tied to a RANKING OUTCOME framed in a verifiable range, never to site-build delivery. We never promise "guaranteed rankings" or a specific jobs/week or leads/week number. We win on ORGANIC regional SCALE, control, and de-risking — not on out-clicking the pack head-to-head (the pack still takes the plurality of local clicks, ~44% vs ~29% organic; mondaydigital.com/blog/google-local-pack-traffic-statistics) and proximity still gates the pack, which we deliver as a proximity-capped byproduct (~5–7mi bubble) and never center. ABSOLUTELY NO PBNs, link schemes, paid links, excessive link exchanges, or automated link creation — Google's spam policy names these explicitly and any paid/placed link must carry rel=sponsored or rel=nofollow (developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies). The review machine is single-path and unscreened BY DESIGN: review gating, incentivizing reviews of a particular sentiment, and review suppression violate both Google's UGC policy AND the FTC Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule (effective Oct 21, 2024; civil penalties up to $51,744 per violation; ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/08). We position on verifiable ACTIONS we ship — the deep unique-content site, one-time on-site link architecture, correct GBP primary category, NAP-consistent one-time citations, credential-gated dofollow manufacturer links (GAF/Owens Corning, measured-dofollow), entity/schema layer, and an unscreened review funnel — never on attestations we cannot back (never "SOC 2 / bank-level / certified / 40%-more-likely"). Ongoing client-managed off-page is out of scope; only one-time shippable off-page is in scope. Polished false confidence is the cardinal sin.

Pages drive ORGANIC, not the pack. The site only tiebreaks the pack when GBP + review velocity are already equal.
